claim: "We have an 80 percent graduation rate in high school after spending more per student than any country in the world other than Liechtenstein, I think, or Luxembourg and a couple other small countries."
rationale: The U.S. four‑year public high school graduation rate in recent years has been around the mid-80s percent (higher than the 80% claimed). It is true the U.S. is among the higher spenders per student internationally, but it is not uniquely behind only Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and a couple small countries — several other countries (and variations by education level and year) rank at or above the U.S. on per‑student spending. Because both the graduation percentage and the absolute ranking phrasing are inaccurate or misleading, the claim is false.

claim: "More black babies are aborted in NYC than born."
rationale: This claim is false. New York City vital statistics and independent fact-checks show that annual live births to Black mothers in NYC exceed the number of abortions among Black women; public-health data do not support the claim that more Black babies are aborted than born. The claim has been circulated by advocacy groups but is inconsistent with official counts when using standard definitions and time frames.

claim: Says the Dickey Amendment "prevents the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from even researching the relationship between gun violence and public health. ... The government can’t study gun violence but is spending $400,000 analyzing the effects of Swedish massages on rabbits."
rationale: The claim misstates the Dickey Amendment and misrepresents a purported $400,000 study. The Dickey language barred use of CDC funds for advocacy and was widely interpreted to chill federal firearm research, but it did not legally ban CDC from studying gun violence and Congress clarified in 2018 that the CDC may conduct such research; federal agencies have funded some gun-violence studies since. The alleged $400,000 “Swedish massage on rabbits” item is a viral, unverified characterization that likely misstates the purpose or context of the grant, so the blanket assertion is false.

claim: "If the Republicans were the majority, (Rep. Barton) would have actually the gavel and the chairmanship."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and cannot be confirmed as a general fact. While committee chairs in the U.S. House are held by the majority party and senior ranking minority members often become chair if their party gains the majority, chair assignments are decided by the majority party caucus and leadership and not automatically given to a particular member. Without specifying which Rep. Barton, which committee, and which Congress, the claim that “he would have the gavel and the chairmanship” is unproven.

claim: Says unlike Tim Kaine, who "invested" in education, Indiana Gov. Mike Pence "slashed education funding."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification. Tim Kaine as Virginia governor did increase state support for education and advanced some education initiatives, but describing Pence as having “slashed” education funding is misleading: while Mike Pence supported some cuts and policy changes (including expanding vouchers) and at times proposed reductions, Indiana’s overall K–12 funding outcomes during his term were mixed and not a straightforward statewide “slashing” of education spending. Thus the comparative binary presented is false.

claim: "There comes a point in the last year of the president, especially in their second term, where you stop nominating" both Supreme Court justices and Court of Appeals judges.
rationale: There is no automatic rule that nominations stop in a president’s final year; practice varies by cycle and is driven by politics and Senate control. Historically the Senate has sometimes refused to consider late-term Supreme Court nominees (e.g., 2016 Garland) while at other times confirming late nominees (e.g., 2020 confirmation of a Supreme Court justice) and presidents routinely continue to nominate Court of Appeals judges. Thus the claim as a blanket statement is incorrect.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said, "When gays stayed hidden we had no mass shootings; we had no public nudity. Society was polite. Now anything and everything goes and I blame them."
rationale: There is no record in credible news reports, transcripts, or major fact‑checking outlets of Ted Cruz making this exact statement; the quote appears to be a fabricated or misattributed line circulated online. Such a provocative remark by a high‑profile senator would have been widely reported and sourced if genuine.

claim: "Lindsey Graham threatens to convert to Democrat if Republicans don’t Dump Trump."
rationale: There is no credible record that Sen. Lindsey Graham has publicly threatened to switch parties to become a Democrat if Republicans do not abandon Donald Trump. Graham has criticized Trump at times but has largely remained a Republican and has not issued such a party-switch threat in major reporting or his public statements through mid‑2024. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or fabrication.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable news report attributing this specific quote to Ted Cruz. Public transcripts and press coverage of Cruz’s remarks around the Josh Duggar controversy do not contain this language; the phrasing appears to be a fabricated or misattributed statement. Given Cruz’s public record on family and sexual morality, he has made conservative comments but not this exact claim as quoted.

claim: Says U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "will be at every polling station" on Nov. 3, 2020.
rationale: This claim is false. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) did not announce and had no plan to be stationed at every polling place on Nov 3, 2020; agency statements and multiple fact-checks debunked viral posts asserting this. Such a widespread deployment would also exceed ICE's legal role and logistical capacity and would have required coordination with states and local election officials that never occurred.

claim: Says Mitt Romney was clear that he "would not provide government assistance to the U.S. auto companies, even if they went through bankruptcy."
rationale: Mitt Romney consistently opposed federal bailouts of the U.S. auto industry during the 2008–2012 period and publicly said he would not provide government assistance to automakers, arguing they should be allowed to restructure through bankruptcy rather than receive taxpayer-funded aid. His campaign statements and debate remarks repeatedly made that position clear, even though precise wording and context varied over time.

claim: "Obama secretly gave citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of nuke deal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama "secretly gave" U.S. citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of the Iran nuclear deal. U.S. citizenship is granted through individual legal processes administered by USCIS and courts, not by executive fiat or international agreements, and fact‑checking organizations investigated and found the claim baseless.

claim: "Actually, on some procedures, you're more likely to die if you're on Medicaid than if you're uninsured."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed observational studies have reported that for certain surgical procedures and emergency care categories, adjusted mortality is higher for patients insured by Medicaid than for uninsured patients. This is not universal across all procedures and likely reflects differences in case mix, delayed presentation, hospital quality, and residual confounding rather than a simple causal effect of insurance status.

claim: Says he didn't cancel a political rally because after Sept. 11, "the New York Stock Exchange was open the following day."
rationale: The New York Stock Exchange did not reopen the day after September 11, 2001; it remained closed and trading resumed on September 17, 2001. Therefore citing the NYSE being open the following day as a reason for not canceling a rally is factually incorrect.

claim: A video shows "the COVID-19 vaccine when it hits your blood."
rationale: There is no credible video that can show a COVID-19 vaccine "hitting your blood" because vaccines are injected into muscle and disperse at the cellular/molecular level, not as a visible bolus entering the bloodstream. Viral clips making this claim have been debunked as showing unrelated microscopy artifacts, chemical reactions, or misinterpreted footage rather than an actual vaccine entering blood.

claim: Wisconsin’s middle class is the "most diminished" in the United States.
rationale: The claim asserts Wisconsin has the single most diminished middle class in the U.S., a superlative that requires a specific metric and timeframe. National data sources (e.g., U.S. Census/ACS and Pew-style analyses of middle‑income share and income change) do not consistently identify Wisconsin as having the largest decline; other states show comparable or larger drops depending on the measure. Without a clear definition and timeframe the assertion is unsupported.

claim: "Maxine Waters Is Getting Criminally Charged!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public court record showing that Congresswoman Maxine Waters has been criminally charged. Major news organizations and court dockets had not reported any indictment or criminal filing against her as of mid-2024. The claim appears to be a rumor or clickbait rather than a factual report of legal action.

claim: "(Pete) Sessions has held at least two fundraisers at adult-themed clubs and made no apologies."
rationale: Contemporary news reporting documented at least one Pete Sessions fundraiser held at an adult-entertainment venue, but I could not verify that he held two or more separate fundraisers at such clubs. Likewise, available reporting does not clearly establish that he categorically “made no apologies” — statements and responses from his office leave room for nuance. Because the claim asserts a specific count and an unequivocal refusal to apologize, it overstates what can be reliably demonstrated.

claim: Says the Security Against Foreign Enemies Act of 2015 would not "pause" the resettlement of Syrian refugees in the United States.
rationale: The Security Against Foreign Enemies (SAFE) Act of 2015 would have required a suspension of Syrian refugee admissions until the president certified that enhanced vetting and identity verification procedures were in place; in other words it would have effectively paused resettlement pending those certifications. Contemporary summaries and the bill’s requirements describe a moratorium/conditional halt rather than allowing continuous resettlement without restriction.

claim: Says Marco Rubio tweeted a verse from the New Testament to shame "his own constituents for flocking to Trump rally."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous news reporting that Marco Rubio posted a New Testament verse specifically to shame his own constituents for attending a Trump rally. While Rubio has at times tweeted Biblical passages, available tweet archives and reporting through mid-2024 do not substantiate this precise claim and it appears to be a misattribution or missing-context claim.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it couldn’t build a factory in South Carolina because South Carolina is a right-to-work state.
rationale: This is false. The NLRB never told Boeing it could not build a factory in South Carolina because the state is right-to-work; right-to-work laws do not prohibit companies from opening plants. The NLRB filed a complaint alleging Boeing unlawfully shifted work from a unionized Washington plant to South Carolina in retaliation (an unfair labor practice) and sought remedies, but that is not the same as a blanket prohibition based on South Carolina’s right-to-work status.

claim: Trump supporters are heading to the border as the migrant caravan approaches.
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks a time, place, or source, so it cannot be verified as a general fact. While news reports from past migrant caravans showed that some pro-Trump activists and groups traveled to the U.S.–Mexico border, that does not support the blanket present-tense statement that "Trump supporters are heading to the border" in all cases or at this moment. Without a specific caravan, date, or corroborating reporting, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "We're the only system of federalism in the world."
rationale: The claim is false. Many countries besides the United States have federal systems — for example Germany, Canada, Australia, India, Brazil, Switzerland, Mexico and others — so the U.S. is one of multiple federal systems, not the only one.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: I judge the claim false because there is no clear, corroborated record (through June 2024) of a Banking Committee formally reporting a 1,336‑page bill in a 21‑minute session with no amendments; such an extremely rapid, amendment‑free handling of a very large bill is inconsistent with typical committee practice and would likely have been widely reported. The quoted wording appears to be a selective or out‑of‑context description rather than a verified factual account of a specific committee action.

claim: "Our economy created over 6.5 million new jobs just last year, more jobs in one year than ever before in the history of the United States of America."
rationale: This statement mixes a largely accurate statistic with an overbroad historical claim. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported roughly 6.6 million net nonfarm payroll jobs were added in 2021 — the largest annual gain in the BLS payroll series — but that series begins in the 1930s/1939 and does not cover the entire history of the United States, so saying "more jobs in one year than ever before in the history of the United States" is imprecise and misleading.

claim: Under his leadership, more people in Wisconsin "have access to health care."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as given because it fails to identify who 'his' refers to, the timeframe, or the metric used for 'access to health care.' Whether more people gained access depends on specific policies (e.g., Medicaid expansion, enrollment changes, provider availability) and measurable data; without that context the claim cannot be verified. Therefore it is treated as false/unsupported in this form.

claim: "Gina Haspel, CIA head is dead!"
rationale: There were no credible reports or official announcements of Gina Haspel’s death through mid‑2024, and she is widely known as the former CIA director (2018–2021). Because major public figures’ deaths are reported by multiple reliable outlets and no such coverage was present in available records, the claim is very likely false.

claim: "I never was in favor of shutting down the government. … (I) voted to fund the government fully."
rationale: The claim gives no speaker or time period, so it cannot be verified as an absolute statement that someone "never" favored a shutdown and also "voted to fund the government fully." Confirming this requires checking specific roll-call votes and public statements; many politicians have mixed records (supporting some funding measures while backing others that risk a shutdown). Given the missing context and the common occurrence of mixed behavior, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "This kind of snowstorm happens every 10 or 15 years."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be supported: it does not define what "this kind" of snowstorm means, nor the location or time period. Storm recurrence intervals vary widely by region, storm type, and multi-decadal climate variability, so a blanket "every 10 or 15 years" statement is unsupported without specific historical or climatological evidence.

claim: "Here's a man who brags about how he made the city safe. It was the Biden crime bill that became the Clinton crime bill that allowed him to do that."
rationale: The statement mixes accurate and misleading points. It is true Joe Biden was a principal author of the 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act and President Bill Clinton signed and promoted that law, but saying it "became the Clinton crime bill that allowed him to make the city safe" implies a direct, singular causal link to a specific official’s ability to make a city safe, which is unproven and oversimplifies historical causation. Crime declines in the 1990s resulted from many factors and attributing a particular city’s policing success solely to that bill is unsupported.

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: This is false. Federal administrations long before Obama authorized the Justice Department to sue states — notably during Reconstruction and repeatedly in the 20th century (for example, numerous civil‑rights enforcement suits in the 1950s–1960s and other federal actions during the New Deal era). Presidents do not personally file suits but act through the executive branch, and historical practice includes many instances of the federal government suing states prior to Obama.

claim: "We’ve got 600-plus police and fire pensions Downstate that are on the cusp of insolvency because they don’t have the revenues that they need to be able to keep those pensions going."
rationale: The claim that there are 600+ Downstate police and fire pensions “on the cusp of insolvency” is not supported by available statewide pension reports or actuarial summaries. While Illinois (and other states) have many local police and fire pension funds and some are severely underfunded, independent and state reports do not document that hundreds of distinct Downstate police/fire pension plans are immediately insolvent; the statement appears to conflate numbers and lacks a clear definition of “on the cusp.”

claim: "More suicide deaths than coronavirus death past two months."
rationale: The claim is too vague and therefore misleading: it gives no location or exact two-month period. Based on available global and national data across the pandemic, COVID-19 deaths over two-month spans have often exceeded typical suicide totals (global suicides ≈700,000/year, and COVID deaths have been in the thousands per day during waves). Without a specified place and time the claim cannot be supported and is likely false in most contexts.

claim: Gas prices during the Obama-Biden administration were $5.49 a gallon.
rationale: The U.S. national average retail gasoline price did not reach $5.49 per gallon during the Obama-Biden presidency (2009–2017). National average data from agencies that track fuel prices show peaks around the high $3s to low $4s (roughly $3.90–$3.95) in that period; isolated stations or premium/diesel prices in specific locations may have been higher but the claim as stated is inaccurate for general gas prices under that administration.

claim: Says President Obama has "doubled" the deficit.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Annual federal deficits rose sharply in 2009 (to about $1.4 trillion) from roughly $0.45 trillion in FY2008, but that spike was driven by the financial crisis, falling revenues and emergency measures, and deficits declined in later years (e.g., around $0.6 trillion by FY2016). Saying Obama “doubled the deficit” without specifying year or whether one means annual deficit versus total national debt is inaccurate.

claim: Says Scott Walker "said that forcing women facing abortion to get invasive ultrasounds was 'just a cool thing.'"
rationale: There is no reliable record or contemporaneous transcript showing Scott Walker explicitly said forcing women to get invasive ultrasounds was "just a cool thing." While Walker publicly supported laws requiring ultrasounds before abortions and used positive adjectives about ultrasound technology, reputable reports attribute no verbatim quote matching that phrasing to him.

claim: "We now consume at the federal level 25 percent of the gross domestic product. Historically we were at 20 percent. So we've taken 5 percent away from the private sector."
rationale: The claim is misleading: a rise in the federal share of GDP from 20% to 25% does not necessarily mean a one-to-one 5% subtraction from the private sector. GDP composition can change (government spending can be deficit-financed, raise total GDP, or complement private activity), and a higher government share can reflect many factors rather than a simple transfer of output away from private firms or households. The statement also omits a clear historical baseline and precise definitions of the percentages.

claim: "A year ago we had the lowest unemployment in history without using taxpayers money."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and misleading. Saying “lowest unemployment in history” depends on the jurisdiction and period — for example, U.S. unemployment hit about 3.4% in 2019 and similar lows in subsequent years, so it is not clearly a unique historical low; and the phrase “without using taxpayers money” is implausible because government fiscal policies, public programs, and services (funded by taxpayers) routinely affect labor markets. Without precise definition of “we,” the time frame, and evidence that no public funds played a role, the assertion cannot be verified and is likely false.

claim: "Across the country, more than half of the U.S. attorney seats remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute without a date; whether a majority of U.S. Attorney seats lacked an Obama-chosen prosecutor depended on timing. There are 93 U.S. Attorney offices and while many were temporarily filled by holdovers immediately after the 2009 transition, the Obama administration nominated and obtained confirmations for a substantial number over the following months, so the blanket claim that “across the country, more than half” remained without an Obama choice is misleading without a specific timeframe. Absent a date, the claim is not reliably true.

claim: "We have completely turned our economy around."
rationale: The statement is an absolute, vague claim without a defined timeframe or metrics; it cannot be verified as true. General economic indicators (GDP growth, unemployment, inflation, wages, and fiscal balance) have shown mixed results in recent years with improvements in some areas and persistent problems in others, so the claim that the economy has been 'completely turned around' is unsupported.

claim: The federal government "now tells us which light bulbs to buy."
rationale: This claim is essentially correct in effect: federal law and Department of Energy rules (notably the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 and subsequent DOE efficiency standards) set minimum efficiency requirements that phased out many traditional incandescent bulbs and limited the types of bulbs that can be sold. The government does not typically direct an individual to a specific brand or model, but its regulations determine which bulb technologies and models are commercially available.

claim: "Historically," Senate ratification of arms control treaties "has been bipartisan."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While several major arms-control agreements (for example the INF Treaty and START I) were approved by wide bipartisan margins, other prominent cases were partisan or failed to be ratified — most notably the Senate's 1999 rejection of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty and the non‑ratification of SALT II. Thus it is not accurate to say Senate ratification of arms control treaties has been uniformly bipartisan historically.

claim: "Look at what’s happening last night in Sweden. Sweden, who would believe this? Sweden. They took in large numbers. They’re having problems like they never thought possible."
rationale: The referenced statement implies a specific major incident “last night in Sweden” and claims Sweden is having unprecedented problems from taking in large numbers of migrants; contemporaneous reporting and Swedish authorities did not corroborate any such major event on that night, and the broad claim is an exaggeration not supported by crime and migration data. While Sweden faces integration challenges like many countries, the tweet’s implication of a recent catastrophic event and dramatic national collapse is false and misleading.

claim: A "majority in every state favors path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants."
rationale: The claim is false. While national polls routinely show a majority of Americans favoring a pathway to citizenship, state-level polling is mixed and there is no evidence that every single state reaches majority support; some conservative states in various polls have shown under-50% support depending on question wording and timing. Therefore the universal "every state" formulation is not supported.

claim: Veterans should vote Republican "because the damn Democrats blocked the VA Healthcare bill again."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific factual event — that Democrats 'blocked the VA Healthcare bill again' — but gives no bill, date, or vote to verify and presents a broad partisan prescription. Congressional action on veterans' legislation varies by bill and session; many VA initiatives have received bipartisan support and procedural blocks can be attributable to specific votes, amendments, or filibuster rules rather than one party uniformly. Because the claim is vague and unsubstantiated as written, it is not supported.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it gives no jurisdiction or baseline date for “when Mark Sharpe first took office,” and no supporting data are provided. Property-tax changes depend on assessed values, millage rates, and budget votes by multiple authorities, so attributing a precise 18% increase to a single official without localized time-series data is unsupported. Without specific local data the claim is therefore treated as false/unverified.

claim: "Three of five detainees swapped (for Bowe Bergdahl) are now ISIS leaders."
rationale: The five detainees exchanged for Bowe Bergdahl in 2014 were senior Taliban figures who, according to US and international reporting, either remained in Qatar under a monitoring agreement or later rejoined the Taliban leadership — they were not documented as becoming leaders of ISIS. While some former Taliban members have later joined ISIS-K (the Afghanistan/Pakistan ISIS affiliate), credible reporting does not support the claim that three of these specific five became ISIS leaders. The statement mischaracterizes widely reported post-release trajectories of those individuals.

claim: After laying off 30,000 people, Carly Fiorina said that in retrospect, "I would have done them all faster."
rationale: Carly Fiorina did oversee roughly 30,000 job cuts at HP, but the specific quote 'I would have done them all faster' cannot be reliably attributed to her from contemporaneous primary sources. Fact-checkers and reporting indicate the line is a misquotation or taken out of context and Fiorina disputed that phrasing. The claim as stated is therefore false.

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: This claim is false. Stephen Curry’s well‑known signature shoe partnership began with Under Armour (he signed with them in 2013) and there is no credible reporting that he ‘split with Nike’ over a Nike ban on Bible inscriptions. Public accounts of Curry’s endorsement history and coverage of his expressions of faith do not support the alleged dispute with Nike about writing scripture on shoes.

claim: "I was speaking out on pension reform almost 17 years ago."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no date or speaker to anchor the phrase “almost 17 years ago.” Without knowing who made the claim and when it was uttered, I cannot confirm whether that person was speaking out on pension reform at the referenced time. Given the missing context, I treat the claim as not proven and therefore mark it false under uncertainty.

claim: The Baucus health care bill would require taxes on medical devices such as X-ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests and surgical needles.
rationale: The Baucus Senate Finance proposals did not impose a direct sales tax on consumer items like X-ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests, or surgical needles. The discussion focused on revenue measures such as an excise on medical device manufacturers (an industry-level tax considered later in the ACA), not a retail tax specifically targeting those listed products; fact-checkers at the time debunked claims that those consumer medical supplies would be directly taxed. The claim conflates manufacturer excise proposals with a new consumer tax on the items named.

claim: "Obamacare isn't helping anyone."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no one has benefited from the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare), which is incorrect. The ACA led to large reductions in the uninsured rate, millions of people gaining marketplace or Medicaid coverage, protections for people with preexisting conditions, and allowing young adults to stay on parents' plans, though some individuals have experienced higher costs or narrower choices in certain markets.

claim: The Biden administration "gifted the Taliban with $80 billion-plus" in military-grade weapons but now "wants your 9mm pistols."
rationale: The claim mixes two misleading assertions. The often-cited '$80–85 billion' figure refers to the cumulative value of U.S. equipment provided to Afghan security forces over many years, not the value of weapons 'gifted' to the Taliban; DoD reporting indicated a much smaller portion of equipment was left behind or could be used by the Taliban. There is also no evidence the Biden administration is pursuing a program to seize private '9mm pistols' nationwide — it has proposed gun-safety measures and supported laws like red-flag orders, but not a mass federal confiscation of common pistols.

claim: Rob Cornilles is a Tea Party candidate.
rationale: There is no clear, documented evidence that Rob Cornilles ran or was publicly identified as a Tea Party candidate. Public references to Cornilles describe him as a Republican candidate/actor in local politics, but do not show explicit Tea Party endorsements or branding that would justify calling him a Tea Party candidate.

claim: Obama said he would "stand with the Muslims should the political winds shift in an ugly direction."
rationale: The quoted line is an accurate statement Barack Obama made; fact-checkers and transcripts show he said he would “stand with the Muslims should the political winds shift in an ugly direction.” The remark was made in the context of defending civil liberties and opposing discrimination, not an unconditional political endorsement of any group.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: The claim broadly asserts that Democrats openly supported riots and that "BLM was burning down cities and killing people in the streets," which is misleading. Public statements from major Democratic leaders during 2020 generally condemned violence while supporting peaceful protest and police reform; while some protests included riots and isolated killings, there is no widespread evidence that Democratic leaders endorsed or celebrated organized mass arson or killings. The statement conflates isolated criminal acts and rhetoric from a few individuals with blanket support from the Democratic Party.

claim: Says a mall Santa beat up a child molester.
rationale: The claim is vague and uncorroborated; no specific incident, location, date, or credible news reports are provided. Without verifiable details or reliable sources, this reads like an unverified viral anecdote rather than a confirmed fact.

claim: The Affordable Care Act alters the "sensible doctor-patient-relationship-centered health care program ... we see today."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act enacted broad changes to insurance coverage, federal regulation of insurers, and payment/delivery models (for example Medicaid expansion, insurance exchanges, essential health benefits, and incentivizing alternative payment models). Those changes did not abolish the doctor–patient relationship but materially altered incentives, access, and administrative rules that shape how care is delivered and experienced, so it is correct to say the ACA altered the existing doctor‑patient‑centered system.

claim: In Virginia, "people are going and getting marriage licenses who are 12 and 13, and 14 and 15 years old."
rationale: This claim is false. Virginia law and policy do not allow 12–15 year-olds to obtain state marriage licenses today; the state has reformed its statutes to set the legal minimum at 18 (eliminating routine issuance of licenses to pre-teens). While historical or extremely rare pre-reform cases existed, current legal practice does not match the claim.

claim: When Terry McAuliffe was governor, "Unemployment went down in every single county, including rural Virginia by nearly 50%.
rationale: Statewide unemployment in Virginia fell during Terry McAuliffe's 2014–2018 term, but county-level BLS/Virginia Employment Commission data show variation and not every single county saw a decline. The claimed "nearly 50%" reduction in rural Virginia is exaggerated: the statewide unemployment rate fell by roughly a quarter to a third, and typical county declines were much smaller and not universal.

claim: Says Joe Biden called ANTIFA "courageous Americans."
rationale: There is no reliable record of President Joe Biden saying the extremist label "ANTIFA" are "courageous Americans." During 2020 protests and afterwards Biden repeatedly distinguished peaceful protesters from violent actors and condemned extremist violence, but he did not praise Antifa by that phrase. Viral posts misattribute praise of peaceful demonstrators or use edited clips to create this false claim.

claim: Says Paul Manafort "played a very limited role" in the Trump presidential campaign.
rationale: Describing Paul Manafort as having "played a very limited role" is misleading. Manafort served as Donald Trump’s campaign chairman from May to August/September 2016, ran strategy, helped with delegate and communications planning, and remained an adviser afterward, so his early and mid-2016 role was substantial even if his involvement declined later.

claim: "Paul Broun Jr. sides with sexual deviants to support sale of 'crush videos.' "
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Representative Paul Broun advocated for or 'sided with' people to legalize or support the sale of so-called 'crush videos.' Federal law and Congressional action have targeted crush videos (which depict animal cruelty) and there is no public record of Broun sponsoring or voting to permit their sale; the claim appears to be inflammatory and unsupported by documented votes or statements.

claim: No one showed up for this Joe Biden and Kamala Harris joint campaign event in Arizona.
rationale: The claim is implausible as stated and lacks a specific date or location; presidential campaign events routinely include staff, security, press, and at least some supporters, so it is highly unlikely that literally no one attended. Without a precise reference to a documented event showing zero attendees, the assertion cannot be substantiated. Images and coverage from Biden-Harris events generally show attendees present rather than an empty turnout.

claim: Rhode Island "charter schools are nationally recognized as outperforming their counterparts across the country."
rationale: This claim is false because there is no national consensus that Rhode Island charter schools (or charter schools generally) uniformly outperform traditional public schools across the country. National studies find large variation: some charter networks and states show positive effects while others show no advantage or worse outcomes, and Rhode Island's small charter sector is not universally documented as outperforming peers. The statement overstates and generalizes inconsistent evidence.

claim: Says television host Steve Harvey authored a pro-Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Steve Harvey authored a pro‑Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators; major news outlets and Harvey's verified social accounts do not contain such a piece and the claim appears to be a fabricated or misattributed viral item. Steve Harvey is a high‑profile figure whose public political statements have been widely covered, and this specific story has not been corroborated by reliable sources. Therefore the claim is not supported.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The claim gives a precise count but provides no timeframe or geographic scope; I cannot confirm a specific figure of 324,000 pregnant people experiencing domestic violence without a cited source. While intimate partner violence during pregnancy is a known problem and various U.S. estimates and surveys produce different annual or lifetime counts, the exact number stated here is not verifiable from my available knowledge. Because prevalence estimates depend on measurement method, population and period, presenting 324,000 as a standalone fact is misleading.

claim: "Babysitter on crystal meth eats 3-month-old baby."
rationale: This dramatic claim (a babysitter on meth eating a 3‑month‑old) would have produced extensive, verifiable national or local criminal reporting and court records; no credible news outlets or official records substantiate it. It matches patterns of sensational rumors or misreported incidents rather than a confirmed factual event.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The claim overstates causation. The Affordable Care Act created coverage standards and employer rules, but it did not directly force universities to dismantle graduate student insurance or compel illegal actions; problems labeled a “#GradInsurance debacle” are normally the result of institutional decisions about benefits, budgets, and plan design or interpretations of compliance, not a direct unilateral mandate from Obamacare. Saying Mizzou “has to break the law to do the right thing” is an unfounded normative assertion without evidence that legal compliance precludes available lawful remedies.

claim: Says "there have been some job gains in the McMansion State since Mr. Christie took office, but they have lagged gains both in the nation as a whole and in New York and Connecticut, the obvious points of comparison."
rationale: Chris Christie took office in January 2010 and New Jersey did add jobs during his tenure, but broad labor‑market data from the post‑2009 recovery show New Jersey’s job growth rates were generally below the U.S. average and trailed neighboring New York (driven largely by NYC) and, in many comparisons, Connecticut. Thus the statement that there were some job gains but they lagged the nation and those neighboring states is accurate in general terms.

claim: Under my platform, "I will make no changes to the current (Medicare) system for current retirees and anyone approaching retirement."
rationale: This statement is a future-looking policy promise that cannot be verified as guaranteed: elected officials cannot unilaterally prevent future legislative or administrative changes to Medicare, and the phrase “anyone approaching retirement” is ambiguous. Without specifying who made the promise, when, or the legal mechanisms, the claim that no changes will ever be made is not supportable. Historically, similar promises have been altered by subsequent policy decisions or legislation.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to keep "an extreme, job-killing Internal Revenue Service paperwork mandate."
rationale: The claim exaggerates and misstates the record. While Sen. Sherrod Brown voted for a 2022 budget/reconciliation package that included IRS funding, the widely-cited ‘‘$600 1099-K’’ reporting rule was changed during negotiation and was not left as an ‘‘extreme paperwork mandate’’ in the final enacted law; labeling Brown as having voted to ‘‘keep’’ such a mandate is misleading. The statement mixes partisan rhetoric with incomplete context about which specific provision and which vote are meant.

claim: "More people, almost twice as many, pay the penalty or take the waiver than signed up for (Obamacare)."
rationale: Available enrollment and tax/IRS data from the Affordable Care Act era show marketplace sign‑ups numbered in the millions (single‑digit to low‑double‑digit millions annually), while the number of people who paid the individual mandate penalty or claimed exemptions was not almost double those enrollment totals. In short, far more people enrolled in ACA coverage in most years than paid penalties or simply took exemptions/waivers. The claim overstates and reverses the relative magnitudes.

claim: "$21T in Pentagon accounting errors. Medicare for All costs ~$32T. That means 66% of Medicare for All could have been funded already by the Pentagon."
rationale: The claim misinterprets the $21 trillion figure: it refers to cumulative accounting adjustments/unsupported entries in DoD books over many years, not missing or seizable cash that could be reallocated. The ~$32 trillion Medicare-for-All number is an aggregate cost estimate that varies by proposal and timeframe, and even if both headline numbers were accepted, accounting adjustments are not equivalent to available funding. Therefore the arithmetic comparison and conclusion are misleading.

claim: A mansion in photo is Joe Biden’s house.
rationale: I cannot verify that an unspecified mansion photo is Joe Biden’s house without the image or provenance; Biden’s publicly known private residence is a modest home in Wilmington, Delaware and as President he primarily resides in the White House. Many large-home photos circulated online are miscaptioned or misattributed, so the claim is unsupported given missing evidence.

claim: Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint against him alleging he used county workers for campaign work, which is an indictable offense.
rationale: I cannot verify that a specific person named Jeff Mann currently has an ethics complaint alleging he used county workers for campaign work; I have no confirmed report or charging document in my training data tying that exact allegation to a named individual. Additionally, whether such conduct is an "indictable offense" depends on the jurisdiction and whether prosecutors have brought criminal charges, not merely an ethics complaint. Because the claim mixes an unverified allegation and a legal characterization that varies by place, I judge it false as presented.

claim: Says as Assembly Speaker he is a "constitutional officer" of Wisconsin.
rationale: While the Wisconsin Constitution establishes the legislature and authorizes each house to choose its officers, the term “constitutional officer” in Wisconsin ordinarily denotes statewide elected executive officers (e.g., governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state, treasurer). The Assembly Speaker is an internal legislative officer chosen by members of the Assembly, not a statewide constitutional officer, so the claim is incorrect in normal legal and political usage.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution "doesn’t say anything about (redistricting) being fair. … it’s set up to be partisan."
rationale: The Constitution does not contain a generic requirement that redistricting be 'fair' or nonpartisan. It apportions representation and leaves drawing district lines largely to the states, subject to constraints like equal-population principles and the Equal Protection Clause; the Supreme Court has also held that federal courts lack a manageable standard to police partisan gerrymandering. Thus the constitutional text and structure do not mandate partisan fairness and allow partisan control.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan’s budget proposal "eliminates Medicare" in 10 years.
rationale: Paul Ryan's budget proposals did not immediately eliminate Medicare for current beneficiaries. They proposed converting Medicare for future enrollees into a premium-support/voucher-style system (phasing in for younger cohorts years later), which critics called an effective end to traditional Medicare but is not a literal immediate elimination within 10 years for existing beneficiaries. Thus the claim as stated is inaccurate.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We need to repeal Daylight Savings Time as a primary measure to decrease the rate of climate change. Less hours of sun shine equal less heat hitting Earth’s surface."
rationale: There is no credible record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez making this statement, and the content reflects a misunderstanding of daylight saving time. Shifting clocks does not change the total hours of sunlight or reduce the amount of solar energy the Earth receives, so the quoted causal claim is incorrect. Given lack of sourcing and the physical inaccuracy, the attribution is false.

claim: Gina Raimondo "paid 70 million in taxpayer dollars to millionaire hedge fund managers."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Rhode Island’s pension system paid tens of millions in fees to outside investment managers over multiple years (part of decisions made while Raimondo was governor), it was not a single $70 million payment directly from Raimondo to “millionaire hedge fund managers.” The amount, timing, and characterization omit key context about pension investment fees versus direct taxpayer giveaways.

claim: "Just on Jan. 1 of this year, there were 40,000 new laws put on the books in one day."
rationale: There is no evidence that 40,000 new laws were enacted or put into effect on a single day. At the federal level only dozens of laws are passed in a year, and while states and localities enact many measures annually, independent fact-checking and legislative data do not support a figure of 40,000 new laws taking effect on one specific day. The number appears to conflate different categories (rules, pages of regulations, or cumulative provisions across many jurisdictions) rather than newly enacted laws.

claim: A video shows Kim Jong Un calling Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable" in a speech.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un delivered a speech calling U.S. President Joe Biden a 'thug,' a 'coward,' and 'mentally unstable.' Videos making that claim have circulated but appear to be edited, mistranslated, or misattributed; North Korean rhetoric is often hostile but major news organizations and primary North Korean releases do not substantiate that specific quote sequence. Absent an original, verifiable transcript or reliable source, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says Tom Barrett "has directed that tens of millions of City of Milwaukee tax dollars be used for the construction of a downtown trolley at the expense of: health and public safety; repair and replacement of public infrastructure; public education; and, job creation and economic development."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes city budgeting. While Milwaukee’s downtown streetcar (The Hop) cost over $100 million and some local financing (TIF/bonds) was used, the project was funded by a mix of federal grants, state/local contributions and dedicated tax-increment financing rather than a unilateral diversion of general-tax “tens of millions” by Mayor Barrett away from health, public safety, education and jobs. There is no clear evidence Barrett personally directed the wholesale reallocation of those service budgets to pay for the trolley, and budgetary decisions involve the Common Council and multiple funding sources.

claim: Ron Klein "sponsored an amendment that specifically allows price gouging."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that former Representative Ron Klein authored or sponsored an amendment that explicitly authorized or "specifically allows" price gouging. Claims like this are typically mischaracterizations of other legislative language (for example liability shields or regulatory preemption) rather than a direct authorization to raise emergency prices. Without a specific bill, text, or date the assertion appears to be a distortion rather than a documented legislative action.

claim: Insulin prices have "gone THRU THE ROOF for patients/taxpayers bc of manufacturer, health plan & PBM biz practices."
rationale: Insulin list prices have risen substantially over the past two decades and many analyses attribute that increase to manufacturer pricing decisions, the rebate/incentive structures used by pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and health-plan designs that shift costs to patients. Those business practices (list-price increases, rebate-driven formularies, high deductibles and coinsurance) have raised out-of-pocket costs for patients and increased public spending through Medicare and Medicaid.

claim: Says the percentage of officers the Chicago Police Board fired after hearing their cases or who chose to resign prior to a board hearing roughly doubled during her tenure.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because it omits who “her” refers to and provides no timeframe or baseline percentages. Without a named official and specific data from Chicago Police Board disciplinary reports or annual summaries, the assertion that the percentage ‘roughly doubled’ cannot be confirmed. Given the missing context and lack of cited figures, the claim should be treated as false until substantiated.

claim: Says Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T-shirt with progressive slogans on it.
rationale: There is no widely reported, verifiable photographic evidence that Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T‑shirt emblazoned with explicit progressive slogans; similar social media claims about celebrities' political attire often lack sourcing. Without a specific image, date, or slogan to check, the assertion is unsubstantiated and cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says the Steele dossier "was—according to (James Comey's) June 2017 testimony—'salacious and unverified.' "
rationale: This is accurate. In his June 2017 testimony before the Senate Intelligence Committee, James Comey described the Steele dossier as "salacious and unverified" when discussing the raw intelligence and memos. He also acknowledged that some elements were subjects of subsequent investigation and partial corroboration.

claim: Says an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying "60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no verifiable audio, video, or reputable news reporting showing an NBC producer saying that line on a hot mic at any Olympics; similar viral “hot mic” quotes have repeatedly been debunked as misattributions or fabrications. The allegation appears to be a social-media rumor rather than a documented incident.

claim: "Many people every year, sometimes over 100,000, and despite the vaccine, die from the flu … we are learning to live with Covid, in most populations far less lethal."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate facts with an incorrect broad generalization. Globally, seasonal influenza does cause many deaths each year (WHO estimates roughly 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths annually, so ‘over 100,000’ can be true on a global scale), and deaths occur despite vaccination. However, the statement that COVID is now “in most populations far less lethal” is misleading: while vaccination, prior infection, and treatments have lowered severe outcomes in many places, SARS‑CoV‑2 has generally caused higher mortality and higher infection‑fatality rates than seasonal flu, especially in older or vulnerable groups, so it is not uniformly “far less lethal.”

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: Authority over whether schools open is not uniformly only a local decision. In the U.S. states set education law and public-health policy and governors or state education/health agencies can and have mandated closures or reopenings; local districts implement operations but are bound by state law and emergency orders. While some states delegate discretion to districts, the blanket claim that opening schools is solely a local determination is inaccurate.

claim: Photo shows Bill Clinton among others not wearing a mask at John Lewis’ funeral.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that a widely circulated photo shows Bill Clinton unmasked at John Lewis’s funeral. Contemporary news photo coverage of the services showed attendees largely following COVID-19 mask guidance, and similar viral images have been debunked or misattributed by fact-checkers. The claim likely stems from a miscaptioned or different-event photo rather than an authentic picture of Clinton unmasked at that funeral.

claim: "The claim ... that we plan to set up panels of bureaucrats with the power to  kill off senior citizens ... is a lie, plain and simple."
rationale: The widely circulated 'death panels' claim about creating panels of bureaucrats with power to kill senior citizens was a demonstrably false characterization. The Affordable Care Act and related proposals did not create bodies authorized to order deaths; disputed items (like reimbursement for advance-care planning and advisory committees) were misrepresented by opponents and debunked by multiple fact‑checking organizations.

claim: "Heitkamp has voted against Trump 68 percent of time."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Public vote-tracking sites that compare senators’ roll-call votes to the president’s stated position show Heitkamp voted with Trump roughly one-third of the time (so ‘against’ him about two-thirds) only for specific windows and using particular definitions; there is no single, constant 68% figure that covers her entire Senate tenure. Without a clear timeframe or methodology the flat “68 percent” statement is not reliably accurate.

claim: President Barack Obama "is the first president to keep a dog-trainer on retainer for $102,000 a year at taxpayer expense."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Barack Obama was the first U.S. president to have professional care for White House pets paid from public funds, and the $102,000 figure is a misleading characterization of existing staff salaries rather than a distinct ‘‘dog‑trainer’’ retainer. Presidents historically have had staff, military aides, Secret Service or maintenance personnel who cared for presidential animals, and press accounts conflated those roles with a standalone trainer contract. The claim therefore overstates novelty and misrepresents how the expense was recorded.

claim: Fox News changed its accreditation to "entertainment."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Fox News was formally reclassified or had its official press accreditation changed to 'entertainment.' Major outlets' White House press credentials and industry status were not altered in that way; occasional platform-specific labels or critiques of Fox's opinion programming have been conflated with an official accreditation change. Claims saying Fox News was reclassified appear to stem from misunderstandings or isolated mislabeling rather than an actual change in accreditation.

claim: Says Marsha Blackburn "voted against the Reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which attempts to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and date rape."
rationale: Marsha Blackburn opposed reauthorization efforts of the Violence Against Women Act; as a member of the House she voted against the 2013 reauthorization and publicly opposed provisions expanding protections and tribal jurisdiction. The claim accurately summarizes that she voted against a VAWA reauthorization that is intended to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and sexual assault.

claim: "Spanish was the first European language spoken in this country."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which country is meant. Many countries were first contacted or colonized by non‑Spanish Europeans (e.g., Portuguese, English, French, Dutch), so asserting Spanish was the first European language cannot be confirmed without specifying the country. Given the ambiguity, the claim as a general statement is therefore false.

claim: "We've seen in this last year tremendous things happening, including our unemployment rate come down 2 percentage points."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no country or specific 12‑month period; unemployment rates are reported monthly and can rise or fall by varying amounts depending on the timeframe. Without the precise start and end dates (and the country) the asserted "2 percentage point" decline cannot be confirmed and is therefore unsupported as presented.

claim: Marc Molinaro "has cut taxes, his budget now is lower than it was six years ago" in Dutchess County
rationale: I cannot confirm that Dutchess County’s overall budget is smaller now than it was six years earlier; nominal county budgets typically rise over multi‑year periods and claims of “cutting taxes” often refer to tax rate changes or individual tax relief rather than a smaller total county budget. Without specific years and whether “budget” means the tax levy, operating budget, or adjusted-for-inflation amounts, the statement is unsupported. Given typical local government spending trends and lack of precise evidence, the claim as stated is likely false.

claim: Takes credit for "reining in" state spending when he was governor.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify because it does not identify who "he" is or provide evidence that the person both claimed credit and actually reduced state spending as governor. Verifying such a claim requires the governor's identity, contemporaneous statements taking credit, and independent budget data showing spending was reduced or restrained. Without that, the assertion cannot be supported.

claim: "For the first time in over a decade, business leaders around the world have declared that China is no longer the world’s No. 1 place to invest; America is."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization without evidence; there has been no single, unanimous global declaration by business leaders that China is no longer the top investment destination and that America is instead. While some surveys and reports in recent years have shown a shifting preference toward the U.S. for certain investors, other surveys and FDI data still show China as a major or top destination depending on region, sector and timeframe. The absolute phrasing (“business leaders around the world have declared” and “for the first time in over a decade”) is not supported by consistent, universal data.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Donald Trump saying the exact phrase 'doesn't make a thing in America.' In fact, Trump has repeatedly promoted U.S. manufacturing and his business activities in the United States, so the claim appears to be a misquote or taken out of context.

claim: "Foster children are disproportionately victims of identity theft."
rationale: Multiple government and child-welfare reports and investigative stories have found that children and youth in foster care are at higher risk of identity theft than their peers. Factors cited include frequent placements and record transfers, wide access to personal data by many adults, and gaps in oversight that make misuse of Social Security numbers and other identifiers more likely. While precise rates vary by study and age cohort, the preponderance of evidence supports that foster children are disproportionately affected.

claim: "COVID internment camps announced in America: Tennessee governor signs EO authorizing National Guard to carry out COVID medical kidnappings."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no credible evidence that any Tennessee governor signed an executive order authorizing the National Guard to carry out “COVID medical kidnappings”; publicly available executive orders and reporting show the Guard was authorized for emergency medical support, logistics, and staffing, not unlawful abductions. The National Guard operates under statutes and civilian law, and detentions would require specific legal authority and due process rather than an EO authorizing blanket kidnappings.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because the U.S. economy was not in multi‑year 'decay' immediately before Trump — unemployment, GDP and stock markets had been improving for years after the 2008–09 recession — and attributing an end to 'decay' solely to Trump reversing prior policies is a causal claim that is not supported by the evidence. Trump's tax cuts and deregulatory actions coincided with continued growth for a time, but independent analyses show the recovery began earlier and the effects and net benefits of those policy changes are debated; correlation does not prove the claimed reversal caused the end of any supposed decay.

claim: "When Marcy Kaptur brought home $42 million for new manufacturing jobs, Dennis Kucinich voted 'no'."
rationale: This claim ties a specific $42 million award secured by Rep. Marcy Kaptur to a single roll‑call 'no' vote by Rep. Dennis Kucinich, but public roll calls and reporting do not corroborate that precise linkage. Kaptur did win federal funding for manufacturing projects at various times, but the statement names no bill or date and there is no clear record that Kucinich cast a direct 'no' on the specific appropriation in question. Without a cited bill and roll‑call, the claim is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: This numeric split is consistent with tallies based on Bureau of Labor Statistics private-sector payroll data since 1961 when job changes are attributed to the party of the sitting president for each month in office. Using that common method, the cumulative net private-sector job gain is about 66 million, roughly 42 million during Democratic presidencies and 24 million during Republican presidencies. The numbers are sensitive to the exact end date and the attribution method, but the claim matches widely reported calculations.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to keep big government in charge" of federally-owned land.
rationale: The claim is false as a general statement about Trump's position. The Trump administration consistently pursued policies to reduce federal control of public lands—seeking to shrink national monuments, transfer more management authority to states, and open lands to energy development—rather than a goal of keeping "big government in charge." While some federal management remained in practice, his stated and implemented policies favored devolving or privatizing control, not maintaining expanded federal authority.

claim: "About 47 percent of able-bodied people in the state of Maine don’t work."
rationale: This claim is not supported by public labor statistics. State and federal data show the majority of working‑age adults in Maine are employed and the employment‑population ratio and labor‑force participation rates are well above 50%, so saying roughly 47% of 'able‑bodied' people don't work is inaccurate and likely conflates different measures. The statement also fails to define 'able‑bodied' or the timeframe, making it misleading.

claim: "After filing a lawsuit in Rhode Island, we reached an agreement with state agencies that resulted in more voters being registered in the first full month after our lawsuit than in the entire previous two-year reporting period."
rationale: The claim is specific and extraordinary but cannot be corroborated from general public records or media reporting through mid-2024. Without the name of the lawsuit, dates, the identity of “we,” or concrete registration numbers, the assertion that one month exceeded an entire prior two‑year reporting period is unverifiable and unlikely without broader public notice. It may be true in a narrowly defined or mischaracterized sense, but as stated it lacks corroborating evidence.

claim: The unemployment rate may be as high as "42 percent."
rationale: As an unqualified statement this is misleading: typical national official unemployment rates (for example the U.S. official rate) have never reached 42% in modern times — the U.S. peak was 14.8% in April 2020 and broader measures stayed well below 42%. While some countries or specific subgroups (youth or certain regions) can have unemployment rates at or above 40%, the claim without context is false.

claim: "We’ve lifted hundreds of thousands of people out of poverty in the last five years."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it fails to identify who 'we' refers to, which country or region, and what poverty metric is being used; without those details and supporting official data, the numeric claim cannot be confirmed. Independent statistics or a cited evaluation over the specified five-year period are required to substantiate that 'hundreds of thousands' were lifted out of poverty.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as given because it provides no timeframe, poll, or source; approval ratings are measured by specific polls and can rise or fall over short periods. Without a cited poll or date I cannot confirm an increase, so I judge the claim false due to lack of evidence. If a specific recent poll were provided the claim could be re-evaluated.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: This is incorrect as stated. The Affordable Care Act added a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax that can apply to capital gains, but it only affects net investment income for taxpayers whose modified adjusted gross income exceeds statutory thresholds and does not automatically apply to sales of a primary residence (which can qualify for large exclusions). It is more likely to affect sales of investment or second properties for high‑income taxpayers than ordinary home sales for typical homeowners.

claim: "Barbara Buono by the numbers: As a Trenton politician, she voted to raise taxes 154 times. Under her, property taxes up 70 percent. Backed a 16 percent sales tax increase. Utilities, nursing homes, cell phones, parking lots, lottery wins, gyms – She taxed them all. Architect of Corzine’s budget, she drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt. Barbara Buono by the numbers: taking New Jersey backwards."
rationale: The claim mixes some accurate elements of campaign attacks with misleading or unsubstantiated numeric assertions. Barbara Buono did serve in the New Jersey Legislature and was involved in budget votes and revenue measures during the Corzine era (including support for a sales-tax increase that raised the rate from 6% to 7%), but the specific counts (e.g., "voted to raise taxes 154 times"), the attribution of a 70% property-tax increase solely to her, and the claim she "drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt" are unsupported or lack necessary context and attribution. Overall the statement is a politically charged aggregation and overstates or misattributes responsibility for complex fiscal outcomes.

claim: Measures taken by my administration "have saved taxpayers $1 billion."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no specifics (which administration, which measures, what time period, or how savings were calculated). Without independent documentation or an audit showing the $1 billion savings net of costs and compared to a clear baseline, the claim cannot be confirmed. Many similar claims depend on accounting choices or projected rather than realized savings.

claim: Says he met a teacher in Dallas "who was only in his third year of teaching and already making more than $90,000 a year in salary."
rationale: Public K‑12 teacher salary schedules in Dallas-area public school districts do not support a typical third‑year teacher earning more than $90,000 in base salary; third‑year teachers are generally near entry pay and far below $90k. While occasional individuals in the region could reach that level through extra duties, stipends, master's/PhD pay, private/charter school arrangements, or significant outside income, the claim as stated (a third‑year teacher in Dallas already making more than $90,000 in salary) is misleading and not supported as a typical or verifiable fact.

claim: "Now, there was a time when someone like Scalia and Ginsburg got 95-plus votes."
rationale: The claim refers to Supreme Court nominees Antonin Scalia and Ruth Bader Ginsburg receiving more than 95 Senate votes. Scalia was confirmed 98–0 in 1986 and Ginsburg was confirmed 96–3 in 1993, so both received 95-plus affirmative votes. Therefore the statement is accurate in historical context.

claim: Wisconsin’s economy has "tanked" under Gov. Scott Walker and "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014."
rationale: The claim combines a subjective assertion (“tanked”) with a specific numeric assertion about layoffs; objective labor indicators under Gov. Walker showed overall job growth and a falling unemployment rate through 2015 rather than an economy that ‘tanked.’ Public labor data (state Department of Workforce Development and BLS mass-layoff/WARN reporting) do not support the statement that ‘so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014’ and the specific layoff total is misleading or inaccurate.

claim: "Every poll you see, the overwhelming majority of people want [E-Verify]."
rationale: The claim is an absolute universal statement that every poll shows an overwhelming majority supporting E‑Verify, which is not true. While many reputable polls record majority support for E‑Verify, results vary by question wording, sample and timing, and some polls show narrower support or mixed results rather than an "overwhelming" majority. Thus the claim overstates the consistency and magnitude of polling evidence.

claim: Says Adolf Hitler said, "The day mankind finds out what I was trying to defend this nation, Germany, from, then that’s the day World War III starts."
rationale: This quotation is not found in any primary sources (Mein Kampf, recorded speeches, Reichstag records) or reputable scholarly compilations of Hitler's words and is absent from authoritative histories. It appears on informal quote collections and internet memes with no verifiable provenance, so the attribution to Hitler is almost certainly fabricated or a modern misattribution.

claim: "Ukraine was the No. 1 donor to Hillary Clinton when she was running for president."
rationale: The claim is false: U.S. federal law bars foreign nationals and foreign governments from contributing to U.S. federal election campaigns, so a country cannot be an official top donor. Hillary Clinton's 2016 fundraising records show top donations came from U.S. individuals, PACs and small-dollar donors, not from the country of Ukraine. There is no evidence that Ukraine as a country was the No. 1 donor to her campaign.

claim: After they bought GST Steel, "Mitt Romney and his partners loaded it with debt, closed the Kansas City plant and walked away with a healthy profit, leaving hundreds of employees out of work with their pensions in jeopardy."
rationale: Bain Capital (which Romney co-founded) did buy GST Steel and the company later closed plants and entered bankruptcy, leaving pensions threatened. However, evidence does not support the specific claim that Romney personally 'loaded it with debt' and then 'walked away with a healthy profit'—Romney was not involved in day-to-day management at the time of the collapse and there is limited public evidence he personally took a large profit from that specific deal. The statement thus overstates Romney's direct actions and personal gain.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted against the Brady Bill five times for background checks on people."
rationale: The claim exaggerates Sanders’ record. While Bernie Sanders opposed some gun measures and voted against certain iterations or procedural motions related to the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, he did not cast five distinct votes specifically ‘against the Brady Bill’ on background checks; counting can vary depending on which procedural or amendment votes are included. The statement therefore overstates and mischaracterizes his voting record.

claim: "Nobody suffered any lasting injuries" from the CIA interrogation program.
rationale: Multiple independent investigations and reporting (including the U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee report, ICRC, medical experts, and human rights organizations) documented that CIA 'enhanced interrogation' caused lasting physical and psychological harm to detainees, and at least one detainee died in custody. The CIA's occasional internal claims that there were no lasting injuries have been contradicted by documented cases of chronic trauma, reports of potential brain injury, persistent PTSD and other long-term sequelae among former detainees.

claim: Says Leah Vukmir "wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault."
rationale: There is no readily available reporting or public record indicating that Leah Vukmir wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault. Her public statements and documented letters covered in major news sources do not include such a plea, so the claim is unsubstantiated as presented.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: The precise claim that undocumented ("illegal") immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs is not supported by authoritative sources. Research estimates of undocumented immigrant workers vary by year and methodology and typically fall in the mid-single-digit millions (roughly 5–7 million employed persons in recent years), and official BLS statistics do not record legal status. The statement also conflates "jobs" with "workers" and gives no timeframe, making the specific 8 million figure unreliable.

claim: "Of all the 62 counties in New York state, all of them, unemployment is going up except for the five counties of New York City."
rationale: The claim asserts a uniform increase in unemployment across all 57 non‑New York City counties, which is implausible and inconsistent with county‑level labor data that show mixed directions in unemployment changes. No specific timeframe or data source is given, and historical BLS/NY labor statistics typically show some counties rising and others falling. Therefore the blanket statement is false absent strong contemporaneous evidence.

claim: Robert Mueller’s investigative team has "13 hardened Democrats, some big Crooked Hillary supporters, and Zero Republicans."
rationale: This specific characterization is inaccurate. Public reporting and campaign-donation records show some Mueller team members had donated to Democratic causes, but the claim that there were exactly '13 hardened Democrats' and 'Zero Republicans' is not supported; the team included career DOJ officials and people without clear partisan donor records, and at least some members were not exclusively Democratic donors. The phrases 'hardened Democrats' and 'big Crooked Hillary supporters' are subjective and unsupported by evidence about the team's professional conduct.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman.
rationale: I was unable to find evidence that the Austin American-Statesman formally endorsed a candidate named Gerald Daugherty. The paper's endorsement records and typical election-coverage archives do not list that name, so the claim is unverified and likely false absent supporting documentation.

claim: U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has blamed the Republicans for the creation of Hamas."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz literally said Republicans “created” Hamas. Public reporting and available transcripts show she has criticized Republican policies or actions for contributing to conditions or failures related to the Israel–Palestine conflict, but the specific claim that she blamed Republicans for the creation of Hamas is a misleading paraphrase not supported by direct quotes.

claim: In the wake of the Republican-backed tax bill, "more than 100,000 American workers have already been laid off in 2018."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or consolidated data showing that more than 100,000 U.S. workers were laid off in 2018 specifically "in the wake of" the Republican tax bill. While some companies announced workforce reductions that year, independent fact‑checking and labor data did not attribute an aggregate six‑figure layoff total directly to the tax law; many firms instead cited market conditions or announced bonuses and buybacks. The causal link and the >100,000 figure are unsupported.

claim: Says Sen. Kamala  Harris "introduced a bill today to forbid a police officers from drawing his/her gun without permission from their supervisor."
rationale: There is no record of Sen. Kamala Harris introducing legislation that would categorically forbid police officers from drawing their firearms without a supervisor's permission. Her known policing-related proposals (e.g., the Justice in Policing Act and related reforms) addressed use-of-force standards, accountability, reporting, and bans on specific tactics, not a blanket supervisory-permission requirement to draw a weapon. The claim appears to misstate or invent a specific rule that did not appear in Harris's legislative record.

claim: Mercedes-Benz USA  moving its headquarters to Atlanta will create at least 800 jobs.
rationale: Reporting on Mercedes‑Benz USA's move to Atlanta indicated roughly 800 employees would be based in the new headquarters, but that reflected relocation of existing positions rather than the creation of at least 800 new jobs. The claim's wording — that the move "will create at least 800 jobs" — is therefore misleading and not supported by the company statements at the time.

claim: Abraham Lincoln "visited and some say even danced in (the Ohio Senate) chamber."
rationale: This claim appears to be a piece of local lore rather than a documented fact. Historians and primary-source records of Lincoln's travels do not provide reliable contemporary evidence that Abraham Lincoln visited and danced in the Ohio Senate chamber; the story surfaces in later anecdotes and is treated as apocryphal.
