Florida’s long-established public trust doctrine and state law generally preserve public access to the intertidal (wet‑sand) zone, and the cited bills change regulatory details rather than wholesale privatization of beaches.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s book "The Art of the Deal" advises: "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated."
rationale: The specific phrasing quoted does not appear in Donald Trump’s 1987 book The Art of the Deal; the book’s published text and widely cited excerpts do not contain that line. While Trump has at times publicly suggested he would claim fraud if he lost elections, that later rhetoric is not the same as the book containing the quoted advice, so the claim that the book advises this is false.

claim: "Instagram has been limiting our posts so that no more than 7% of our friends see our posts."
rationale: There is no evidence Instagram enforces a universal hard cap that only 7% of followers see every post. Instagram uses an algorithmic feed and organic reach varies widely by account, post time, engagement and other factors; some analytics studies report single-digit average reach for some accounts but not a platform-wide fixed limit. The claim states a specific enforced percentage as a rule, which is not supported.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't believe in equal pay."
rationale: There is no authoritative record of Donald Trump literally saying the words "I don't believe in equal pay." While Trump has opposed specific equal-pay legislation and has downplayed the gender pay gap in interviews and statements, the precise quoted sentence appears to be a paraphrase or political characterization rather than a documented verbatim quote.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: The claim asserts a universal rule that races always tighten at the end of campaigns; that is false. While some elections do see late shifts or narrowing margins, many contests remain steady or even widen toward one candidate, so tightening is not guaranteed or universal.

claim: "When I go on Letterman" the "ratings go up."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented: it lacks a named speaker, timeframe, and specific episodes, and there is no general rule that any single guest consistently causes ratings to rise. Individual celebrity appearances can sometimes boost viewership for a particular night, but proving a consistent causal effect requires episode-by-episode Nielsen data and controls for other factors. Without that evidence this blanket statement cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says El Chapo testified in court that he paid off Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open for drug cartels.
rationale: There is no record in the U.S. trial transcripts or credible news reporting that Joaquín ‘El Chapo’ Guzmán testified he paid Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.–Mexico border open. The claim appears to originate from social-media misinformation; reliable coverage of the 2019 New York trial does not include any such accusation.

claim: Says there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold for confirming Supreme Court nominees."
rationale: False — there was no formal, always-applied "traditional" 60-vote requirement to confirm Supreme Court nominees. What existed was a Senate cloture practice (since 1975 three-fifths of senators, typically 60 of 100) to end debate if a filibuster was attempted; when no filibuster occurred nominees could be confirmed by simple majority, and in 2017 the Senate removed the filibuster for Supreme Court nominations entirely.

claim: Says "Every time the Legislature 'suspended' the kicker, most recently the corporate kicker in 2007, Salem spent every penny and failed to stabilize the state's revenues."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. Oregon’s ‘kicker’ has only been altered or redirected a few times, and the Legislature’s responses and use of those dollars have varied by episode; it is not true that on every occasion Salem simply “spent every penny” and uniformly failed to stabilize state revenues. Whether a suspension or redirection occurred, the outcomes differed and some actions were intended as temporary budget fixes rather than permanent spending of all funds.

claim: "Last year, there were an additional 81,000 pages of government regulations. If you stack that up, it would be a three-story building."
rationale: The claim mixes an imprecise page-count with a physical analogy and is misleading. While the Federal Register has run on the order of tens of thousands of pages in recent years (figures around 70k–90k some years), saying there were an "additional 81,000 pages of government regulations" overstates or mischaracterizes what those pages represent (they include notices, proposed rules, and other items, not only new final regulations). The stacking math (81,000 pages ≈ 20–30 feet using typical paper thickness) makes a roughly 2.5–3‑story pile under generous assumptions, so the "three-story building" claim is an approximate rhetorical exaggeration rather than a precise factual statement.

claim: "When President Obama landed in Cuba on Air Force One, no leader was there, nobody, to greet him -- perhaps an incident without precedent in the long and prestigious history of Air Force One."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: when President Obama arrived in Havana on March 20, 2016 Raúl Castro did not meet him on the tarmac, but senior Cuban officials (including First Vice President Miguel Díaz-Canel and other ministers) did greet him at the airport and Castro met Obama later at the Revolution Palace. Thus it is false to say “no leader was there” and the implication that this was unprecedented is overstated.

claim: Wisconsin is "38th in the country in terms of proficiency standards" in student testing.
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported: there is no single, universally accepted national ranking that definitively places Wisconsin 38th on 'proficiency standards' across student testing. Rankings of state proficiency standards vary by dataset, year, and methodology (e.g., NAEP cut scores, state assessments, or third‑party reports), and I could not confirm a consistent 38th-place placement for Wisconsin. Without a specified source or metric the claim is misleading and unverified.

claim: Says Rick Perry's proposal on driver licenses and high school dropouts has been state law since 1989.
rationale: The statement is incorrect as written. There is no clear evidence that the specific rule Rick Perry cited — suspending driver’s licenses for high‑school dropouts — had been a statewide law continuously since 1989; similar dropout/licensing penalties were enacted or enforced at different times and often at the district or later-state statute level, not uniformly in 1989. Prior fact-checks and legislative histories show the relevant Texas policies were modified or implemented after 1989 rather than established statewide that year.

claim: "Hillary (Clinton), one time late at night when she was exhausted, misstated and immediately apologized for it, what happened to her in Bosnia in 1995."
rationale: This claim mixes truth with an incorrect detail. Hillary Clinton did misstate during the 2008 campaign that she came under sniper fire in Bosnia and later said she had "misspoken" (attributing it to being tired/exhausted) and apologized; however the Bosnia trip in question took place in January 1996, not 1995, and the wording about timing of the apology is imprecise. Because of the incorrect year and slight sequencing imprecision, the claim as written is false.

claim: Facebook is changing its hate speech policy to ban "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: False. Meta (Facebook) has not announced a categorical hate-speech policy change specifically banning the phrase "Let’s go Brandon." The slogan is a political insult directed at a public figure, and Facebook’s hate-speech rules focus on protected classes; posts using the phrase could be moderated for harassment or other violations depending on context, but there is no announced blanket ban.

claim: "Tony Evers is cutting child support."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Tony Evers has enacted a blanket cut to child support payments. Governors can propose budget changes, but actual reductions to child support payments or statewide programs would require legislative action and public reporting; news and public records through mid‑2024 do not show such an enacted cut by Evers. Some discussions have involved funding for child support enforcement or administrative changes, which is not the same as cutting child support benefits to families.

claim: "Over the past decade, drug prices have risen at three times the rate of inflation."
rationale: The claim is too general and not supported as a uniform fact. Trends depend on which country, which ten‑year window, and whether one measures list prices, consumer out‑of‑pocket costs, or net prices after rebates; some list prices rose faster than inflation in parts of the past decade, but other measures did not, and overall increases are not reliably “three times” inflation across the board. Because of these ambiguities and mixed empirical findings, the categorical claim is false as stated.

claim: In the plot to kidnap Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, "the perps were ANTIFA and BLM anarchists."
rationale: Federal indictments, arrests, and reporting tied the plot to right-wing, anti-government militia members (commonly described as the Wolverine Watchmen and allied individuals), not to ANTIFA or Black Lives Matter activists. Court filings, law-enforcement statements, and defendants' own statements and social-media activity demonstrate ties to far‑right militia ideology rather than left‑wing anarchist groups.

claim: Mitt Romney previously believed "that abortion should be safe and legal in this country." Now he is "prolife."
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly said during his 1990s Massachusetts Senate campaign that abortion should be "safe and legal," and over subsequent years he changed his stance, identifying as pro‑life by the time of his later presidential campaigns. The claim accurately summarizes this documented shift in his stated positions on abortion.

claim: Amazon will ship baby formula to U.S. addresses if you change your preferred country on its website from the U.S. to Canada.
rationale: This is false as a general rule. Amazon's marketplaces and product listings are tied to the shipping address and seller policies, and Amazon and many sellers block or restrict cross‑border shipment of regulated items like infant formula because of customs, export/import rules, and vendor restrictions. While individual third‑party sellers or freight‑forwarding services might sometimes send Canadian purchases to U.S. addresses, simply changing the preferred country setting will not reliably cause Amazon to ship baby formula to U.S. addresses.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: The claim is false because high-quality evidence and public-health guidance show that commonly used masks (cloth, surgical, N95) do not cause clinically meaningful reductions in blood oxygen (SpO2) or widespread CO2 retention in the general population, and there is no credible evidence that mask use has killed “quite a few people.” While masks can be uncomfortable and rarely might exacerbate breathlessness in people with severe respiratory failure, that is not the same as masks being broadly dangerous or lethal to those with cardiac or respiratory disorders.

claim: "As your Lieutenant Governor…I cut your taxes."
rationale: As worded the claim is misleading: a lieutenant governor does not have unilateral authority to cut taxes. Tax changes generally require legislative approval and the governor's signature (or voter referendums), so claiming "I cut your taxes" without specifying law enacted and role in its passage overstates what the office can do.

claim: "2 million rounds of ammo that ‘went missing’ under Obama turns up in enemy hands"
rationale: There is no publicly verifiable evidence that exactly “2 million rounds” went missing under President Obama and were later recovered in enemy hands. Department of Defense oversight and reporting acknowledge some diversion of U.S.-provided weapons and ammunition in Afghanistan, but they do not substantiate the specific 2 million-round figure or a confirmed recovery of that exact cache. Media reports that repeat the claim rely on anonymous or unverified sources and conflate different time periods and accounting categories.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: Public reporting and federal campaign finance disclosures showed Rep. John Culberson used campaign committee funds to buy collectibles, including Civil War-era items and fossils. Media coverage characterized these expenditures as discovered in filings, supporting the claim that he was found to have spent campaign cash on such items.

claim: "I've seen (life) from the factory floor when I was working the graveyard shift ...and I'd be ankle-deep in water at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant where I was running a machine that was so loud I couldn't hear myself yell if I wanted to."
rationale: I cannot corroborate the specific personal anecdote that the speaker worked the graveyard shift running a machine at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant and stood ankle-deep in water. Public biographies and news reports about the likely speaker and about Murray Ohio do not provide independent verification of this employment or the described conditions. Because the claim is a personal recollection with no reliable third‑party sourcing, it remains unverified and is judged false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Military tribunals start Jan. 20, 2021."
rationale: There is no evidence that any official U.S. military or federal authority scheduled nationwide "military tribunals" to begin on January 20, 2021. The claim originated from conspiracy talking points and contradicts normal legal requirements: military tribunals need explicit legal authorization or orders and are not simply started on a calendar date for civilian suspects. January 20, 2021 was the presidential inauguration and no credible government announcements or actions implemented such tribunals on that date.

claim: "Kenosha car dealer kills himself after insurance won’t cover … damages caused by the riots."
rationale: I find no credible news reports or official records confirming that a Kenosha car dealer killed himself because insurance wouldn’t cover riot damages. The claim appears to originate from unverified social-media posts that were not corroborated by local or national outlets, and fact-checkers previously debunked similar viral allegations. Without independent reporting or official confirmation, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Attention hunters: Voting in North Dakota could cost you your out-of-state hunting licenses."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Simply voting in North Dakota would not automatically revoke someone’s out-of-state hunting licenses — hunting residency and license eligibility are determined by each state’s statutes and proof of domicile, and agencies typically require more evidence than a single vote to change residency status. That said, registering to vote or otherwise establishing domicile in a different state can be used as strong evidence of a change of residency and could, in some circumstances, affect license eligibility after a residency determination is made.

claim: "We are No. 1 among all large states in having fully vaccinated teenagers. We are No. 2 in all large states for having fully vaccinated five- to 11- year-olds."
rationale: The claim lacks a specified actor (which state is “we”), a date, and a clear definition of “large states,” so it cannot be verified as stated. Rankings of fully vaccinated teens and 5–11 year‑olds come from time‑sensitive state vaccination data that vary by source and week; without those specifics the assertion is unsubstantiated. Because such claims are verifiable only with a named state and date, this undated, contextless statement is judged false for lack of evidence.

claim: The Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. "cannot account for creating one single job."
rationale: This absolute claim is false. State audits and reporting found WEDC had significant documentation and accountability problems for many incentive deals and could not substantiate all claimed jobs, but the agency did report and document job outcomes in numerous cases — it was not true that WEDC “cannot account for creating one single job” in any comprehensive sense. The criticism reflects real record-keeping failures but overstates them into a total inability to account for any jobs.

claim: Police are "20.8 times more likely to kill than be killed by a criminal."
rationale: The 20.8× figure appears to be a simple ratio of annual raw counts (roughly ~1,000 civilians killed by police vs ~48 officers murdered by felons in a single year) and therefore is misleading. Reliable statistics vary by year and by definitions (what counts as a police-caused death, what counts as an officer being killed), and comparing raw totals without normalizing by number of officers, incidents, or other context does not support a general ‘‘20.8 times more likely’’ statement.

claim: The $1.9 trillion relief package is "about a bridge for Chuck Schumer, a tunnel for Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: The phrasing is a rhetorical/opinionated jab, not a factual description of the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan. The law provided broad pandemic relief (stimulus checks, enhanced unemployment, state and local aid, vaccine and public-health funding) rather than specific "bridge" or "tunnel" projects earmarked for Chuck Schumer or Nancy Pelosi. There is no evidence the package primarily consisted of or intentionally funded infrastructure projects for those leaders personally.

claim: "Before we even passed health care, 4 millions kids got health insurance that didn't have it before, through the Children's Health Insurance Program."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) has covered millions of children since its 1997 start, there is no clear, verifiable evidence that exactly four million children newly gained insurance through CHIP in the narrow period “before we passed health care” (the ACA). Total CHIP enrollment has typically been reported in the 6–8 million range, and reauthorizations/expansions added coverage over many years, but the specific 4‑million figure tied to the immediate pre‑ACA period is not substantiated.

claim: ﻿﻿"Since Mayor Kennedy O’Brien took office Sayreville has issued 22,081 building permits! Now O’Brien is holding secret meetings with big developers."
rationale: The claim combines a very specific permit total and an allegation of "secret meetings," but I cannot verify the 22,081 figure or the meetings from available public information. Building-permit totals are public records and would need a cited time range and source; similarly, allegations of secret meetings would typically be supported by reporting, meeting minutes, or public-records evidence. In the absence of corroborating sources the precise numeric claim and the meeting allegation are unsubstantiated.

claim: In the 1970s, "the swine flu broke out . . . under another Democrat, President Jimmy Carter."
rationale: The major U.S. ‘swine flu’ scare and national vaccination program occurred in 1976 following an outbreak at Fort Dix, New Jersey, while Gerald Ford (a Republican) was president. Jimmy Carter took office in January 1977 and there was no comparable swine‑flu outbreak in his term; any mixing of dates likely confuses the 1976 events with later, unrelated influenza activity.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: This is false. Louisiana receives money related to offshore oil through state severance taxes and royalties on production in state waters and submerged lands, and it also receives federal revenue-sharing from Gulf of Mexico offshore lease revenues under laws like GOMESA and from BP Deepwater Horizon settlement/RESTORE Act distributions. While historically large portions of federal Outer Continental Shelf royalties went to the U.S. Treasury, mechanisms exist that direct substantial offshore-related funds to Louisiana.

claim: Says Joe Biden took a knee during the national anthem.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified video showing Joe Biden taking a knee during the national anthem at a public event. Viral clips claiming he did have been debunked or shown to be misinterpreted/manipulated; at major public ceremonies and sporting events he has been recorded standing for the anthem. Without a specific event or reliable source, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "The number of people who just got their voting rights restored in Florida is greater than the populations of Wyoming, Vermont, Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Delaware, Rhode Island, Montana, Maine and New Hampshire."
rationale: Florida's 2018 Amendment 4 affected roughly 1.4 million people whose voting rights were to be restored, and that figure is larger than the population of each listed state individually (those states have populations roughly between 0.58 million and 1.36 million). Therefore the statement is true if read as comparing the Florida number to each state's population separately.

claim: "With 320,000 net Ohio manufacturing jobs lost, (Sen. Rob) Portman calls NAFTA a ‘proven success’."
rationale: Ohio manufacturing employment declined by roughly 300–330 thousand jobs when comparing the post‑NAFTA period (mid‑1990s) to the mid‑2010s in BLS/state series, matching the commonly cited ~320,000 figure. Separately, Sen. Rob Portman has publicly described NAFTA as a "proven success" in speeches and interviews, so the two parts of the claim are supported by available employment data and his quoted statement.

claim: "Obamacare … means that for up to 20 million Americans, they will lose the insurance they currently have, the insurance that they like and they want to keep."
rationale: Wide independent analyses found the number of Americans who would be forced to lose noncompliant individual-market plans was in the single-digit millions, not 20 million. CBO, HHS, Kaiser and academic estimates generally pointed to roughly 4–8 million affected in the individual market, while employer-sponsored coverage was largely preserved; therefore the "up to 20 million" figure substantially overstates mainstream estimates.

claim: "U.S. agricultural & food exports are expected to increase more than $2 billion annually under #USMCA"
rationale: Official U.S. government statements made during USMCA negotiation (notably from the U.S. Trade Representative and related USDA materials) presented projections that U.S. agricultural and food exports would rise by more than $2 billion per year under the agreement. Those figures were presented as model-based expectations rather than observed results.

claim: The longest filibuster in U.S. history was 75 days and "took place in 1964, when Democrats tried to block the Civil Rights Act."
rationale: The longest continuous U.S. Senate filibuster is widely recorded as the 75-day obstruction from March to June 1964 against the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The effort was carried out mainly by Southern Democratic senators who opposed the bill; the Senate ultimately invoked cloture and the Act passed.

claim: "The Defense Department received only one-half of 1 percent of the nearly trillion-dollar stimulus package funding."
rationale: This is false: the Department of Defense received substantially more than 0.5% of the nearly trillion-dollar stimulus commonly referenced (the 2009 ARRA). The stimulus included tens of billions for military construction, procurement and related defense activities, so a 0.5% share (only a few billion dollars) would greatly understate DoD’s funding. The exact share depends on which stimulus bill and accounting method is used, but the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: "More than half of women under 30 who give birth do so outside of marriage..."
rationale: The claim as stated is too general and unsupported: it gives no country or time period. In many national datasets (for example U.S. vital statistics), unmarried birth rates are high among teens and women in their early 20s but substantially lower for women aged 25–29, so the combined share of births to women under 30 occurring outside marriage is not clearly and universally above 50%. The statement might be true for specific countries, age subgroups, or years, but not as a blanket fact without context.

claim: A state report’s "projection is that approximately half of public employees" would live outside municipal boundaries in a decade if the state bans local residency requirements.
rationale: I cannot verify any authoritative state report that projects "approximately half of public employees" would move outside municipal boundaries within a decade solely because local residency requirements are banned. Available research and reporting on residency-requirement bans show mixed and usually modest shifts in where employees live, and such a precise, large projection would require named methodology and context that are not provided. Without identification of the state and the specific report, the claim is unsubstantiated and likely inaccurate.

claim: He "stood up to Barack Obama by passing legislation that prevents you from being forced to join government health plans or buy health insurance against your will."
rationale: The claim is false as stated: there is no single federal law that broadly prevents the government from requiring people to enroll in government health plans or buy health insurance. The Affordable Care Act originally included an individual mandate, and Congress later set the federal penalty to zero in 2017, which removed the enforcement penalty but did not create a permanent legal bar preventing future mandates. The statement also lacks a specific identify for “He” or the precise legislation, so it overstates and mischaracterizes the legal situation.

claim: "Already, the Affordable Care Act is helping to slow the growth of (Medicare’s) health care costs."
rationale: The ACA included multiple Medicare payment and delivery reforms (reductions in Medicare Advantage benchmarks, productivity adjustments, ACO and value-based payment initiatives) that federal analysts (CBO and the Medicare actuary/Trustees) have identified as reducing projected Medicare spending. Early post-ACA years also showed slower Medicare spending growth, though the degree directly attributable to the law versus macroeconomic and secular trends is debated. Overall, evidence supports that the ACA has helped slow Medicare cost growth, but attribution is not exclusive or precise.

claim: Says county parties representing more than half the state’s Republican voters approved resolutions "demanding changes" in Texas House leadership.
rationale: Contemporary news reporting tallied county Republican party resolutions and found that the counties whose party organizations had approved resolutions calling for changes in Texas House leadership represented a majority of the state’s Republican electorate (typically measured by past Republican primary turnout). The claim matches those reports that aggregated county-level votes into a share of Republican voters and concluded the affected counties exceeded 50%.

claim: "I haven't switched my position" on the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it omits who is speaking and when; without identifying the person and timeframe, we cannot confirm that their stance on the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) never changed. In practice many public figures shifted their TPP positions over time, so a blanket assertion of no change is implausible without evidence. Given the missing context, the claim cannot be validated as true.

claim: "Texas now has the second-highest high school graduation rate in the country. And it has the highest graduation rate for African Americans and Hispanics."
rationale: Available national data through mid‑2024 do not support a clear claim that Texas is currently the second‑highest state overall or the top state for African‑American and Hispanic graduation rates. While Texas has improved its graduation rates in recent years, NCES and state‑by‑state reports typically show states such as New Jersey, Massachusetts, and others ranking at or above Texas overall and often leading for Black and Hispanic subgroups.

claim: "David McCormick paid for attacks on Donald Trump."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that David McCormick (the former hedge‑fund executive and 2022 Pennsylvania Senate candidate) paid for attacks on Donald Trump. Reporting and campaign‑finance records through mid‑2024 do not show McCormick funding anti‑Trump ads; he sought GOP support rather than running an anti‑Trump campaign. The claim is unsubstantiated as presented.

claim: Photos show "diesel generators" at the COP26 climate change conference.
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and COP26 organisers reported that viral photos were misattributed or showed temporary, ancillary equipment rather than diesel generators powering the summit. The main COP26 venue was supplied from the grid and images circulating online were either unrelated, taken out of context, or depicted small temporary units for side events, not diesel power for the conference itself.

claim: The book Little Red Riding Hood is something "that’s been banned in America," but not assault weapons.
rationale: The claim is misleading. While some local schools or libraries have at times removed or restricted certain editions of Little Red Riding Hood, there is no nationwide permanent ban of the tale across the United States; conversely, 'assault weapons' are not banned federally today but several U.S. states do impose legal bans or strict restrictions. The statement treats both topics as absolute when the reality varies by jurisdiction and edition/time period.

claim: Sen. Mark Kelly voted "for benefits to illegals."
rationale: The claim is vague and contains a pejorative term; there is no specific roll‑call or bill that matches the description "voted for benefits to illegals." Sen. Mark Kelly has supported immigrant‑relief measures (e.g., DACA protections and some pathway proposals), but that is not the same as a definitive vote described in those words. Without a specific bill, the broad assertion is unsupported.

claim: "George Bush never suggested that we eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The claim is implausible because at least one President Bush (George W. Bush) presided over and publicly supported policies that sought to restrict federal funding for organizations associated with abortion services, such as reinstating the Mexico City policy and backing funding limits like the Hyde approach. Those actions and statements were commonly applied against providers like Planned Parenthood, so the categorical statement that “George Bush never suggested” eliminating their funding is incorrect.

claim: Says the CEO of Camping World told Trump supporters "Frankly, don’t shop at my business."
rationale: I could not find reliable, corroborated reporting that the CEO of Camping World explicitly told Trump supporters the quoted line “Frankly, don’t shop at my business.” While Camping World CEO Marcus Lemonis has publicly criticized political rhetoric and expressed strong views about customers and employees, there is no clear evidence he uttered that exact, attributable statement; the claim appears to be a misquote or lacks context.

claim: "8 Syrians caught at Texas border in Laredo."
rationale: I cannot corroborate the specific claim that exactly "8 Syrians" were caught at the Texas border in Laredo; no clear, verifiable reports matching that precise wording appear in my training data through mid-2024. The claim may be plausible in the abstract (migrants of many nationalities are frequently apprehended), but without a date, source, or official confirmation this precise assertion is unverified and therefore judged false for lack of evidence.

claim: Data on violent crime shows Wisconsin "has become less safe than it was when Scott Walker took office."
rationale: The claim is presented as a definitive, data-backed decline in safety statewide since Scott Walker took office in January 2011, but statewide violent-crime trends are mixed and depend on the metric and time period chosen. Violent crime in Wisconsin fell in the early-to-mid 2010s, rose in some years (notably around 2020–2021 with increases in homicides), and varies substantially by locality; therefore it is not accurate to say the data uniformly show Wisconsin has become less safe than in 2011. Without specifying which violent-crime measure and end year, the claim overstates what the data consistently demonstrate.

claim: No openly gay man has ever been elected to the Georgia Legislature.
rationale: The claim is false. Sam Park, an openly gay man, was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives in 2016 (becoming the first openly gay man in the Georgia General Assembly), and other openly gay men such as Matthew Wilson have since been elected as well. These election results were widely reported and are reflected in public legislative records.

claim: The "president of Drag Queen Story Hour" was "arrested, charged with child pornography."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the national or official "president" of Drag Queen Story Hour was arrested and charged with child pornography. Multiple reputable fact-checkers and mainstream news outlets investigated viral posts and found they misidentified individuals or conflated unrelated arrests with the organization's leadership. The claim appears to be a viral misattribution rather than a verified arrest of the organization's president.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Casten has held numerous "invite-only" town halls.
rationale: There are isolated reports and criticism that Rep. Sean Casten held some pre-screened or invitation-based virtual constituent events, but I did not find clear, verifiable evidence that he has held 'numerous' invite-only town halls as a widespread, documented pattern. The claim overstates the available public reporting, which tends to describe a few specific instances rather than many such events. Without a defined timeframe or supporting documentation, the assertion is not reliably proven.

claim: Bernie Sanders has "never taken corporate lobbyist money in his *entire political career.*"
rationale: The claim is absolute but inaccurate. While Bernie Sanders has prominently refused corporate PAC money in his recent Senate and presidential campaigns, reporting and campaign-finance records show he has received donations tied to corporate interests or from individuals who worked as lobbyists or for corporations at various points earlier in his political career. Therefore the statement that he has "never" taken corporate lobbyist money is false.

claim: "Not only is there no scientific evidence that CO2 is a pollutant, higher CO2 concentrations actually help ecosystems support more plant and animal life."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: there is abundant scientific evidence that CO2 is a greenhouse gas whose rising concentrations drive global warming and associated harms to human health, ecosystems, and infrastructure. While elevated CO2 can stimulate photosynthesis in some plants (the “CO2 fertilization” effect), that benefit is frequently limited by nutrients, water, pests and other factors, can reduce plant nutritional quality, change species composition, and is outweighed by negative impacts of warming and ocean acidification on many ecosystems and species.

claim: Says private-sector job growth in 2011 "places New Jersey in the top third among all of the states."
rationale: State-level employment data for 2011 show New Jersey’s private-sector job gains were modest relative to many other states; growth that year was concentrated in energy- and Sun Belt-states and several faster-recovering economies. Given those patterns, New Jersey did not rank in the top third of states on private-sector job growth for calendar-year 2011 in commonly used BLS/state rankings.

claim: "8% of the votes cast" in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary, 864 mailed ballots, came from dead voters. "NOTHING TO SEE HERE!!!"
rationale: The claim conflates a raw dataset count (864 absentee-related records) with confirmed ballots cast by deceased people and misstates the percentage. Fact-checks and Michigan election officials explained the 864 figure reflects administrative/recordkeeping issues (duplicate requests, ballots mailed to registrants who later died, or other flags) and not 8% of votes being cast by dead people; the number of actual ballots cast in the name of deceased voters was negligible.

claim: "Moderna has been pulled in Iceland and pulled for everyone under age 30 in Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark due to heart issues."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes national policies. While Nordic health authorities and the EMA have noted a small increased risk of myocarditis/pericarditis with Moderna and several countries issued age- or sex-based recommendations favoring Pfizer for younger people, the age cut-offs and scopes differed by country and changed over time — and Iceland did not issue a blanket permanent “pull” of Moderna for all ages. Therefore the statement that Moderna was pulled in Iceland and for everyone under 30 across Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark is inaccurate.

claim: "As a 27 year old staff attorney for the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate investigation, Hillary Rodham was fired by her supervisor, lifelong Democrat Jerry Zeifman. When asked why Hillary Rodham was fired, Zeifman said in an interview, ‘Because she was a liar. She was an unethical, dishonest lawyer, she conspired to violate the Constitution, the rules of the House, the rules of the Committee, and the rules of confidentiality.’"
rationale: Contemporary reporting and later interviews confirm that Jerry Zeifman, who served as counsel to the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate impeachment inquiry, said in a 1994 interview that he had fired Hillary Rodham (then about 27) and called her a "liar" and "an unethical, dishonest lawyer," alleging she violated committee rules. The basic elements of the claim — her role/age, Zeifman’s role as her supervisor, and his quoted criticism — are supported by contemporaneous accounts and Zeifman’s own statements.

claim: "Violent crime is now going down for the first time in a long while."
rationale: The statement is unqualified and therefore not verifiable: violent crime trends differ by country, state, and city and by specific time windows. Some jurisdictions have seen recent declines after earlier increases, but others have not, and aggregate/global trends are not uniformly 'going down for the first time in a long while.' Without a specified place and timeframe the claim is misleading.

claim: Says Quaden Bayles committed suicide.
rationale: Claims that Quaden Bayles committed suicide are false. Multiple media reports and public statements from his family have confirmed he was alive after the viral bullying incident, and previous death rumors about him have been debunked. There is no credible evidence that he died by suicide up to the assistant's knowledge cutoff.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: The statement is unsupported by public records and contemporary reporting: there is no credible evidence that Governor Scott Walker personally received a one-time $7,300 pay raise. Governor salaries and adjustments in Wisconsin are public and handled by a compensation process; major media and fact-checkers did not report such a discrete $7,300 increase to Walker’s pay. The claim is likely a misrepresentation or lacks context (e.g., comparing different years, benefits, or statutory adjustments).

claim: Officials "recommend that women who get one of these (COVID-19) shots should absolutely not get pregnant for at least the first two months after they’ve been injected."
rationale: Major public health authorities (CDC, WHO, FDA and similar national agencies) did not issue a blanket recommendation that women must avoid pregnancy for two months after receiving COVID-19 vaccines. Some clinical trials required participants not become pregnant during the study follow-up, which is different from public vaccination guidance, and early guidance evolved as data accumulated. The claim appears to conflate trial protocols or misinformation with official public-health recommendations.

claim: During the lead-up to the American Revolutionary War, "some guy in Boston got his head blown off because he tried to secretly raise the tax on tea."
rationale: There is no historical evidence that someone in Boston had their head blown off for trying to secretly raise the tax on tea. The key incidents in the lead‑up to the Revolution — the Boston Massacre (1770) in which colonists were shot by British soldiers during a street confrontation, and the Boston Tea Party (1773) in which colonists dumped taxed tea — do not match that description. Taxes on tea were imposed by Parliament (the Tea Act), not covertly raised by a single Bostonian who was executed in that manner.

claim: "They tried to give us $400 million to build a high-speed train that goes 39 miles an hour."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a $400 million federal or state grant was offered specifically to build a “high‑speed” train that would run only 39 miles per hour. Major U.S. high‑speed rail grants (for example under the 2009 stimulus) were in the billions for projects that planned much higher operating speeds; 39 mph is characteristic of slow commuter or construction‑phase speeds, not high‑speed rail. The claimant appears to conflate or misstate funding amounts and the intended speeds of planned projects.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker doesn't make his calendar public -- "he's on our dime and we don't know where he is."
rationale: This is an overbroad characterization. While critics complained that Gov. Scott Walker did not disclose a complete, detailed personal calendar and often withheld private meeting times, his office did publish public schedules and event listings. Saying he "doesn't make his calendar public" ignores that public appearances were routinely posted even though comprehensive calendars were not.

claim: Says Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam said, ‘You will give up your guns, if you don’t I’ll have the National Guard cut your power, your phone lines, and your internet. Then, if you still refuse to comply I’ll have you killed.’"
rationale: This quotation is a fabrication; there is no record, transcript, audio, or credible news reporting showing Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam ever said anything like threatening to cut utilities or kill people to force gun turn-ins. Established fact-checkers and archives of Northam’s public remarks show he has advocated gun-safety measures but has not issued the claimed threat, which has circulated as a viral misattribution. The claim appears to originate from social media and political misinformation rather than any verifiable primary source.

claim: Says Josh Mandel bet against Ohio families
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Josh Mandel personally placed financial 'bets against Ohio families.' The wording resembles a political-ad accusation and no credible reporting documents specific trades or transactions showing he intentionally bet against Ohio families.

claim: "The EPA has tried to define a puddle or a drainage ditch on your farm to be navigable waters and thus subject to massive environmental regulations."
rationale: Federal agencies (EPA and the Army Corps) have in past rulemakings and guidance sought broad definitions of “waters of the United States” that would bring some small features—including certain ditches, ephemeral streams and wetlands—under the Clean Water Act. Those proposals triggered widespread concern by landowners that very small or intermittent features on farms could be regulated, though courts and later rulings limited the agencies’ reach.

claim: State budget cuts for local schools resulted in "nearly 4,000 educator layoffs"
rationale: The statement is unverified as written because it lacks any identifier of which state or what budget cycle produced the layoffs. Public reporting shows that state budget cuts have led to educator layoffs in some places, but the specific round figure “nearly 4,000 educator layoffs” cannot be confirmed without a named state and timeframe. Absent that context or a reliable source, the claim cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Says this photo shows Joe Biden kissing and biting a child on the cheek.
rationale: This claim is false. Available photographs and reporting show Biden leaning in to kiss or whisper to a child and do not provide evidence that he bit the child; credible fact-checks and contemporaneous reports have not corroborated any biting. The "biting" interpretation appears to come from a misleading angle or timing of the photo rather than an actual action.

claim: Says the case of a Texas judge who refused to perform heterosexual weddings exposes a double standard in the case against Kentucky clerk Kim Davis.
rationale: The claim is unsupported: Kim Davis was a county clerk who refused to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples after the Supreme Court’s Obergefell decision and was legally sanctioned; there is no well-documented, directly comparable Texas judge who refused only to perform heterosexual weddings and thereby created an established precedent showing a double standard. Reports about Texas officials typically described recusals or refusals affecting same-sex marriages or ceasing to perform all weddings, so the asserted parallel and resulting ‘double standard’ is not substantiated by the public record.

claim: "America’s least-trusted news sources are also its most popular."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. National surveys and audience-measurement data show that some widely used outlets or platforms (e.g., social media and partisan cable) are distrusted by many, but the least-trusted sources are not uniformly the top-ranked by overall audience; likewise, many of the most-watched news sources (local TV and network evening news) often command higher general trust. Thus popularity and trust do not map cleanly in the absolute way the claim asserts.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: The claim gives a definitive rank but omits a year and specific metric; available state-by-state rankings (such as those compiled by the Center for American Women and Politics) vary by year and by whether they count only state legislatures or include federal offices. I do not recall Georgia being 49th in the commonly cited recent composite rankings, and such rankings change over time. Without a cited year or source this precise numeric claim is not supported.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I cannot confirm a reputable, peer-reviewed economic impact study that specifically reports that every $1 invested in Pennsylvania pre-K generates $1.79 in total in-state spending. While numerous impact and input–output analyses find positive short-term spending multipliers from early childhood investment, reported multipliers vary by study, methodology, year and scope; the exact $1.79 figure appears to be an unverified or misattributed summary without the original source.

claim: "Phony" ballots "were printed without my name on it."
rationale: The statement is unverified and too vague: it asserts that "phony" ballots were printed without the speaker's name but gives no jurisdiction, time, or supporting evidence. Election ballots are typically produced by official election authorities with chain-of-custody and printing controls, and allegations of missing names require independent evidence (chain-of-custody, affidavits, or audits) which is not provided here. Without such corroboration this claim cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Says that politicians who approved collective bargaining restrictions for public employees "exploited a loophole exempting themselves from Senate Bill 5."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that politicians who approved Senate Bill 5 secretly 'exploited a loophole' to exempt themselves from its restrictions. The 2011 Ohio SB 5 broadly limited collective bargaining for many public employees but included explicit statutory exceptions for certain roles (as many such laws do); those were part of the bill text and widely reported, not a concealed self-exemption by vote proponents. The claim appears to conflate ordinary exemptions with an allegation of deliberate self-dealing without supporting specifics or documentation.

claim: "Before Congress, (Tom) Cotton got paid handsomely working for insurance companies and corporate interests."
rationale: Public biographies and reporting show Tom Cotton’s pre‑Congressional career centered on military service, Harvard Law education, and legal clerkships and short stints in private practice rather than a documented history of being a paid lobbyist for insurance companies. There is no clear evidence that he ‘got paid handsomely working for insurance companies and corporate interests’ as a primary pre‑Congress role; the claim appears to conflate generic private‑sector work with direct employment by insurers or corporate lobbying.

claim: "We could build 30 walls with the $150 billion Obama gave to Iran."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the Obama administration did not "give" Iran $150 billion in US cash. The JCPOA and related sanctions relief allowed Iran access to some frozen assets (estimates vary, commonly cited $50–150 billion) and the US separately settled a $1.7 billion claim, but most funds were foreign-held and not a direct US cash transfer. Moreover, "30 walls" is undefined — border-wall cost estimates vary widely, so a precise 30-wall calculation is unsupported.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum is running "from the FBI."
rationale: The claim implies Andrew Gillum was fleeing or evading the FBI; there is no public evidence he has run from or been on the run from federal agents. While Gillum and his associates were subject to an FBI probe after the 2018 Florida governor’s race, he was not reported to have fled investigators or been evading arrest.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no record in AOC’s verified tweets, speeches, or reputable news reports of her making this quote; it appears to be a fabricated social-media attribution. The phrasing (including a grammatical error) and the content praising an ISIS affiliate as "more of a hero than our veterans" is inconsistent with Ocasio-Cortez’s known public statements and was circulated as a meme rather than a verifiable quote.

claim: "Nancy Pelosi, Adam Schiff, and the rest of the corrupt Democrats made a promise to their crazy left-wing base that they would impeach me even BEFORE I took office."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi, Adam Schiff, or Democratic leadership publicly promised to impeach Trump before he took office. Pelosi publicly urged giving Trump a chance after the 2016 election, and formal impeachment proceedings against Trump did not begin until years into his presidency based on actions while in office. While some activists and fringe figures discussed impeachment pre-inauguration, that does not substantiate the broad claim about party leaders making a promise.

claim: Says "Donald Trump himself contributed $100,000" to the Clinton Foundation.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public donor record showing that Donald J. Trump or the Donald J. Trump Foundation gave $100,000 to the Clinton Foundation. Major fact-checkers and Clinton Foundation donor lists do not list such a gift, and Trump’s documented charitable giving does not include a $100,000 contribution to that foundation. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute other donations.

claim: Photo shows Rihanna is pregnant
rationale: A single photograph alone is not reliable proof that someone is pregnant. Visual cues (body shape, clothing, pose, or image editing) can be misleading, and pregnancy is normally confirmed by the person or credible sources rather than by photos. Without corroboration from a reputable announcement or multiple trustworthy reports, the claim is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: "If you want out of the individual mandate... all you have to do now is tick off the box that says 'hardship' and you're out."
"We jumped 11 places since beginning this year in terms of being job-friendly."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no subject (who is “we”), no named ranking or index, and no source or dates. Rank changes require a specific, published metric and data; absent that information there is no evidence to support the assertion, so I rate it false. If specific country/region and the ranking dataset were provided the claim could be checked.

claim: The Baucus health care bill "would drastically restrict the use of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) in order to help pay for health care reform."
rationale: The Baucus Senate Finance Committee health care draft included provisions that would limit tax-favored flexible spending account use (notably by capping annual FSA contributions) as part of the revenue offsets to finance reform. While it did not eliminate FSAs entirely, the proposed cap reduced the tax-advantaged amount people could set aside, which opponents reasonably described as a substantial restriction.

claim: Says author J.K. Rowling was the first billionaire to fall off Forbes billionaire list because of charitable giving.
rationale: While Forbes removed J.K. Rowling from its billionaire list (reportedly influenced by her charitable giving), she was not the first billionaire to disappear from Forbes due to philanthropy. Prominent donors such as Chuck Feeney gave away vast portions of their fortunes and fell off billionaire lists earlier, and historical records do not support the claim that Rowling was uniquely the first.

claim: Wisconsin was embroiled in a "constitutional crisis" brought on by the Democratic senators fleeing the state for Illinois to block Gov. Scott Walker's budget-repair bill.
rationale: In February–March 2011 fourteen Democratic Wisconsin state senators left the state (traveling to Illinois and elsewhere) to deny the Senate the two‑thirds quorum needed for certain fiscal actions, stalling Governor Scott Walker’s budget‑repair/collective bargaining measures. The move produced a prolonged interbranch standoff and was widely reported and debated at the time as a constitutional or legislative crisis because normal legislative procedures were rendered inoperative.

claim: "Registered Republican not allowed to vote."
rationale: The blanket claim that a “registered Republican [is] not allowed to vote” is false in general. Party registration does not bar someone from voting in general elections; it only affects primary participation in some states (closed primaries) and separate legal issues (felony disenfranchisement, removal from voter rolls, or declared incompetence) can prevent individuals from voting. Without a specific jurisdiction or case, the statement is incorrect as a general assertion.

claim: "So that 2005 energy bill was a big step backwards on the path to clean, renewable energy. That's why I voted against it."
rationale: The statement combines a subjective policy judgment (“a big step backwards”) with an unverifiable claim about the speaker’s vote without identifying who made it. The 2005 Energy Policy Act included both fossil-fuel favorable provisions (tax breaks, drilling incentives) and some support for nuclear and renewables, so whether it was a “big step backwards” is a matter of interpretation, and the claim about voting cannot be checked without the speaker’s identity and roll-call. Because key factual details are missing and the core claim is evaluative, the statement cannot be verified as true.

claim: Federal spending is "the highest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years (and) revenue is the lowest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years."
rationale: The first part (spending) is essentially correct: federal outlays surged in 2020 and were at levels not seen since World War II, making them unusually high as a share of GDP. The second part (revenue) is incorrect: federal receipts as a share of GDP were lower during the 2009 Great Recession than in the recent pandemic year, so revenues were not the lowest in 60 years. Because one of the two linked claims is false, the combined claim is false.

claim: The number of children in seven countries "missing so far this year" range from 20,000 to 460,000.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated and likely false: it gives a precise range (20,000–460,000) for 'children in seven countries missing so far this year' without naming the countries, the year, or a source. Official missing‑children figures vary widely by country, definition (e.g., missing vs. abducted vs. unaccompanied), and reporting period, and I could not confirm a reliable dataset showing exactly seven countries with counts in that specific range.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: There is no credible record, verified transcript, or reputable news source attributing this speech or that wording to Keanu Reeves. The line circulates on social media and quote sites but has not been traced to any of Reeves's known interviews, appearances, or speeches and has been flagged as a misattribution in prior checks. Given the lack of primary-source evidence, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "I investigated Abramoff and people ended up in jail."
rationale: Federal and congressional investigations into lobbyist Jack Abramoff produced multiple guilty pleas and prison sentences: Abramoff himself was convicted and imprisoned, his partner Michael Scanlon was convicted and jailed, and several public officials and aides (notably Rep. Bob Ney) pleaded guilty and received prison terms or criminal penalties. Thus the broad claim that an investigation of Abramoff led to people ending up in jail is accurate. The phrasing 'I investigated' is ambiguous about who conducted the probe, however.

claim: "While (Chris Christie) talks about job creation, we don't see jobs being created in this state."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no jobs were created in the state while Christie discussed job creation. That is contradicted by publicly reported employment data for the period of his tenure, which show net job gains in several years and declining unemployment at times. The statement overstates the case and ignores measurable job-creation episodes.

claim: "Before Leaving, Obama Enacts Rules to Take $3,000 From EVERY American."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Obama enacted any rule that took $3,000 from every American before leaving office. Such a sweeping, per-person confiscation would require legislation or widely reported executive action, and no credible news outlets or legislative records document such a measure. The claim matches patterns of viral misinformation or misinterpretation of unrelated policy changes.

claim: Says Virginia Republican "Scott Taylor has been convicted in at least four different courts across the country, at times failing to even appear, and having a warrant issued for his arrest."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Virginia Republican Scott Taylor has been criminally convicted in at least four different courts nationwide; major reporting and public records about the former congressman note civil judgments and disputes but do not document multiple criminal convictions or widespread arrest warrants. The claim appears to conflate unrelated civil cases, traffic citations or administrative issues with criminal convictions and warrants, which would have generated substantial media coverage.

claim: In Liberia, "a girl is more likely to be married by 18 than to know how to read."
rationale: Available demographic data for Liberia indicate that literacy among girls and young women (especially the 15–24 age group) is higher than the proportion married by 18. Surveys and UNESCO/World Bank indicators show youth female literacy rates substantially above the reported child‑marriage prevalence for Liberia, so the statement as a general national comparison is not supported.

claim: According to a recent CDC report, "almost everyone — 85% — who got the coronavirus in July was wearing a mask, and they were infected anyway. So clearly (wearing a mask) doesn’t work the way they tell us it works."
rationale: This is a misinterpretation/misrepresentation of CDC-related data. No CDC report concludes that 85% of people who got COVID-19 in July were wearing masks and therefore masks don’t work; at best some surveys report high self‑reported mask use among cases, but those data are confounded (self‑reporting, improper mask use, exposure in unmasked settings like households) and do not demonstrate that masks are ineffective. Public-health evidence and CDC guidance show mask use reduces transmission risk at the population and individual level when used properly.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation folded."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation has not ceased operations; it continues to exist, file tax returns, and run programs and events. While it has scaled back some activities and faced controversy, it did not 'fold' or shut down entirely.

claim: "More than half of last year's U.S. college graduates are unemployed or underemployed."
rationale: Official labor statistics and multiple independent studies show unemployment among recent U.S. college graduates is well below 50%, and most credible underemployment estimates for recent graduates fall below or around the 30–40% range; combining the two does not support a claim that more than half of last year’s graduates were unemployed or underemployed. While underemployment definitions vary and some short‑term or narrowly defined measures can be high, the blanket statement that over 50% of last year’s graduates are unemployed or underemployed is not supported by mainstream data.

claim: "Medicare does just as good, if not better, at keeping people healthy" as Medicare Advantage.
rationale: The evidence comparing traditional (Original) Medicare and Medicare Advantage is mixed and does not support the blanket claim that Original Medicare does "just as good, if not better" at keeping people healthy. Many studies find Medicare Advantage enrollees receive equal or higher rates of preventive services and have similar or better outcomes on measures like hospital readmissions and some quality metrics, though results vary by outcome, plan, and population. Because outcomes depend on measure selection, risk adjustment, selection effects, and plan variation, the general claim is not consistently true.

claim: Says a video shows Iranian rockets being launched toward U.S. airbases in Iraq.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified from a generic video alone and is therefore likely false as stated. Video footage without provenance, geolocation, metadata, or munitions identification cannot reliably show that rockets were launched by Iran or that their intended target was U.S. airbases in Iraq; such attributions require independent open-source or official confirmation. Many similar clips have been misattributed to Iran or to strikes on U.S. facilities in the past.

claim: "By any measure, New Jersey has one of the most segregated school systems in the country."
rationale: The claim is overly broad. While multiple studies (e.g., Civil Rights Project and census-based analyses) show New Jersey ranks near the top of states for certain measures of school segregation—particularly Black-white segregation and poverty/isolation indices—it is not true that it ranks as one of the most segregated “by any measure” across all metrics, populations, and years. Some measures and comparisons put other states higher or show variation by subgroup and time period.

claim: "From 1990 to 2015 under (Democratic) control, W. Va. teacher pay rank plummeted from 30th in the nation to 48th."
rationale: The core idea — West Virginia teacher pay fell relative to other states between 1990 and 2015 — is broadly correct, but the claim as stated is inaccurate. Published salary rankings (NEA/NCES) show a fall from roughly the 30s in the early 1990s to the mid‑to‑high 40s by the mid‑2010s, and West Virginia was not continuously under Democratic control for the entire 1990–2015 period (e.g., a Republican governor served 1997–2001 and the legislature flipped GOP in 2014). Because the control assertion and the exact rank numbers are misleading, the claim is false as presented.

claim: Says Jennifer Aniston said, "Me and all the Trump supporter celebrities decide to make a company named ‘celebrities for Trump’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence Jennifer Aniston ever said she and Trump-supporting celebrities formed a company called 'celebrities for Trump.' Aniston is publicly associated with liberal causes and has not endorsed Trump, and no reputable news or primary-source record supports this quote; it appears to be a fabrication or misattribution.

claim: Says "$30 million gap" in stadium funding forced the Portland Beavers to leave.
rationale: The Portland Beavers’ relocation in 2010–11 was driven by failure to secure a new or renovated baseball stadium and by the sale/relocation of the franchise, but contemporary reporting shows differing cost estimates and multiple factors (including PGE Park’s conversion for MLS). While owners cited a public funding shortfall, there is no single authoritative fact that a precisely "$30 million gap" alone forced the move — the figure is a simplification of disputed financing estimates. Thus the claim as stated is not fully accurate.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The claim asserts certainty that cameras will discourage robberies, but empirical research shows mixed effects: visible CCTV can deter some opportunistic crimes and aid identification/prosecution, yet it does not reliably prevent determined or masked offenders and effects vary by context and implementation. Therefore the absolute claim of certainty is unsupported.

claim: Atlanta Tea Party co-founder Debbie Dooley "wants gas taxes raised."
rationale: Debbie Dooley is a Tea Party activist and founder of Conservatives for Energy Freedom who has publicly argued for policies to lower gasoline prices (e.g., expanding domestic production and pipelines) and has opposed tax increases on fuel. There is no clear, corroborated record that she broadly advocates raising gas taxes, so the claim that she “wants gas taxes raised” is misleading or incorrect.

claim: The seven nations identified in Donald Trump's travel ban were "identified by the Obama administration as the seven most dangerous countries in the world in regard to harboring terrorists."
rationale: The seven countries in Trump’s 2017 travel ban (Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Yemen) were not officially labeled by the Obama administration as “the seven most dangerous countries” for harboring terrorists. While several of those countries had active terrorist groups, travel advisories, or were on various U.S. lists (e.g., State Sponsors of Terrorism, travel warnings), there was no Obama-era government ranking that identified these seven specifically as the seven most dangerous. The claim therefore misstates or invents an official Obama administration designation.

claim: America’s federal business tax rate is the highest "in the world."
rationale: This is false. After the 2017 tax reform the U.S. federal statutory corporate tax rate is 21%, and even when state-level corporate taxes are added the combined U.S. top statutory rate is not the highest globally. Numerous countries have higher statutory or combined corporate tax rates (and effective rates vary), so the U.S. is not the world leader by this measure.

claim: Says she is a registered nurse.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it gives no identity or supporting evidence—"she" is unspecified. Without a named individual and documentation (e.g., a nursing license, employer record, or official statement), I cannot confirm the assertion, so I default to FALSE per instruction to prefer false when uncertain.

claim: "The amount of money that we put into running our own state legislature is nearly as much as we put into the University of Rhode Island."
rationale: The operating budget for a state legislature is generally in the tens of millions of dollars, while the University of Rhode Island receives well over $100 million annually in state appropriations and has a much larger total budget when tuition and other revenues are included. Therefore the legislature's running costs are not "nearly as much" as the funding put into URI.

claim: "U.S. Department of Homeland Security has told banks -- in writing -- it may inspect safe deposit boxes without warrant and seize any gold, silver, guns or other valuables it finds inside those boxes!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Department of Homeland Security issued a written blanket instruction to banks allowing warrantless inspection and seizure of safe-deposit box contents. U.S. law generally requires a warrant or court order (or clear exigent/custodial exceptions) for searches and seizures of private property; while civil asset forfeiture and law-enforcement seizures can occur, they normally follow legal process rather than a unilateral DHS directive.

claim: "As we near the 10th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, we should not forget that some of the hijackers used New Jersey driver’s licenses to board those aircraft."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence in official investigations or widely accepted reporting that any of the 9/11 hijackers used New Jersey driver’s licenses to board the planes. The 9/11 Commission and subsequent reporting document that some hijackers obtained U.S. state IDs and driver’s licenses, but claims specifically naming New Jersey licenses are not supported by primary investigative records. Given ambiguity in popular accounts, the specific assertion about New Jersey IDs is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The Republican from Georgia [U.S. Rep. Jack Kingston], he hasn’t even been to a NASCAR race."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute fact (that Rep. Jack Kingston has never attended a NASCAR race) but there is no verifiable evidence to support such a categorical statement. Kingston served many years as a Republican congressman from Georgia, a state with strong NASCAR ties, and politicians from that region commonly attend racing events for constituent outreach; absent reliable documentation proving he never attended, the claim is implausible. Because the statement is absolute and unsubstantiated, it is judged false.

claim: "We have pay equity. When you think about that wage gap, we all know it's 78 cents to the dollar. Well, in New York state it's 90 cents to the dollar."
rationale: The numbers in the claim are not consistently accurate. The often-cited “78 cents” figure is an older national estimate and more recent Census/BLS measures of median annual earnings for full-time workers show women earn roughly 81–84 cents on the dollar, and New York’s gender pay ratio varies by year and definition and is not reliably 90 cents across standard measures. Thus the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
rationale: The claim combines an exaggerated factual assertion with an unsupported causal claim. Public data show year-to-year fluctuations in NFL TV ratings and generally stable in-person attendance rather than a consistent, dramatic collapse, and there is no reliable evidence that a large share of fans are skipping games primarily "because they love our country." The attribution of declines to patriotism is speculative and not supported by surveys or viewership analyses.

claim: Says "we are overcharging students . . . to help pay for the health care law."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as a general statement: there is no broad evidence that students are being systematically "overcharged" specifically to pay for the health care law. While some colleges have changed student health fees for a variety of reasons (insurance market changes, expanded services, administrative costs), attributing a widespread overcharge solely to the health care law is unsubstantiated without specific institutions, amounts, and documentation.

claim: Photo shows Kim Jong Un’s weight loss
rationale: A single photo is insufficient to prove an actual change in Kim Jong Un’s weight because posture, clothing, camera angle, lighting, and possible editing can create the appearance of weight loss. There is no independent medical confirmation or consistent, verified sequence of images publicly available that conclusively demonstrates the claimed weight loss from that photo alone.

claim: "Over 97 percent of the scientific community … believe that humans are contributing to climate change."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies find about 97% agreement that humans are the primary cause of recent global warming, but that figure refers specifically to climate scientists or to peer-reviewed climate science papers, not the entire "scientific community." Surveys of broader groups of scientists or the public show lower percentages and results depend on question wording and sampling. Therefore the claim as phrased (about the whole scientific community) is not supported.

claim: The federal government only ordered BP to pay "to do one of those six segments" of sand barriers for Louisiana.
rationale: This claim misstates the record from the Deepwater Horizon response. Federal agencies negotiated with BP and approved funding for multiple sand‑berm segments; the U.S. government did not issue an order that BP pay for only one of six segments. Public reporting and agency actions show the berm project involved several segments and negotiations over scope and funding rather than a single mandated payment for only one segment.

claim: Paul Ryan would "outlaw in vitro fertilization."
rationale: There is no clear public record of Paul Ryan explicitly saying he would outlaw in vitro fertilization or sponsoring legislation to ban IVF. While Ryan is a long-standing pro-life advocate who supports legal protections for embryos and restrictions on abortion, asserting he "would outlaw IVF" overstates the available evidence and attributes a specific policy action he has not publicly endorsed.

claim: Says Scott Walker rejected legislation to make college loan payments tax deductible and the result was "to raise taxes on students."
rationale: Rejecting a bill to create a new tax deduction does not itself raise taxes; it simply preserves the existing tax treatment by preventing a proposed cut. There is no evidence that Walker enacted a new tax specifically on students as a result — at most his veto or rejection denied them a potential tax break, which is not the same as increasing their tax burden above the prior baseline.

claim: "Hillary Clinton invented ISIS with her stupid policies. She is responsible for ISIS."
rationale: The claim is false. ISIS (Islamic State) evolved from Al‑Qaeda in Iraq (founded after the 2003 U.S. invasion) and expanded amid the 2011 Syrian civil war and sectarian Iraqi politics; it was not ‘invented’ by a single U.S. official. While Hillary Clinton supported certain foreign policy positions as Secretary of State, there is no credible evidence she created or is solely responsible for ISIS.

claim: "The national unemployment rate has been above 8 percent for a record 36 months."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated. For the U.S., the unemployment rate stayed above 8% for a longer continuous stretch during the Great Recession (roughly early 2009 through mid-2012, about 40+ months), so saying it has been above 8% for a record 36 months is not accurate. The statement also lacks a specified country and timeframe, which changes the evaluation.

claim: Says "Karen Handel’s office budget increased a whopping 42 percent."
rationale: The claim is misleading: public budget records and prior fact-checks do not support an unqualified 42% increase solely attributable to Karen Handel’s office. The cited percentage appears to conflate different funding streams and time periods (including one‑time grants/capital items) rather than showing a straightforward rise in the regular operating budget.

claim: A video shows "Dems caught not wearing masks" at the White House.
rationale: The claim is misleading and cannot be verified as stated. Publicly circulating clips purporting to show "Dems caught not wearing masks" at the White House lack context—mask policies changed over time and many videos show mixed-party groups or brief moments (e.g., for photos or eating) rather than a targeted rule-violating episode by Democrats alone. Without a specific, corroborated incident, the assertion that the video proves Democrats were uniquely caught not wearing masks is false.

claim: The federal deficit is "growing."
rationale: The claim lacks a timeframe or jurisdiction. U.S. deficits fell from the pandemic peak into 2022 but rose again in FY2023, and CBO projects deficits will grow over the coming decade; without a specified period the blanket statement 'is growing' is not reliably true as stated.

claim: Bill Nelson’s vote for the Affordable Care Act "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The Affordable Care Act included roughly $400–$500 billion in reductions to Medicare spending relative to prior projections (mainly from lower payments to Medicare Advantage plans and providers), but these were reductions in projected spending growth and payment rates—not a direct $500 billion cash cut taken out of Medicare benefits and handed over to "new government programs." While some savings helped finance coverage expansions and subsidies, it is inaccurate to say Nelson's vote simply "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
