Without a specific year, office, or citation showing the NRA grade and Farmer's stated claim, calling his statement an 'absolute lie' cannot be substantiated. Given the lack of confirmatory evidence in my knowledge, I rate the assertion as likely false but with low confidence.

claim: Says Marco Rubio took "three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives" during the 2016 Senate election.
rationale: Campaign finance records and public reporting do not support a clear, single-source payment of "three quarters of a million dollars" from fossil-fuel executives to Marco Rubio's 2016 Senate campaign. While Rubio received money from the energy sector (including PACs, company employees, and industry-affiliated donors), donors are reported by employer/industry and the claimed $750,000 figure for individual executives is not substantiated by FEC/OpenSecrets summaries or contemporaneous fact-checks. The claim appears to conflate different energy-industry contributions and types of donors (PACs, employees, bundlers) into a single, precise sum attributed to "executives."

claim: Says a California surfer was "alone, in the ocean," when he was arrested for violating the state’s stay-at-home order.
rationale: Contemporary news reports and official statements indicate the surfer was contacted and detained after coming ashore and was not literally arrested while alone in the water. Witnesses and police noted other people were present on the beach and officers boarded the shore to detain him, so the claim that he was "alone, in the ocean," at the moment of arrest is misleading and incorrect.

claim: "The average life expectancy for African Americans in Saint Louis and Saint Louis County varies by as much as 18 years compared to the white population, with nearly half of all African-American kids under the age of 18 living in poverty."
rationale: Contemporary public‑health analyses of St. Louis neighborhoods and countywide data document very large racial life‑expectancy gaps — reports and maps have shown differences of roughly up to about 18 years between predominantly Black and predominantly white neighborhoods in the St. Louis area. Census and local poverty statistics likewise show extremely high child poverty rates for African‑American children in St. Louis (city and parts of the county), on the order of nearly one‑half in many summaries and datasets.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was asked repeatedly to provide security in Benghazi on several occasions, including direct cables."
rationale: Multiple State Department cables and other communications from U.S. personnel in Benghazi requested enhanced security on several occasions in the months before the 2012 attack, and oversight reports documented those repeated requests. While many of the cables were routed through State Department channels that reach senior leadership, it is less certain whether Secretary Clinton personally read every message.

claim: "(Texas Republicans) believe in abolishing Social Security, abolishing V.A. health care."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. While some Texas GOP activists and elements of past state party platforms have endorsed privatization or major reform of Social Security and supported shifting VA services toward private-care options, it is not accurate to say Texas Republicans as a whole uniformly ‘believe in abolishing’ Social Security and VA health care. Many elected Texas Republicans and voters support preserving veterans’ benefits and Social Security in some form.

claim: "Texas mothers are dying during childbirth at the highest rates in the nation."
rationale: This is not accurate as an absolute statement. Texas has had elevated maternal mortality and notable reporting artefacts (a spike after adopting a pregnancy checkbox on death certificates), but it has not consistently had the highest maternal-death rate in the U.S.; other states (for example Louisiana) have reported higher maternal mortality ratios in many official datasets and rankings depend on year and measurement method.

claim: Says Russ Feingold supported a stimulus plan that allowed a company to create 3,000 jobs in China.
rationale: This claim is unsupported by available evidence. While Russ Feingold voted for the 2009 economic stimulus (ARRA), that law did not contain provisions that specifically enabled or funded a firm to create 3,000 jobs in China, and there is no documented link showing Feingold’s vote directly caused a company to hire 3,000 workers in China. The claim appears to conflate general support for stimulus with unrelated corporate decisions to offshore jobs.

claim: Says Baltimore police are "trained by Mossad and Shin Bet."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Baltimore Police Department as an institution is trained by Israel’s intelligence agencies Mossad or Shin Bet. While some U.S. police departments have occasionally used private trainers or exchanged practices with Israeli security professionals, formal training by foreign intelligence services would be highly unusual and has not been substantiated for Baltimore. The claim appears to conflate private or former-Israeli personnel involvement with direct training by those agencies.

claim: Sarah Palin "already has more executive experience" than Barack Obama and Joe Biden "combined."
rationale: Sarah Palin’s executive service (Wasilla mayor ~1996–2002 and Alaska governor 2006–2009, roughly 8–9 years total) is less than the combined presidential terms of Barack Obama (8 years as president) and Joe Biden (4+ years as president as of 2025). Even if one disputed whether the vice presidency is an executive-post in the same sense, Biden’s presidential time alone plus Obama’s totals well exceed Palin’s executive time. Therefore the claim is false.

claim: "In 1960, most black children were raised in two-parent, monogamous families." Today "we have only 20 percent of black children being raised in two-parent, monogamous families..."
rationale: Historical U.S. Census data show that a clear majority of Black children lived with two married parents in 1960, so the first part is broadly correct. However, the contemporary share of Black children living with two parents is substantially higher than 20%—most reputable sources (Census/Pew analyses) put it in the ~30–45% range depending on whether cohabiting couples are counted—so the claim that only 20% are raised in two-parent monogamous families today is inaccurate.

claim: "Over the last 40 years, real wage growth has been flatlined because of the policies of the Federal Reserve ... It was all driven by the Federal Reserve."
rationale: The claim that real wage growth over the last 40 years was flat and that this outcome was "all driven" by Federal Reserve policy is incorrect. While median real wage growth has been weak for many workers since the 1970s–1980s, numerous structural factors (globalization, technological change, declining union power, policy choices on taxation/minimum wage, and changes in labor market institutions) explain much of the trend; monetary policy affects inflation and cyclical unemployment but is not the sole or primary driver of multi-decade wage distribution and productivity-wage divergence. Thus attributing the entire 40-year pattern to the Fed overstates monetary policy’s causal role.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker is making voting more difficult by closing Department of Motor Vehicles offices where "low-income voters" live.
rationale: While Wisconsin under Gov. Scott Walker did make budgetary changes that included consolidating or reducing DMV services, there is not clear, documented evidence that offices were closed specifically to target ‘low-income voters’ or to directly make voting harder. DMV closures can indirectly affect access to voter ID, but claims of intentional targeting and a direct causal effort to suppress votes are not substantiated by authoritative reporting or official documents. The statement conflates potential disparate impacts with proven intent and targeted policy placement.

claim: "House Bill 6627 also requires the applicant to attest to their eligibility to vote, as is required by the National Voter Registration Act and used by all other states that have (automatic voter registration)."
rationale: This claim is overbroad and not verifiable as stated. The National Voter Registration Act’s federal form does include an attestation of eligibility, and many automatic voter registration (AVR) programs incorporate some form of applicant affirmation, but state AVR implementations vary. I cannot confirm that the unspecified House Bill 6627 in question actually contains that specific attestation requirement, nor that every other AVR state uses the identical attestation mechanism described.

claim: Says a new report shows the "devastating tax hikes (in the health care law) will have on middle-class Kentuckians."
rationale: The statement that a new report shows “devastating tax hikes” on middle‑class Kentuckians is misleading. The major tax changes in the federal Affordable Care Act primarily targeted higher‑income households (e.g., 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax and 3.8% net investment income tax) and certain industries (insurer and medical device taxes), not broad middle‑class wage earners; any pass‑through effects on premiums do not substantiate a blanket claim of ‘devastating tax hikes’ on the middle class. Without a named report showing clear, direct, widespread middle‑class tax increases in Kentucky, the claim overstates the law’s tax impact.

claim: More than 500,000 mail in ballots in Virginia and 200,000 in Nevada were sent to dead people or pets
rationale: Independent fact‑checks and statements from state election officials found no evidence that Virginia mailed over 500,000 ballots to deceased people or that Nevada mailed 200,000 to dead people or pets. Large mailings did occur to registered or inactive voters ahead of recent elections, but the numbers of mailings actually sent to known deceased registrants or to non‑humans were far smaller and often the result of outdated rolls or clerical errors rather than massive fraudulent mailings. The claim conflates different lists and inflates isolated errors into implausibly large totals.

claim: "Some even advocate wiping out 401(k)s entirely and replacing them with government-run accounts."
rationale: The claim is accurate in the sense that a number of economists, policy advocates, and some politicians have proposed eliminating or radically restructuring private 401(k) plans in favor of government-run retirement accounts. Those proposals have appeared in policy papers, op-eds, and legislative suggestions as a way to reduce costs, improve retirement security, or simplify savings. This is not a description of mainstream enacted policy, but it correctly reports that such advocacy exists.

claim: Says he could be "the first president in modern history to be outspent."
rationale: The statement is misleading and likely incorrect: U.S. history includes multiple instances where sitting presidents or incumbents were outspent by challengers, so calling someone "the first president in modern history to be outspent" is not supported without a precise definition of "modern history." The claim also lacks necessary context (who "he" is and the time period), so as stated it is not a factual claim.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which election or what metric of "closeness" is being used; without that context one cannot determine whether the result was unusual compared with historical margins. Claims about an election’s closeness require specific vote margins, turnout, and a historical baseline to compare against, none of which are provided. Therefore I treat the unqualified claim as false until clarified or supported with data.

claim: "Faced with $1 million in campaign debt," Scott Walker "is unloading his campaign security costs onto the backs of Wisconsin taxpayers."
rationale: The claim asserts Walker purposely shifted campaign security costs to Wisconsin taxpayers because of $1 million in campaign debt. Publicly available rules and reporting indicate that the state pays for official gubernatorial security, while campaigns are generally responsible for security at campaign events, and there is no clear, documented evidence that Walker systematically offloaded campaign security bills onto taxpayers to retire campaign debt. At best this is a misleading conflation of routine state security for official duties with campaign expenses.

claim: "Many Nevadans relied on Uber for work, but after accepting $70,000 from taxi companies, Catherine Cortez Masto went after Uber ... (driving) them out of town."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Catherine Cortez Masto accepted exactly $70,000 from taxi companies and then personally led an effort to 'drive Uber out of town.' While Nevada officials and regulators debated and enacted rules affecting ride‑hail services, campaign finance records do not clearly support the specific $70,000 payment or the causal claim that her actions single‑handedly expelled Uber from Nevada. The claim conflates regulatory debates and routine contributions into a direct quid pro quo that is not supported by public records.

claim: "We now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and, as stated, is not generally true. Worldwide and in major economies the oil and gas industry (upstream, midstream, downstream and services) still supports more jobs overall than solar, although solar employment has grown rapidly and in some localities or specific categories (e.g., installers vs. oil extraction) solar employment may exceed certain oil subsectors. Without a specified country, year, and definitions of “oil” the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "Biden is computer generated."
rationale: This is false: Joe Biden is a living human being with decades of public records, verified identity documents, and countless in-person appearances and interactions that corroborate his existence. While images or video of him can be digitally manipulated or deepfaked, that does not make the person himself computer-generated.

claim: "There's not a single, solitary example that" signing the bill to end Glass-Steagall "had anything to do with the financial crash."
rationale: The claim is false: the repeal of key Glass–Steagall restrictions in the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act (1999) has been widely cited by investigators and economists as a contributing factor to the 2007–2008 crisis because it allowed commercial banks to affiliate with investment banking activities and grow large exposures to mortgage-backed securities. Concrete examples include Citigroup’s expansion into securities and Bank of America’s acquisition of Merrill Lynch, both of which produced large losses and required government support; major investigations (e.g., the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission) and many academic studies identify the erosion of Glass–Steagall as one of multiple contributing causes.

claim: Says the U.S. Postal Service has taken no taxpayer aid since 1971, funds operations entirely from the sale of stamps and related products and makes an "operational profit year after year."
rationale: The claim is not accurate. Although the Postal Service is intended to be self‑funded and generally does not receive annual appropriations for routine operations, it has received targeted federal appropriations, emergency loans/support and statutory reimbursements at times, and it has reported operating losses in many recent years rather than making an "operational profit year after year" (losses largely driven by a 2006 prefunding mandate for retiree health benefits).

claim: "Not even Tim Kaine is willing" to say he trusts Hillary Clinton.
rationale: False. Tim Kaine, Hillary Clinton's 2016 running mate, publicly expressed trust and support for Clinton on the campaign trail and in media interviews; he did not categorically refuse to say he trusted her. The absolutist phrasing "Not even Tim Kaine is willing" contradicts his repeated public endorsements and statements of confidence in her.

claim: Says Bill O’Reilly spoke 40 percent of the words in an interview with President Barack Obama.
rationale: There is no reliable, broadly accepted transcript analysis showing O’Reilly spoke 40% of the words in any high-profile interview with President Obama. Publicly available transcripts and media analyses of their notable interviews indicate Obama’s share of words was larger; the 40% figure appears to be an unverified claim that depends on choice of episode and counting method.

claim: "Most" of the Bush tax cuts went to people "in the top 3 percent of this country."
rationale: Nonpartisan analyses of the 2001/2003 Bush tax cuts find the benefits were tilted toward higher-income households but the top 3% did not receive a majority (>50%) of total dollar benefits. Instead a large share went to the entire top quintile or top decile, with the top few percent receiving a substantial but not majority portion. Different studies and measurement methods change exact shares, but none support that most of the cuts went solely to the top 3%.

claim: "Our state economic development agency under Walker, WEDC, actually isn’t even using the funds that are appropriated to it."
rationale: The statement that WEDC 'isn’t even using the funds that are appropriated to it' is not supported by available evidence. Under Governor Walker, the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation disbursed grants, loans and operated programs using appropriated funds, and state audits and budget documents show expenditures and commitments rather than a wholesale refusal to use appropriations. While WEDC faced criticism and audit findings about oversight, compliance, and some misspending, those findings do not equate to the agency not using its appropriated funds.

claim: Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas said: ‘Hey, all you wrinkly, white-aged has-beens: It’s time for you to die and let the next generation have your spot on the planet.’
rationale: There is no credible record — no mainstream news reports, congressional transcript, or verifiable video — showing Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee ever saying that quote. Such an incendiary remark by a sitting member of Congress would have been widely reported and archived, but searches of reputable sources and public records turn up no instance of it. The phrasing resembles viral misattributions or satirical fabrications rather than a documented remark.

claim: Says "Former President Barack Obama arrested for ESPIONAGE."
rationale: This is false. There are no credible news reports, Department of Justice filings, or reliable public records indicating that former President Barack Obama was arrested or charged with espionage; such an action against a former president would be major, widely reported news. The claim matches patterns of hoaxes, satire, or conspiracy posts rather than verified reporting.

claim: It's "not true" that since he's been the president, executions in Iran have increased by four times.
rationale: Independent human-rights monitors and reporting since August 2021 document a sharp, multi-fold rise in executions in Iran compared with the immediate prior period; several organizations and news reports characterized the increase as roughly three- to four-fold in the years after this president took office. Therefore the blanket statement that "it’s not true" that executions increased four times is incorrect. Variation exists by exact baseline years and counting methods, but the overall trend is a substantial increase.

claim: "Kelly Ayotte voted to give big oil more than $20 billion in tax breaks."
rationale: There is no clear legislative record showing Kelly Ayotte cast a single identifiable vote that directly ‘gave big oil more than $20 billion in tax breaks.’ Ayotte did vote for some tax and budget bills that contained provisions benefiting the energy sector, but the claim packages those diffuse provisions into a single >$20 billion gift without a specific bill, time frame, or authoritative scoring linking her vote to that total. Absent a named bill and a CBO or scoring estimate that attributes $20+ billion to provisions she supported, the statement is misleading.

claim: Says the Obamas are connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack or Michelle Obama were connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal. The DOJ investigation and indictments named Rick Singer, a number of parents, coaches, and college administrators, and extensive media reporting does not include the Obamas. Claims tying the Obamas to the scandal appear to be unsupported misinformation.

claim: "Under the federal Controlled Substance Act, marijuana is listed in the same Schedule I as heroin," even though "marijuana is not a killer drug like heroin."
rationale: The federal Controlled Substances Act currently places cannabis (marijuana) in Schedule I, the same schedule that includes heroin. Heroin is well documented to cause frequent fatal overdoses and high addiction risk, whereas marijuana has not been shown to cause fatal overdoses and is generally considered far less acutely lethal, so the comparison is factually supported though simplified.

claim: "Under @BarackObama illegal immigration dropped to a 50-year low."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While illegal immigration flows and the estimated unauthorized-immigrant population fell from a post-2007 peak during the Obama years, the unauthorized population did not fall to a 50-year low, and whether a multi-decade low occurred depends on which metric (e.g., Border Patrol apprehensions vs. population estimates) and year you pick. The claim overstates and lacks the necessary metric and timeframe to be true as written.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The statement is misleading as phrased. Historical employment data and contemporary fact-checks show the post-2008 job recovery was unusually slow compared with post–World War II recoveries, but it is not accurate to say it was the slowest since the Hoover/Great Depression era without specifying metrics or time windows; the 1930s decline and recovery were uniquely severe. Thus the blanket claim overstates the comparison.

claim: "We had 6,000 oil and gas spills in 2012" with "more oil and gas spreading in the United States than the entire Exxon Valdez spill."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions that are not supported by authoritative records. While there were thousands of reported oil- and gas-related incidents in various 2012 datasets and news summaries, the precise figure “6,000” as a definitive national total for 2012 is not corroborated by single authoritative federal summaries, and the vast majority of reported incidents are very small. Likewise, the Exxon Valdez spill released roughly 10–11 million gallons; regulator-compiled incident volumes for 2012 do not clearly show a single-year, nationwide confirmed total of released oil/gas exceeding that amount when accounting for reporting thresholds and types of releases.

claim: "One in 19 Americans today get SSDI or SSI. That's one in 19 Americans (who) are disabled."
Says a picture he posted on Facebook of a man posing in front of five decapitated human heads is "one of the subhuman mongrels our president set free."
rationale: The assertion reports a specific quoted Facebook post but gives no name, date, screenshot, or other verifiable source. Such an inflammatory and graphic post would likely have been documented by major outlets or archived, yet no corroborating evidence is provided here, making the claim unverified and judged false in this context. Without specific identifying information it cannot be reliably confirmed.

claim: "Iraq is costing each household about $100 a month."
rationale: The statement is unqualified and therefore misleading — costs of Iraq depend on which country’s households are meant, the time period, and which expenditures (direct military spending, veterans’ care, interest, reconstruction) are included. Different reputable estimates (CBO, academic projects) produce widely varying per-household monthly figures, so a blanket claim that it is “about $100 a month” without specification is not supportable.

claim: Says Barack Obama "founded ISIS. I would say the co-founder would be crooked Hillary Clinton."
Says Republican lieutenants to House Speaker Joe Straus "aired radio ads supporting Democrat(ic state Rep.) Mark Homer... helping the Democrat to a narrow win."
"State revenue projections have missed the mark month after month."
"Why was there no news coverage of this raid on the Arizona border? … Seizure was just five days ago. Right on the Arizona border!"

"In the past year, Floridians, not government, created almost 135,000 new private sector jobs. We netted more than 120,000 total jobs in the first 11 months of 2011; the third most of any state in the nation."
Says Governor Cooper has vetoed "every single teacher pay raise we've ever passed."
rationale: The absolute claim that Governor Cooper vetoed “every single teacher pay raise” is incorrect. Since becoming governor he has both signed some measures that raised teacher pay and vetoed other budget bills, so the record is mixed rather than a universal pattern of vetoing all pay raises. The claim’s categorical wording is therefore false.

claim: Says Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Democratic lawmakers are "granting free tuition to illegal immigrants while closing Excelsior Scholarship applications to citizen students."
rationale: There is no evidence New York ‘‘closed’’ Excelsior Scholarship applications to citizen students while exclusively granting free tuition to undocumented immigrants. New York has expanded some state financial-aid access for certain undocumented residents, but Excelsior remained governed by residency, income, enrollment and application rules and any pauses or limits were fiscal and affected all applicants rather than blocking citizens. The claim misstates policy scope and timing.

claim: "For more than 80 years, there has not been a nomination and confirmation of a Supreme Court Justice in a presidential election year. This is simply not the time to break with decades of bipartisan practice."
rationale: Historical records show the last time both the nomination and Senate confirmation of a Supreme Court Justice occurred within a presidential election year was in 1940 (Frank Murphy), which is more than 80 years ago. Since then there have been nominations in election years (e.g., Merrick Garland in 2016) or confirmations in election years following earlier nominations, but not both actions within the same presidential election year.

claim: Chris "Sununu supported Obama’s Common Core agenda, taking away local control of our schools."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. Common Core was a state-led set of standards that the Obama administration encouraged through incentives (eg. Race to the Top), rather than a direct federal takeover, and Chris Sununu has publicly positioned himself as favoring local control and has criticized federal overreach on education rather than endorsing an Obama-led takeover. The statement conflates federal incentive policies with a direct ‘taking away’ of local control and mischaracterizes Sununu’s record.

claim: "BREAKING: Queen Elizabeth II Dead At 94"
rationale: This is inaccurate: Queen Elizabeth II died on 8 September 2022 and was 96 years old at the time, not 94. The death was announced by Buckingham Palace and widely reported by major news organizations, and her birth date (21 April 1926) confirms her age of 96 at death.

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: The statement mixes different government lists and presents an imprecise, misleading claim. The U.S. “no‑fly” list is intended to prevent boarding commercial flights, but the frequently cited figure of “more than 2,000” refers to people on broader terrorism-related watchlists (not specifically the no‑fly list) and reporting on gun purchases by watchlisted individuals has varied by dataset and time period. Because the claim conflates lists and lacks clear sourcing or timeframe, it is not accurate as written.

claim: Photos show "Ukrainian Christians pray outdoors, in the snow, for their country in this phase of war danger."
rationale: The claim asserts that photos depict Ukrainian Christians praying outdoors in the snow for their country during the current phase of war, but no images or provenance are provided to verify date, location or who is pictured. While similar scenes have been photographed in Ukraine, images are often miscaptioned or reused from different times/places, so this specific assertion cannot be confirmed. Without original images and metadata the claim is unverified and therefore rated false.

claim: Says "New Jersey’s $1 billion horse racing industry … employs 13,000 individuals and ensures the preservation of 176,000 acres of horse farmland."
rationale: The figures (about $1 billion in economic impact, ~13,000 jobs, and ~176,000 acres) correspond to New Jersey’s broader equine industry in state reports, not specifically the horse racing sector. The claim misattributes statewide equine-industry totals to “horse racing” alone and overstates that these numbers are a direct guarantee of land preservation.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on abortion.
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly identified as pro‑choice during his 1994 Massachusetts governor campaign but later adopted a pro‑life stance in his 2008 and 2012 presidential campaigns and as a senator, changing votes and public statements on abortion. Those documented shifts in position are widely characterized as a political flip‑flop.

claim: Says Mike DeWine "flip-flopped on the gun issue and has earned an F from the NRA."
rationale: The statement bundles two claims (a ‘flip‑flop’ and an NRA ‘F’ grade) that aren’t supported as presented. Mike DeWine has a long record of pro‑gun votes earlier in his career but as governor backed limited gun‑safety measures after 2019, which opponents call a flip‑flop; that characterization is subjective. Public record and common NRA scorecards do not clearly show the NRA assigning him a formal overall “F” rating, so the blanket claim as stated is not supported.

claim: The Republican replacement for Obamacare does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans.
rationale: Major Republican proposals to replace the Affordable Care Act (for example the 2017 AHCA and related Senate bills) included repeal or reduction of ACA-related taxes (such as the net investment income tax and additional Medicare surtax) and other provisions that analyses found disproportionately benefited high-income households. Independent assessments by the Congressional Budget Office and tax-policy analysts concluded those changes produced sizable tax savings for wealthy Americans, so the blanket claim that the replacement “does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans” is incorrect.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Rep. Bob Dold "continues to side with his Republican leadership and the NRA in blocking consideration of a bill that would keep firearms out of the hands of people on the terrorist watch list."
rationale: The claim asserts Rep. Bob Dold was actively siding with GOP leadership and the NRA to block consideration of a specific 'terrorist watch list' firearms bill. Public roll-call and reporting around the relevant debates show leadership and the NRA opposed some "No Fly/No Buy" proposals, but there is not clear evidence that Dold personally led or consistently voted to block consideration; his record on guns is mixed and he supported some gun-safety measures at times. Because the statement presents a definitive partisan coordination claim without a specific vote or date tying Dold to a blocking action, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: Hillary Clinton "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her."
rationale: The statement presents a precise nationwide figure without citation or context. Public-opinion measurements of Hillary Clinton’s support or unfavorability have varied across polls, times, and question wordings, so there is no single established fact that she “starts off with 47 percent of the country against her.” At best some individual polls at certain moments showed about 47% unfavorable, but that does not validate the blanket claim as stated.

claim: "Mass media destroyed! Blackout for mass arrests event!"
rationale: The claim that the "mass media destroyed" and there was a "blackout for mass arrests event" is unsubstantiated. There are no credible reports or evidence of a coordinated destruction of mass media outlets or a widespread blackout enacted to facilitate mass arrests; mainstream news organizations and independent outlets continued reporting. The phrasing also resembles a rallying slogan rather than a factual report, and extraordinary events of this scale would have multiple verifiable sources.

claim: "Over 65% of the country believes that (the) 2020 election was fraudulent. That number was around 35% a year ago."
rationale: No reputable national poll showed more than 65% of all U.S. adults believing the 2020 election was fraudulent; most national surveys found roughly 30–45% of all adults endorsing fraud claims, while much higher percentages occur only within the Republican subset. The claim’s second part (about ~35% a year ago) roughly matches some earlier national estimates, but conflating a party subgroup with the whole country makes the overall statement misleading.

claim: "Mayor Bloomberg was busy blaming African Americans and Latinos for the housing crisis in 2008."
rationale: There is no reputable record that Mayor Michael Bloomberg publicly blamed African Americans and Latinos for the 2008 housing crisis. Contemporary reporting and his public statements attributed the crisis to subprime lending, mortgage-backed securities, lax regulation, and financial institutions rather than blaming minority communities. Without a specific quote or reliable source, the claim appears to be an unfounded or misattributed accusation.

claim: Says science shows the physiological effects of wearing masks include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shortness of breath, toxicity and increased muscle tension.
rationale: This claim is false because numerous peer-reviewed studies and public-health agencies report that routine use of surgical and cloth masks (and most respirators in healthy people) does not cause clinically significant hypoxemia or hypercapnia; oxygen saturation and CO2 measurements generally remain within normal ranges. While some individuals report subjective shortness of breath, discomfort, or increased breathing effort (especially with tight-fitting respirators), these subjective effects are not the same as documented systemic toxicity or widespread low oxygen/high CO2.

claim: Say Bernie Sanders "won Nevada after all."
rationale: The claim provides no timeframe and thus is ambiguous. Bernie Sanders lost the 2016 Nevada Democratic caucuses to Hillary Clinton, but he did win the Nevada Democratic caucuses in 2020—so saying simply that he "won Nevada after all" is misleading without specifying the year.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: Broadly true for the United States: violent crime rates fell for roughly three decades after the early 1990s, then rose again around 2019–2021. FBI and mortality data show murders (homicides) jumped sharply during the 2020 pandemic year (about a 25–30% increase from 2019), so an increase of more than 20% over a short two‑year span is supported by official counts.

claim: The "state bureaucracy" Jane Norton managed "grew by $43 million in just three years."
rationale: The claim is misleading and unsupported: Jane Norton served as Colorado lieutenant governor, a largely ceremonial post without direct control of a single large “state bureaucracy” whose budget she could unilaterally expand by $43 million in three years. Publicly available records and standard descriptions of the lieutenant governor’s office show small operating budgets for that office and that major departmental budget changes are enacted through the governor and legislature, not a lieutenant governor managing a standalone bureaucracy.

claim: A Mack Trucks employee told Joe Biden, "You can’t drive anything besides the country into the ground."
rationale: There is no credible contemporaneous reporting or verifiable video showing a Mack Trucks employee telling Joe Biden the quoted line. The phrase appears to be a social-media paraphrase or fabrication that isn’t corroborated by reputable news outlets or primary footage from Biden’s events. Given the lack of evidence, the claim is likely false.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "opposes faster broadband internet in small towns" and "got nearly $90,000 in campaign contributions from the telecom special interests."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Sen. Johnson has opposed specific federal subsidies, regulatory changes, and some municipal broadband initiatives favored by telecom critics, but he has not credibly argued against ‘faster broadband’ in small towns as a general goal. The contribution figure is roughly in the right ballpark over multiple cycles (telecom companies and workers have donated on the order of tens of thousands of dollars to his campaigns), but the claim bundles a vague policy position and a loosely framed dollar amount into a definitive accusation, which overstates and mischaracterizes his record.

claim: Quotes Albert Einstein as saying "I fear the day technology will surpass human interaction. The world will have a generation of idiots."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence (writings, speeches, or contemporaneous records) that Albert Einstein ever said or wrote this line; it first appears in modern internet memes and social-media posts. Fact-checkers and scholarship on Einstein's quotations have traced the sentence to later online fabrications rather than any verifiable Einstein source.

claim: "In 2011, (Debbie) Wasserman Schultz missed 62 congressional votes — one of the worst records of any member of Congress."
rationale: Official roll-call records and contemporary news/fact-check reports show Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz missed 62 House votes in the 2011 calendar year. That total was among the larger numbers of missed votes by members that year (though it was not the single highest), so the statement is accurate though slightly imprecise in absolute ranking.

claim: The employer mandate "affects only 5 percent of businesses in this country."
rationale: This is essentially correct in ordinary usage: the Affordable Care Act employer mandate applies to firms with 50 or more full‑time‑equivalent employees, and only about 5% of employer firms meet that size threshold. The statement is nonetheless potentially misleading because those firms employ a large share of private‑sector workers and other rules (aggregation, subsidiaries) can change applicability.

claim: The Biden administration’s American Jobs Plan will be "the biggest non-defense investment in research and development in the history of our country."
rationale: This is a promotional claim about a future outcome rather than a verifiable historical fact. The American Jobs Plan included large proposed R&D spending (on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars in headlines), but historical federal non‑defense R&D outlays — especially when inflation‑adjusted and counting major past programs like the 1960s space/health research build‑ups — have been larger, so the assertion that it would be the largest ever is not supported as a factual guarantee.

claim: Charlie Crist stopped "layoffs of some 20,000 school teachers during the global economic meltdown."
rationale: There is no solid, contemporaneous evidence that Charlie Crist personally 'stopped layoffs of some 20,000 school teachers.' During the 2008–09 recession Crist used federal stimulus (ARRA) money and state actions to shore up education funding and likely reduced or delayed some education job losses, but the specific claim that he prevented roughly 20,000 teacher layoffs is an unsubstantiated or exaggerated figure. Reports at the time referenced varying numbers of education jobs saved or supported, not a verified count of 20,000 teacher layoffs averted attributable solely to Crist.

claim: "Newgard owed more than $13,000 for unpaid taxes on his $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex."
rationale: I could not find credible reporting or public records confirming that any person named Newgard owed more than $13,000 in unpaid taxes on a $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex. The claim omits a first name and time frame, and publicly available local tax and news records through my knowledge cutoff do not support that specific assertion. Given the lack of verifiable evidence, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Supreme Court issues its first bench warrant ever."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: supreme courts (including the U.S. Supreme Court and many national high courts) have long exercised contempt powers and have issued arrest/bench-warrant-like orders historically. Saying the Court issued its "first bench warrant ever" ignores prior instances of courts ordering arrests or warrants for contempt or failure to comply. Without a specific jurisdiction and timeframe the "first ever" assertion is implausible.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke is "the only candidate to the U.S. Senate to call for" impeaching President Donald Trump.
Says new figures he released showing Wisconsin job gains for 2011 are "the final job numbers."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks who “he” is and provides no source for the quote. In general, official job totals for a year are produced and periodically revised by state and federal labor agencies, so an unsourced statement that privately released 2011 figures are the “final job numbers” is not reliably supported. Without a specific speaker and citation, the assertion that someone legitimately labeled those figures as final is unproven.

claim: Says Bruce Poliquin "voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance."
rationale: Poliquin did vote for Republican health-care repeal measures in 2017 that nonpartisan analysts said would increase the uninsured, but there is no authoritative, contemporaneous estimate showing his vote directly 'stripped 117,000 Mainers of their insurance.' State- and federal models projected varying losses over different timeframes, so stating the precise figure as a direct result of his single vote is misleading and unsupported by a clear source.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: There is no verifiable public reporting or hospital confirmation that a 13‑year‑old in Halifax went into critical care because her heart stopped immediately after receiving a vaccine. While very rare cardiac events (e.g., myocarditis) have been associated with some vaccines in adolescents, claims of immediate cardiac arrest require independent medical confirmation and are often unsubstantiated when circulated without sources. Without named sources, dates, or a hospital statement, the causal assertion is not supported by available evidence.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's Iran nuclear deal "lined the pockets of the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism with your money."
rationale: I could not verify that Hillary Clinton specifically said the exact line quoted. While Clinton and many critics argued the Iran nuclear deal freed significant Iranian funds and posed risks, this exact phrasing appears to be a paraphrase or rhetoric used by opponents rather than a documented direct quote from Clinton. Absent a clear source attributing those precise words to her, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Says "Obama’s deadliest cover-up (in an explosion that killed 29 miners) has been uncovered" by internal government documents.
rationale: The claim appears to refer to the Upper Big Branch mine explosion (April 2010) that killed 29 miners, which was investigated by the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) and the Department of Justice; those official investigations found extensive violations by the mine operator Massey Energy and led to fines and criminal charges. There is no credible evidence that the Obama administration orchestrated or concealed a “deadliest cover-up,” and official internal reports and prosecutions were publicly released and reported. The assertion of an Obama-directed cover-up is unsupported by the available investigation records and mainstream reporting.

claim: "Never mind that no red light camera, no speed camera, nor any radar gun has ever stopped one accident from occurring."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that is contradicted by empirical evidence. Numerous peer-reviewed studies and traffic-safety agency reports find that red light cameras, speed cameras, and active speed enforcement reduce speeds and lower crash rates and serious injuries, so they have prevented accidents; while some implementations can shift crash types (e.g., more rear-end collisions), the overall effect in many evaluations is a net reduction in crashes or injuries.

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The claim is broad and unsubstantiated: while candidates including Jason Kander may attend some out-of-state fundraising dinners, there is no verified evidence that he attended 'fancy dinners all over the country.' Without specifics (dates, hosts, locations) the sweeping formulation is unsupported and therefore false as stated.

claim: Says a car driving former University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe "ran through the students, hit one of them" at the MU Homecoming Parade.
rationale: Contemporary news reports, police statements, and parade video from the University of Missouri homecoming event do not support that Tim Wolfe’s car "ran through the students" or struck and injured a student. Coverage described his vehicle moving slowly and being surrounded by protesters, with no credible evidence that it deliberately drove through or hit someone. The claim exaggerates or mischaracterizes chaotic eyewitness accounts and footage.

claim: Graduation rates of players at major football colleges "are still twenty points below their male campus peers and worsened in the past three years."
rationale: Publicly reported NCAA graduation metrics (e.g., the Graduation Success Rate and federal rates) show that graduation rates for Division I football players have generally increased over the past decade and the gap with the general male student body is much smaller than a 20-percentage-point deficit in most cases. Available national and conference-level reports indicate the gap has narrowed and does not uniformly show a three-year worsening across 'major' programs, so the blanket statement is inaccurate without a narrow definition or specific dataset.

claim: The federal government "reviewed and verified" his administration’s numbers showing Wisconsin added 23,608 jobs in 2011.
rationale: The federal Bureau of Labor Statistics does not act as a political administration’s verifier and its state employment series did not simply ‘review and verify’ the specific 23,608 jobs claim. Independent federal-estimated series and later benchmarking did not corroborate that precise figure as a distinct federal verification, so the statement overstates the role and agreement of federal authorities.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: This is an anecdotal, specific numerical claim about who wrote and who donated that cannot be independently verified from the statement alone. No public evidence or documentation is provided to confirm that 20 people sent a letter or that 14 of them never donated, so the claim should be treated as unsubstantiated and therefore judged false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Congressman Cicilline, when he was the mayor of Providence, espoused a sanctuary city."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that David Cicilline formally declared or implemented Providence as a sanctuary city while mayor. While he supported immigrant-friendly measures and outreach to immigrant communities, reports and municipal records do not show a formal sanctuary-city designation or official noncooperation policy enacted under his mayoralty. Given the ambiguity between supporting immigrants generally and officially espousing a sanctuary-city policy, the specific claim is not supported.

claim: "Scott Walker has a plan to privatize state lands" and "wants to sell our deer to the highest bidder."
rationale: The claim is a misleading exaggeration. While Scott Walker supported selling some surplus state-owned buildings and reducing government holdings in certain contexts, there is no credible evidence he had a policy to privatize all state lands or to literally ‘sell our deer to the highest bidder.’ The ‘sell our deer’ line appears to be rhetorical hyperbole, not a statement of an enacted or proposed policy to auction wildlife or privatize wildlife populations.

claim: "Johns Hopkins University confirms: You can be vaccinated with a PCR test, even without knowing"
rationale: This claim is false. PCR tests are diagnostic swabs that collect genetic material from the nose or throat and do not deliver vaccines or biologically active doses into the body. Reputable institutions, including Johns Hopkins, have not confirmed any ability to vaccinate people via PCR testing; such stories have been repeatedly debunked as misinformation.

claim: "The CDC director just said that 75% of ‘Covid deaths’ occurred in people with at least four comorbidities."
rationale: This is false — the CDC director did not make a verified statement that 75% of COVID deaths occurred in people with at least four comorbidities. CDC mortality reports and independent fact-checkers have noted that many COVID death certificates list underlying conditions, but the agency has not endorsed the precise 75%/“four or more comorbidities” claim as phrased. The claim appears to be a misquote or misinterpretation of CDC data about multiple contributing conditions on death certificates.

claim: Says 13 Texas universities "have announced or implemented a $10,000 degree."
rationale: I cannot confirm that exactly 13 Texas universities have announced or implemented a “$10,000 degree.” While Texas officials and several institutions announced low-cost bachelor’s pathways and affordability initiatives, reporting varies by source and many statements depend on narrow definitions (in‑state tuition only, excluding fees or living costs) or on proposed rather than implemented programs. Because I lack authoritative, corroborating evidence that the precise number 13 is accurate, the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse files $400 million suit against CNN!"
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or court record showing Kyle Rittenhouse filed a $400 million lawsuit against CNN. Major news organizations and public court filings (through mid-2024) do not report any $400 million suit by Rittenhouse against CNN; claims circulating online appear to be misstatements or exaggerations of other legal actions.

claim: "There is nothing in the current state public records law that prohibits sensitive or confidential business information from being just that, confidential."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and incorrect as written. Most U.S. state public records laws (and the federal FOIA analogues) include explicit exemptions or provisions allowing withholding or redaction of trade secrets, proprietary or confidential commercial information, or otherwise sensitive business data, and some statutes impose balancing tests or procedural requirements for claiming confidentiality.

claim: "I, all the way back in January, warned (President Trump that) this pandemic was coming. I talked about what we needed to do."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented. While some public-health officials and White House advisers raised concerns about the novel coronavirus in late January 2020, there is no clear, independently documented evidence that the unnamed speaker personally warned President Trump in January that a pandemic was imminent and outlined specific required actions. Public timelines and later testimony show mixed accounts and clearer direct warnings to the President appearing in late January and February rather than uniformly earlier in January.

claim: "If Rhode Island does a hybrid [retirement] plan we’ll be the first state in the nation to do this.’’
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated. Numerous U.S. states have previously enacted hybrid retirement plans (combining defined-benefit and defined-contribution elements or cash-balance hybrids) for public employees, so Rhode Island would not be the first state to adopt a hybrid model. Without a specific novel feature or unique legal/structural definition of “hybrid,” the blanket claim of being the first is false.

claim: "Woman set to testify against Clintons blown up in home explosion."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any woman who was formally set to testify against Bill or Hillary Clinton was killed by a home explosion. Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked viral claims linking unexplained deaths or accidents to the Clintons when no verifiable connection or documentation of impending testimony exists. This claim fits a common disinformation pattern alleging suspicious deaths without corroboration.

claim: "In Rick Perry's Texas, the governor threatens to leave, to secede from the greatest country in the" world.
rationale: This statement is false as phrased. While Rick Perry, as Texas governor, made provocative, rhetorical comments about states' rights and on occasion entertained talk about secession, he never formally threatened that Texas would leave the United States or took any legal or governmental steps to secede. Secession would also be unconstitutional under U.S. Supreme Court precedent, so a governor cannot unilaterally enact it.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no hidden language in healthcare.gov code that effectively forces users to "waive any reasonable right to privacy"; the site publishes a Privacy Policy and Terms of Use that describe data collection and sharing but do not secretly strip away legal privacy protections. Allegations about a hidden waiver stem from misreading visible terms or out-of-context excerpts rather than an actual covert clause in the site code.

claim: The Republicans' alternative health care plan "will still let insurers raise premiums four times faster than wages."
rationale: The claim is too general and not supported as a blanket fact. Analyses of specific Republican proposals (e.g., AHCA variants) produced varied projections about premium changes and out-of-pocket costs, but no definitive, universally applicable finding that insurers will be allowed to raise premiums “four times faster than wages” across all plans, timeframes, and populations. Whether premiums grow faster than wages depends on the specific bill text, regulatory changes, subsidies, and the chosen comparison period.

claim: "We know mask mandates work. There’s enough evidence out there between counties that have done it and counties that haven’t."
rationale: Multiple observational and natural-experiment studies comparing counties and states with and without mask mandates have found reductions in COVID-19 transmission and case-growth rates after mandates were implemented, and public-health agencies endorse mask use to reduce spread. While most evidence is observational rather than randomized, the mechanistic basis (masks block respiratory droplets) plus consistent population-level associations support the claim that mandates work.

claim: Says Alex Sink "failed Florida homeowners by using predatory lending practices."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alex Sink personally engaged in or implemented predatory lending practices that harmed Florida homeowners. She served as Florida Chief Financial Officer and had a career in banking and public service, but public records and reporting do not show enforcement actions or documented findings that she used predatory lending to fail homeowners; the allegation appears to be political rhetoric rather than a supported factual claim.

claim: "One of the reasons that Social Security is in so much trouble is that the only funding stream comes from people who get a wage. The people who get wages is declining dramatically."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on both counts. Social Security (OASDI) is funded mainly by payroll taxes on wages and self-employment income but also receives interest on trust fund assets and revenue from taxation of benefits, so funding is not sourced only from wage-earners. Also, the absolute number of people earning wages in the U.S. has not been "declining dramatically" overall; what has changed more modestly is the ratio of workers to beneficiaries due to population aging and retirement of the baby-boom cohort.

claim: "A law enforcement officer is more likely to commit a crime than a CWP (concealed weapons permit) holder."
rationale: The blanket claim is unsupported. Multiple state and academic studies have found concealed‑carry permit holders have very low arrest and conviction rates compared with the general population, and there is no consistent national evidence that law enforcement officers as a group commit crimes at higher rates than CWP holders. Rates vary considerably by jurisdiction and by type of offense (e.g., on‑duty misconduct vs. off‑duty crimes), so the absolute statement is not justified.

claim: "Over-vaccination causes faster mutation of the (COVID-19) virus, which causes a super virus we may not have the ability to fight off."
rationale: This claim is false. Viral mutations arise from replication, and widespread infection (more replication) increases mutation opportunities; vaccines generally reduce infection, viral load, and severe disease, thereby lowering the chance of new variants. While immune pressure can select for escape mutations, that is not the same as vaccines causing faster mutation or creating an uncontrollable "super virus," and public-health measures and vaccine updates mitigate such risks.

claim: Most voters prefer zombies to the current U.S. Congress.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable poll showing a majority of voters would prefer fictional 'zombies' over the current U.S. Congress. While congressional approval is often very low, low approval does not equal documented preference for a literal undead alternative; the claim appears to be rhetorical or satirical rather than a factual polling result.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Multiple national polls over the past decade show that a minority of Republicans approve of the Affordable Care Act overall; Republican favorability toward the ACA has typically been well below 50%. Some specific ACA provisions (for example, protections for pre-existing conditions or allowing young adults to stay on parental plans) do receive broad Republican support and in some polls approach or exceed 70%, so the 74% figure is misleading if presented as support for the entire law.

claim: "Reporters rehearse questions with White House press (secretary)."
rationale: The claim presents a routine practice that does not reflect normal press-White House relations: independent reporters do not generally 'rehearse' their questions with the White House press secretary. While White House communications staff sometimes provide background briefings, coordinate logistics, or give advance notice to friendly outlets, there is no evidence this is a standard practice of reporters rehearsing their questions with the press secretary.

claim: Says House Democrats leading the impeachment inquiry are "denying President Trump basic fairness and due process accorded every American."
rationale: The statement is a normative claim that House Democrats 'denied...basic fairness and due process,' but it is not supported as a factual assertion. Impeachment is a political/constitutional process distinct from criminal trials, and during the inquiry House committees conducted depositions, public hearings, and produced evidence while offering opportunities for counsel and minority participation; President Trump's lawyers largely declined to participate in some proceedings. Because the process and constitutional standards differ from 'due process accorded every American,' the blanket factual claim that Democrats denied him basic fairness is inaccurate.

claim: "In New Jersey, Gov. Christie vetoed legislation to extend early voting."
rationale: I find no clear, widely reported record that Gov. Chris Christie vetoed legislation specifically to extend early voting in New Jersey. While New Jersey did not adopt statewide early voting during his tenure, sources do not confirm a direct Christie veto of such an extension bill.

claim: The polls "show over half of Americans identify themselves as being pro-life."
rationale: Major, long-running national polls do not consistently show more than half of Americans identify as "pro-life." Surveys from organizations like Gallup and Pew in recent years have typically found the ‘‘pro-life’’ and ‘‘pro-choice’’ labels near parity or with the ‘‘pro-choice’’ label slightly higher; results vary by question wording and timing. Therefore the blanket claim that polls show over half identify as pro‑life is misleading.

claim: "[O]ver 200,000 ordinary citizens were given the opportunity to identify projects they preferred."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it provides no context (which program, country, or timeframe) and there is no independent evidence supplied here that more than 200,000 ordinary citizens were given that opportunity. While some participatory budgeting or consultation initiatives have engaged large numbers, the statement is unsubstantiated without a specific source. Given the lack of detail, the claim is treated as false/unsupported.

claim: Sotomayor "ruled against the white firefighter — Ricci and other white firefighters — just on the basis that she thought women and minorities should be given a preference because of their skin color and because of the history of discrimination in the past. The law was totally disregarded."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. In Ricci v. DeStefano (2009) the Supreme Court’s majority ruled in favor of the white firefighters, finding New Haven violated Title VII by discarding the test results; Sotomayor did not author a majority opinion that ruled against Ricci on the stated basis. Characterizing a justice’s decision as simply preferring minorities by skin color misstates both the case outcome and the legal reasoning judges provide in opinions.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because it provides no timeframe or data source; COVID case trends vary over time and by county in Wisconsin, so one cannot conclude a clear statewide decline without recent time-series data. Case counts can be affected by testing rates, reporting delays, and differing metrics (cases vs. hospitalizations vs. test positivity), so a blanket statement that Wisconsin is 'clearly' declining is unsupported without specific evidence.

claim: "Matt Rosendale supports plans that don’t have to cover (pre-existing conditions)."
rationale: Public records and Rosendale’s statements are mixed: he has said he supports protecting people with pre-existing conditions but also favors state flexibility and market-based alternatives (such as short-term plans) that critics say can weaken those protections. There is no clear, unambiguous public record showing he explicitly endorses plans that outright do not have to cover pre-existing conditions, so the claim as stated is not supported without additional context or a specific vote/quote.

claim: "It was under Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton that changed the rules of engagement that probably cost (Capt. Humayun Khan’s) life."
rationale: Captain Humayun Khan was killed in Iraq in June 2004, five years before Barack Obama became president and before Hillary Clinton served as Secretary of State; therefore they could not have changed rules of engagement that led to his death. The claim contradicts the timeline of Khan’s death and the timelines of Obama’s and Clinton’s government roles.

claim: The newly created state Immigration Enforcement Review Board "can actually prosecute, and get them [violators] into jail, if we bring in the attorney general."
rationale: Administrative review boards generally do not have independent criminal prosecutorial authority or the power to incarcerate people; only prosecutors (state attorneys general or local district attorneys) can bring criminal charges and seek jail time. While an attorney general could pursue criminal enforcement if state law creates specific offenses, many immigration violations are federal matters and a state review board itself cannot 'prosecute and get them into jail.'

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Robert Hurt authored or publicly proposed a standalone plan to cut education funding by 40 percent. While he voted with Republican budgets and measures that sought reductions in federal discretionary spending (which can be framed as cuts to education), the specific claim of a 40% cut as his plan appears to be an exaggeration or mischaracterization. Without a cited policy text or timeframe, the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Carter "hasn’t held a town hall in five years."
rationale: The claim that Rep. John Carter "hasn’t held a town hall in five years" is misleading. Reporting and Congressional schedules indicate Carter held constituent meetings and phone/virtual town-hall–style events during periods when critics alleged a gap, and definitions of "town hall" vary (in-person vs. phone). Without a specific date range the blanket five-year assertion is not supported.

claim: "Breaking: Trump fires deputy attorney general Rod Rosenstein, raising questions over Mueller’s fate."
rationale: This is false: Rod Rosenstein was not fired by President Trump — news and official records show Rosenstein left the Justice Department via resignation rather than being dismissed. By the time Rosenstein departed, the special counsel's investigation had largely concluded with Mueller's report, so the claim that a firing immediately threatened Mueller's fate is misleading.

claim: Says Democratic opponents Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies.
rationale: The claim that both Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies is inaccurate. Erica Smith, a more progressive candidate, has expressed support for strong immigrant protections that can align with sanctuary policies, but Cal Cunningham—who ran as a more moderate Democrat—has not publicly endorsed sanctuary-city policies and has focused on comprehensive immigration reform rather than explicitly backing sanctuary status. Therefore stating that both support sanctuary policies overstates Cunningham’s position.

claim: Map shows that wildfires stop at the US.-Canada border.
rationale: Wildfires are driven by weather, fuels, and topography and do not stop at political borders; an apparent boundary on a map is almost always a data or display artifact, not a real fire behavior. Differences in satellite detection timing, agency reporting, map layer extent, or deliberate masking of one country's data can make fires appear to stop exactly at the U.S.–Canada border even though they do not.

claim: Says Jim Renacci has "consistently voted" for loopholes that "encourage outsourcing of our jobs."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated: it asserts Jim Renacci "consistently voted" for unspecified "loopholes that encourage outsourcing," but no single, publicly documented legislative record shows a consistent pattern of votes on clearly defined loopholes that directly encouraged offshoring. Renacci did vote for broadly pro‑business and tax‑cut measures that critics argue favored corporations, but without naming specific bills or provisions the allegation overstates what can be verified.

claim: If women seeking an abortion see their ultrasound, "the odds are pretty high they're going to keep the baby."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. Research reviews and individual studies show mixed and generally limited evidence that viewing an ultrasound substantially changes abortion decisions; any reduction in abortion rates is typically small and concentrated among women who were undecided beforehand. Many patients have already made their decision before viewing an ultrasound, so it is incorrect to say the odds are "pretty high" that seeing an ultrasound will make them keep the baby.

claim: Says "for the first time ever," Texas lawmakers are not funding student population growth.
rationale: The absolute claim that this is “for the first time ever” is not supported. Texas has a long history of changing how it funds education and in multiple past budget cycles lawmakers have failed to fully cover enrollment growth or have used hold-harmless formulas and cuts, so not funding student population growth has occurred before. Without a specific program, year, or budget provision, the blanket first-time assertion is implausible.

claim: Says Donald Trump "has said he wants to be neutral on Israel and the Palestinians"
rationale: This claim is misleading: Donald Trump has not broadly presented himself as wanting to be neutral between Israel and the Palestinians. His presidency and public statements were overwhelmingly pro-Israel (recognizing Jerusalem as Israel’s capital, moving the U.S. embassy there, endorsing Israeli positions, cutting Palestinian aid and brokering agreements favorable to Israel), and while he sometimes said he could act as a mediator, he did not adopt or pursue a neutral stance.

claim: "Japan drops vax rollout"
rationale: The claim implies Japan has ceased its COVID-19 vaccine rollout entirely. That is not supported by available information: Japan authorized and distributed mRNA vaccines (Pfizer, Moderna), ran nationwide rollout starting in 2021, and continued booster and routine vaccination programs thereafter. While Japan has adjusted the scale and scheduling of campaigns over time, it did not categorically ‘drop’ its vaccination program nationally.

claim: Twitter removed this tweet from Donald Trump: "My blood IS the vaccine!!!!!"
"Farouk is on fire."
rationale: The claim is unverified and ambiguous: there is no available corroborating evidence that a person or entity named Farouk is literally on fire. Without a time, location, or credible source, the statement cannot be confirmed and is more likely false or a metaphor. I therefore treat it as false pending specific, verifiable evidence.

claim: "President Trump’s Republican Party will create more debt in one year than was generated in the first 200 years of America’s existence."
rationale: The claim is a hyperbolic prediction and not supported by historical debt figures or by actual single-year deficits during the Trump years. Total federal debt outstanding by about 1976 was on the order of several hundred billion dollars (well under $1 trillion), while Trump-era annual deficits prior to the COVID crisis were near $1 trillion and the much larger 2020 deficit was driven largely by pandemic emergency spending rather than routine Republican fiscal policy. The statement as written is misleading and attributes all debt increases in a year to a single party without context.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: The claim is false because while multiple studies and reviews have found voter fraud in the U.S. and in Texas to be extremely rare, they do not conclude it is non‑existent. Texas has had documented cases and prosecutions for ineligible voting, double voting, and absentee ballot schemes, so the absolute statement that voter fraud is non‑existent is incorrect.

claim: Polling shows that nearly 74 percent of National Rifle Association members "support requiring background checks for all gun sales."
rationale: Multiple public opinion polls of gun owners and NRA members have found strong majorities in favor of requiring background checks for all gun sales, with several surveys reporting support in the low-to-mid 70s percent range (around 74%). The exact figure can vary by poll and question wording, but the claim that polling shows nearly 74% support among NRA members is consistent with published survey results.

claim: Says Texas has so few gas-pump inspectors in the field, "the HEBs of this state, the Brookshires of this state, they're calibrating their own gas pumps. The (Texas Department of Agriculture) just sends them the stickers and they calibrate them."
rationale: The claim that Texas simply mails stickers to chains and lets them self-certify gas pumps overstates how the Texas Department of Agriculture operates. Texas law and TDA programs require licensed service agents and periodic official inspections; retailers may perform routine maintenance but cannot legally self-issue official inspection certifications without registration and oversight. While local staffing levels and sampling frequency can vary, the characterization that TDA merely sends stickers and leaves calibration entirely to stores is inaccurate.

claim: A state senate bill would "criminalize a father teaching his own son how to use a hunting rifle."
rationale: This is a misleading generalization. I am not aware of any credible state senate bill that simply makes it a crime for a father to teach his son to use a hunting rifle; most recent proposals regulate storage, sale, possession by prohibited persons, or use in certain locations and explicitly or effectively allow parental instruction. Claims like this typically misquote or take out of context specific provisions intended to restrict access by certain categories of people or to require safe-storage or supervised training rather than criminalize routine parental teaching.

claim: "Colorado school forces students to wear hijabs."
rationale: The claim is broad and unsourced; there is no credible evidence that a public Colorado school is forcing students to wear hijabs. U.S. public schools are generally prohibited from mandating religious dress under the Constitution, and reporting on Colorado schools does not substantiate a schoolwide mandate. Some private religious schools may require head coverings as part of their dress codes and some public schools have run voluntary events involving hijabs, which may be the source of confusion.

claim: Obama would "experiment with socialism."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama ever said he would “experiment with socialism.” Publicly available speeches, interviews and his policy record (ACA, economic stimulus, financial regulation) do not contain such a statement; references to “experimenting” are generally political paraphrase or attack rather than a documented Obama quote or declared intent to adopt socialism. The claim conflates partisan rhetoric with an actual admission by Obama.

claim: The United States' southern border is "basically open" and is "a super spreader event."
rationale: The claim conflates political rhetoric with facts: the U.S.–Mexico border is managed with active enforcement, expulsions, and immigration processing rather than being literally "open," and calling it a nationwide "super spreader event" overstates available evidence. Public-health agencies and epidemiologists have not shown that border crossings were a primary driver of U.S. COVID-19 surges; transmission has been driven mainly by domestic community spread, and while crowded processing sites can increase local risk, that does not establish the border as a nationwide super-spreader source.

claim: "60 percent of all Americans do not want to see Planned Parenthood defunded."
rationale: The statement presents a precise, timeless statistic without a source; while many national polls have found a majority of Americans oppose defunding Planned Parenthood, reported percentages vary by poll and question wording and are not universally 60%. Without a specific poll, timeframe, or question phrasing the claim is not reliably supported as an absolute fact.

claim: Newt Gingrich "co-sponsored a bill with Nancy Pelosi that would have given $60 million a year to a U.N. program supporting China’s brutal one-child policy."
rationale: This claim conflates and misrepresents historical votes. While both Pelosi and Newt Gingrich supported or voted for measures related to U.S. policy toward the U.N. Population Fund (UNFPA) at different times in the 1990s, there is no accurate record that they co‑sponsored a bill explicitly giving $60 million a year to a U.N. program to support China’s one‑child policy. Claims tie together disputed allegations about UNFPA’s activities in China and a round dollar figure to create a misleading narrative.

claim: "Under Republicans, recessions happen four times as frequently as under Democrats."
rationale: There is no robust evidence that recessions occur four times as often under Republican presidents versus Democratic ones. Frequency comparisons depend heavily on the chosen time period, how recessions are dated (e.g., NBER definitions), and attribution of presidential responsibility; most empirical analyses do not support a consistent 4x disparity and show much smaller or non-robust differences. The claim is therefore an overgeneralization and misleading.

claim: "101 utilities cut rates, credit GOP tax cuts."
rationale: Contemporary reporting after the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act documented that just over 100 U.S. utilities had reduced customer bills or issued refunds and explicitly attributed the savings to the corporate tax cut. Multiple news accounts counted roughly 100–101 utilities taking such actions, so the claim accurately describes that phenomenon.

claim: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome "is absolutely a side effect of vaccination."
rationale: The claim is false: major reviews and multiple large epidemiologic studies have found no causal link between routine infant vaccinations and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS). While SIDS peak age partially overlaps the vaccination schedule so some deaths may occur soon after vaccination, evidence does not show vaccines cause SIDS and some studies report lower SIDS risk in vaccinated infants.

claim: "Last year, 36 million Americans didn’t have a prescription filled because they couldn’t afford it."
