claim: Untaxed corporate earnings used to be "$2.5 trillion … I guess it’s $5 trillion now. Whatever it is, it’s a lot more. So we have anywhere from 4 (trillion) to 5 or even more trillions of dollars sitting offshore."
rationale: The claim overstates widely reported estimates. Prior to the 2017 U.S. tax reform, unrepatriated foreign earnings of U.S. multinationals were commonly estimated at roughly $2.4–2.6 trillion; after the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and the transition tax those balances fell and subsequent growth has not been credibly documented as reaching $4–5 trillion in 'untaxed' earnings. The phrase 'untaxed' and the time reference are also imprecise, making the larger $4–5 trillion figure unsupported by mainstream data.

claim: Says he "helped to draft parts of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform bill."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “he” refers to; without a named individual there is no way to confirm whether that person helped draft parts of Dodd–Frank. Public records and reporting name specific congressional staff, committee lawyers, and lawmakers (not unnamed people) as drafters, so a generic claim like this cannot be confirmed. To verify, a specific person and documentary evidence (credits, contemporaneous reporting, staff lists, or acknowledgments) would be needed.

claim: Trade deals are negotiated in "secret" and, unlike corporate interests, politicians never invite "the leaders of the AFL-CIO or steelworkers or the mine workers to come in and sit down in these meetings."
rationale: The claim is overly absolute. While many trade negotiations are conducted with limited public access and business interests often have greater formal access, labor leaders have not been universally excluded: U.S. trade officials have historically met with labor unions, and labor representatives participate in advisory processes (e.g., labor advisory committees and consultations) even if they are less frequently in closed negotiating rooms than corporate advisors. Saying politicians 'never' invite leaders of the AFL-CIO or major unions is false.

claim: Zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago; major news outlets and the Chicago zoo issued statements that animals were secured and none were freed. Social media rumors circulated during protests but were debunked by fact-checkers and official sources.

claim: Says Joe Biden repeatedly told Americans he's going to raise their taxes.
rationale: This is misleading. Throughout his campaign and presidency Biden repeatedly pledged not to raise federal taxes on households making under $400,000 and framed tax increases as targeted at corporations and high‑income earners, not 'Americans' generally. While he has said he will raise taxes on the wealthy and on corporations, he did not repeatedly tell the general public that their own taxes would rise.

claim: "On average, one person dies by suicide every 22 hours in West Virginia."
rationale: Saying ‘one person dies by suicide every 22 hours’ implies about 399 suicides per year (365*(24/22)). That corresponds to a suicide rate of roughly 22 per 100,000 in a state of ~1.8 million. State-level suicide totals and rates fluctuate year-to-year and recent CDC/state data do not consistently support that exact figure without specifying a year, so the blanket claim is misleading and likely incorrect as stated.

claim: Says swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball is a "safe, easy way" to remove them from skin.
rationale: Major public-health guidance does not endorse swabbing or smothering ticks with soap as a 'safe, easy' removal method. Authorities recommend using fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick close to the skin and pull straight out because smothering or irritating a tick can cause it to regurgitate or leave mouthparts, potentially increasing infection risk.

claim: Bing Energy said it decided to move to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s "plan to eliminate the corporate tax."
rationale: I found no reliable public record or company press release showing that a firm named Bing Energy explicitly said it moved to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s plan to eliminate the corporate tax. Coverage of corporate relocations around Scott’s tenure sometimes noted his pro-business tax proposals, but the specific quoted attribution to Bing Energy is not supported by available reporting. Given lack of primary-source evidence, the claim appears to be a misattribution or unverified.

claim: "Because of my policies, Black Unemployment has just been reported to be at the LOWEST RATE EVER RECORDED!"
rationale: The claim mixes a factual measurement with an unsupported causal attribution. While U.S. Black unemployment did hit a post-1972 low in 2019, saying it is the "lowest ever recorded" ignores that the BLS race series only begins in 1972, and claiming it occurred "because of my policies" is not demonstrably supported — the labor-market recovery began years earlier and multiple factors influence unemployment. Therefore the causal claim is misleading and not established.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted against the bipartisan Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: The Senate reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act in 2013 was widely described as bipartisan, and Marco Rubio voted against that reauthorization. He publicly said he supported reauthorizing VAWA in principle but opposed the 2013 bill because of provisions he objected to (such as expanded jurisdictional and other protections).

claim: Says Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio "had it set so that the winner takes everything, because they wanted to make sure that I didn't get anything" in the Florida primary.
rationale: There is no evidence that Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio personally “set” Florida’s primary to be winner-take-all to deny another candidate delegates. Delegate allocation rules are adopted by the state Republican Party (and constrained by national party rules), not unilaterally by individual candidates, and reporting does not support a private scheme by those two to rig the allocation. While home-state politicians sometimes favor rules that help favorites, the claim that Bush and Rubio arranged it personally is unsupported.

claim: Says of El Paso that some years, "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
rationale: The statement mixes accurate context with incorrect specifics. El Paso's population is about 680,000 and the August 2019 Walmart shooter killed 22 people (which did exceed a typical annual total), but official counts show El Paso's annual homicides in the recent decade were generally in the low-to-mid teens — not years with as few as five — and the claimed 10-year average of 18 is imprecise. Thus the combination of facts as presented is misleading and not supported by available crime-data summaries.

claim: "On average, 65% of gun deaths in America are from suicides."
rationale: This claim slightly overstates the typical share. CDC mortality data show that a majority of U.S. firearm deaths are suicides, but the share in recent years has been roughly around 55–63% depending on the year, not a steady 65% average. Saying "on average, 65%" is misleading without specifying the time period or source.

claim: "Trump Management was charged with discriminating against African-Americans and breaking federal law."
rationale: The Trump organization (including Trump Management/Trump Management, Inc.) was the subject of a 1973 U.S. Department of Justice civil suit alleging discrimination against Black renters in violation of the federal Fair Housing Act. The case was resolved with a 1975 consent decree requiring nondiscriminatory practices; the company did not admit guilt but was accused and legally constrained by federal action.

claim: "We have the lowest beer tax in the nation."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no jurisdiction or time period; U.S. beer taxes vary by state and by measurement (per gallon, per barrel, ad valorem, keg vs retail). Multiple states historically have had extremely low excise rates, so a blanket assertion of “the lowest in the nation” is unlikely to be correct without specifying which tax and when. Because the statement lacks necessary detail it cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: Say Ohio Reps. Marcia Fudge, Marcy Kaptur and Dennis Kucinich are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Marcia Fudge and Marcy Kaptur are longtime Democratic members who have not publicly identified as "socialists," and Fudge left the House in 2021 to serve in the Biden administration. Dennis Kucinich has been described as a progressive/populist but did not openly identify as a socialist while serving and has not been a current member of Congress in recent years. Labeling them as "socialists openly serving in the U.S. Congress" misstates their self-identification and current office status.

claim: "The American people don't want us to raise taxes."
rationale: The statement is an unjustified universal claim about "the American people." Public opinion on taxes varies by the type of tax, wording of the question, timing, and partisan identification. Polling routinely shows opposition to broad tax increases but substantial support for raising taxes on high earners or corporations, so the absolute claim is false.

claim: Says Iranian Gen. Qassem Soleimani "was a designated terrorist by President Obama, who didn't do anything about it."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The Obama administration did not formally designate Qassem Soleimani as a State Department Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) during his presidency, though U.S. sanctions lists (Treasury) targeted the Quds Force and individuals tied to it including measures affecting Soleimani. Saying Obama “didn’t do anything about it” ignores that his administration imposed sanctions and pursued other counterterrorism measures even though it did not carry out a killing or an FTO label for Soleimani.

claim: "Nobody’s invited us" to the Obama events in Atlanta.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable and implausible as an absolute claim because it gives no specifics about which people ('us') or which Obama events in Atlanta are meant. Political events typically include a mix of invited guests and public/ticketed attendees, so asserting that 'nobody' was invited is unlikely without corroborating evidence and thus should be treated as false until details are provided.

claim: When the United States "first created the federal income tax, frankly, nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything."
rationale: The 1913 federal income tax (after the 16th Amendment) did tax incomes above modest exemptions — for example, a normal tax applied to net incomes above about $3,000 (with a surtax starting at much lower levels than $1,000,000). Many people earning well under $1,000,000 paid federal income tax from the start of the modern income tax; earlier Civil War–era income taxes also existed. The claim that “nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything” is therefore incorrect or a gross exaggeration.

claim: "We’ve saved over $100 million of (health care) costs" in Milwaukee County. "I did that."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific, attributed claim that Milwaukee County has had over $100 million in health care cost savings directly caused by the speaker. Public budget and news summaries typically report various reforms and projected or cumulative savings, but the claim is precise about amount and personal credit without independent audit evidence. Given the lack of corroborating, independently audited figures tied solely to one individual's actions, the claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "We sell 40 percent of our guns without a background check."
rationale: As stated, the claim is misleading. Federal law requires licensed firearm dealers to conduct background checks on retail sales, so licensed sellers do not lawfully sell 40% of their guns without checks; the commonly cited “40%” figure typically refers to certain private-party transfers or is a misinterpretation of survey data rather than routine dealer practice. Empirical surveys and legal requirements show private transfers (which may lack checks in some states) are a distinct category and are not equivalent to dealer sales.

claim: In first week as governor, Tim Kaine "proposed a nearly $4 billion tax increase, $4 billion, including a tax increase on people earning as little as $17,000 a year."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported by clear evidence. Tim Kaine’s incoming 2006 budget proposals sought to close a significant shortfall and included tax and fee changes over the biennium, but there is no clear record that in his first week he proposed a single, nearly $4 billion immediate tax hike specifically described as taxing people earning as little as $17,000. Advertisements and summaries at the time condensed a mix of revenue changes, fee adjustments and policy shifts into alarming figures that misstate who would be directly taxed or when the revenue would be raised.

claim: "Our minority graduation rate went from levels below Milwaukee and Madison, to above 80%" when I was Beloit school superintendent.
rationale: The claim ties a specific numeric change and cross-district comparison to the speaker's tenure but provides no dates, data source, or definition of “minority.” I was unable to verify the asserted move from below Milwaukee and Madison to “above 80%” with publicly available, contemporaneous graduation-rate reports. Because the claim is specific yet unsubstantiated and ambiguous, I judge it not provable and mark it false pending concrete evidence.

claim: Says a "Pro-Stimulus economist admits it is not working … "
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable because it provides no named economist, quote, date, or specific stimulus program. Without those details there is no evidence I can check that a self-described pro‑stimulus economist publicly "admitted it is not working." While some pro‑stimulus economists have criticized aspects of policies, that is not the same as a documented blanket admission of failure.

claim: An email from Hillary Clinton to Donna Brazile Oct.17th, 2016 stated: "If that f-----’ bastard wins, we’re all going to hang from nooses! You better fix this s---!"
rationale: There is no evidence in the publicly released Podesta/Clinton/DNC email archives or reputable news/fact-check reporting of an October 17, 2016 email from Hillary Clinton to Donna Brazile containing that quoted language. Such a provocative quote would have been widely reported and archived if authentic, but searches of the released emails and established fact-checkers find no match. The claim appears to be a fabrication or misattribution.

claim: "Florida ranks first in the nation for access to free prekindergarten."
rationale: The statement is too definitive. While Florida operates a large free Voluntary Prekindergarten (VPK) program that provides widespread access for 4‑year‑olds, national comparisons vary by metric and year, and other states (notably Oklahoma and Georgia) have historically matched or exceeded Florida on universal access/enrollment. Without a specified year or metric, claiming Florida ranks first is not supported.

claim: Henry Kissinger "said that we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition."
rationale: Henry Kissinger publicly advocated meeting with the Iranian leadership and has been quoted urging talks 'without preconditions' in interviews and opinion pieces. While the exact punctuation or phrasing (‘guess what’) may vary across appearances, the substantive claim — that Kissinger said we should meet Iran without precondition — matches his recorded public position.

claim: "The (health care) law does not demand that all of these cancellations go out."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act (ACA) did not include a line that literally ordered insurers to cancel existing individual policies en masse. Instead it set new minimum coverage and benefit standards and barred noncompliant plans from being sold or renewed in the individual market after implementation, and many cancellations resulted from insurers' renewal decisions and regulatory implementation rather than an explicit statutory command to cancel every affected plan.

claim: "More college graduates are living at home than in decades."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated. While overall rates of young adults living with parents rose after the 2007–09 recession and again during COVID, that trend primarily affected non-college-educated young adults and is sensitive to the exact age range and time period used; available evidence does not show a clear, sustained increase in the share of college graduates living at home that is higher than “in decades.” Without a specific timeframe and age definition, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "I never had a filibuster-proof Senate."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it uses “I” with no identified speaker; without a known person and timeframe it cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false. Additionally, some recent presidents did in fact have a filibuster‑proof Senate (e.g., Democrats briefly held 60 seats in 2009 after Senator Arlen Specter’s party switch), while others (e.g., Joe Biden) never did—so the statement is not universally true.

claim: "Greg Casar passed paid sick leave."
rationale: The claim is misleading as stated. Greg Casar helped author and advocate for local paid-sick-leave measures while serving on the Austin City Council and has sponsored federal paid-leave proposals as a U.S. Representative, but he did not single-handedly “pass” a nationwide paid sick leave law; local ordinances faced legal challenges and no federal paid-sick-leave law he authored has been enacted into law.

claim: "The collective net worth of Americans has taken a $5.5 trillion hit ... mainly due to plummeting home values."
rationale: While U.S. household net worth has fallen by amounts on the order of $5–6 trillion in some quarters, those declines have generally been driven primarily by drops in stock and financial asset values rather than by a sudden, large fall in home values. Housing wealth is a large but typically less volatile component, and reports from the Fed/BEA attribute the biggest swings to equity market movements.

claim: Says Joe Biden "blackmailed Ukraine with a billion in tax dollars to drop an investigation into his son and Democrats want to impeach President Trump for simply asking if it was true?"
rationale: The claim misstates known facts. Biden did pressure Ukraine in 2015–16 to remove prosecutor Viktor Shokin by threatening to withhold U.S. assistance, but that demand reflected a broad U.S./international view that Shokin was corrupt and not pursuing corruption cases; there is no credible evidence Shokin was investigating Hunter Biden or that Joe Biden acted to protect his son. Democrats impeached Trump in 2019 over allegations he solicited Ukrainian investigations and conditioned aid on such help (and for obstruction), not simply for asking a question.

claim: Miami-Dade County is the "No. 1 donor county in the state."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as an absolute fact — it does not specify the state, the time period, or the metric (total dollars, number of donors, contributions to a party/candidate). While Miami‑Dade is Florida's most populous county and frequently ranks near the top for political contributions in many election cycles, donation rankings change by cycle, metric, and party, so the blanket claim cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "COVID cases in India plummet after government promotes ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine use."
rationale: The claim implies a causal link that is not supported by evidence: randomized trials and major health agencies found no reliable benefit of ivermectin or hydroxychloroquine for preventing or treating COVID-19, and India’s declines in cases have been attributed to a combination of prior infection waves, vaccination, public health measures and other factors rather than mass drug effectiveness. While some Indian bodies and states at times recommended or used these drugs early in the pandemic, temporal correlation does not establish that promotion of these drugs caused case counts to plummet.

claim: Says Don Lemon’s show has been canceled and he is leaving CNN.
rationale: CNN announced in April 2023 that Don Lemon’s primetime program had been canceled and that he was leaving the network. The network terminated his contract following an internal review of allegations, so he departed CNN and the show ended.

claim: "Hedge fund managers and others in private equity pay much lower (tax) rates on their income than do truck drivers and teachers and nurses."
rationale: Many hedge fund and private equity managers receive a large portion of compensation as carried interest or long-term investment income, which is typically taxed at the long-term capital gains rate (and subject to the 3.8% net investment income tax) rather than ordinary wage rates. Wage earners such as truck drivers, teachers, and nurses pay ordinary income tax rates plus payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare) on virtually all their earnings, so their effective tax rates on that income are often higher than the preferential rates available to investment-manager compensation. While not universal (some managers are taxed as ordinary income and state taxes vary), the broad pattern of lower effective tax rates for carried interest/investment income is well established.

claim: Cover Florida "is available to any Floridian, offering basic coverage for about $150 a month, instead of the typical $600 a month."
rationale: There is no broadly available Florida program called “Cover Florida” that guarantees any Floridian basic individual health coverage for about $150/month in place of a typical $600/month. Health insurance prices vary by age, income, plan metal level and subsidies, and historically programs named CoverFlorida were limited in scope or administrative (not a universal $150 plan). The claim therefore overstates availability and understates typical costs without accounting for eligibility or subsidies.

claim: "Leonardo DiCaprio explains why he’s moving to Casselberry, Florida."
rationale: There are no credible reports or direct statements from Leonardo DiCaprio indicating he’s moving to Casselberry, Florida. DiCaprio’s property holdings and any major relocations are widely reported by reputable media, and no such coverage supports this claim—it appears to be a rumor or satirical item.

claim: "The president campaigned against this type of legislation."
rationale: The statement cannot be confirmed as presented because it fails to identify which president or what category of legislation is meant; without those specifics there is no evidence to verify that any particular president campaigned against it. Determinations about campaign positions require documented statements, ads, or policy platforms, none of which are supplied here.

claim: "Even with full control of the House, Senate and White House, Republicans have still failed to deliver on their promise of higher wages for working families."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad assertion that Republicans never delivered higher wages even when they controlled the House, Senate, and White House. Historical wage data show that in some periods of unified Republican control (notably 2017–2019 and parts of the mid-2000s) wages and median incomes rose on several common measures, so the blanket statement that they “still failed” is inaccurate. Wage outcomes also depend on timeframe, inflation adjustments, and which wage metric is used.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Michael McCaul is "the sixth-richest person in Congress."
rationale: The claim lacks a date or source and is not supported by consistent, publicly available congressional wealth rankings. Michael McCaul is a relatively wealthy member of Congress, but annual estimates and official financial disclosures do not reliably place him as the sixth-richest overall; rankings change by year and by valuation method and other members are commonly ranked higher. Therefore the blanket statement that he "is the sixth-richest person in Congress" is not supported as a general fact.

claim: " ‘Obamacare’ puts the federal government between you and your doctor."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The Affordable Care Act increased federal involvement in financing and regulating health insurance (Medicaid expansion, federal exchanges, subsidies, and insurer rules) but it did not nationalize health care or directly replace the doctor‑patient relationship for most people. Government mainly influences coverage, reimbursement and rules, rather than literally standing between every patient and their physician.

claim: "Mike Morell testified and told Congress that the reason Obama has not bombed ISIS' oil fields is they're concerned about global warming."
rationale: This is a mischaracteration. Mike Morell did testify that U.S. policymakers were reluctant to strike ISIS oil infrastructure because of potential environmental damage, civilian harm and safety/strategic concerns, but he did not say the reason was concern about 'global warming' specifically. News reports and the testimony referenced environmental and humanitarian consequences, not climate-change motivations.

claim: "Tens and tens of thousands of bridges are in disrepair, some on the verge of collapse."
rationale: In the United States there are well over half a million bridges and federal data have shown that tens of thousands are rated in poor or structurally deficient condition (on the order of 40,000+ in recent years). That supports the claim that "tens and tens of thousands" are in disrepair. Saying "some on the verge of collapse" is vaguer but plausible: a small subset are fracture‑critical or sufficiently deteriorated to pose elevated safety risk, though outright imminent collapses are rare.

claim: Between 2000 and 2006,  "health insurance company profits quadrupled."
rationale: Available industry data and contemporaneous reporting do show that health insurer earnings rose in the early 2000s, but there is no clear, industry-wide basis for the claim that health insurance company profits quadrupled between 2000 and 2006. Some individual firms had large profit increases and specific measures (e.g., earnings per share for a single company) can jump dramatically, but aggregate net income for the industry did not uniformly increase fourfold over that period.

claim: Clips of Dr. Anthony Fauci show he "flip-flopped" on guidance for wearing masks, whether kids should be in school and whether people should change how they interact.
rationale: The claim that clips show Fauci simply 'flip-flopped' is misleading. His public statements on masks, school attendance, and social interaction changed over time largely because scientific evidence (including asymptomatic spread and mask efficacy) and public-health context evolved, and some early comments were made to preserve scarce medical supplies or were situation-specific. Cherry-picked clips that omit timing and context distort those evidence-driven shifts.

claim: "Biden’s Air Force One is not the same as Trump’s Air Force One," which indicates Biden is not the real president.
rationale: The claim is false. “Air Force One” is a callsign applied to any U.S. Air Force aircraft while the president is aboard, and the presidential airlift consists of a fleet of specially configured planes that can be reassigned, replaced, or repainted between administrations. Differences in which specific aircraft, tail number, or livery are used do not indicate that the person aboard is not the legitimate president.

claim: Says more Austinites voted in the city’s 1973 election featuring a mayor’s race than in the city’s most recent mayoral election.
rationale: This is unlikely to be true: Austin’s population and voter rolls have grown substantially since 1973, so recent mayoral elections almost always involve higher absolute vote totals than elections in the early 1970s. Without specific vote counts from the 1973 race and the named “most recent” race we cannot be certain, but general population and turnout trends make the claim improbable.

claim: Says Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger "faces espionage charges."
rationale: There are no credible reports or criminal indictments charging Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger with espionage. Public news coverage and court records show he has been a public official and witness in election-related disputes, but not a defendant in any espionage case. Espionage is a federal charge that would be widely reported, and no such reporting exists for Raffensperger.

claim: The Washington D.C.-area "never has a recession."
rationale: The claim is incorrect — the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area has experienced economic downturns during national recessions. For example, the region saw job losses and higher unemployment during the 2008–2009 Great Recession and the 2020 COVID‑19 recession, especially in tourism, hospitality, and contracting sectors; while the large federal payroll can cushion impacts, it does not prevent recessions entirely.

claim: "The Doherty Campaign, unlike the Cicilline Campaign, is funded mostly by individual donors -- not the big PACs that Cicilline relies on."
rationale: The statement asserts a categorical funding difference but is not verifiable as phrased: campaign finance records typically show both individual and PAC contributions for most House campaigns, and the exact mix varies by cycle and filing period. While David Cicilline and other incumbents have attracted substantial PAC/committee money, that does not prove Cicilline “relies on” PACs nor that any “Doherty” campaign is funded mostly by individuals without checking FEC/OpenSecrets data for the specific candidate and time frame.

claim: Florida Democrats "put my Social Security number and my wife's Employment Identification Number in a mail piece."
rationale: There is no credible public reporting or verifiable evidence that the Florida Democratic Party mailed a piece containing an individual's Social Security number and their wife's Employer Identification Number. Including such sensitive identifiers in political mailings would be an extraordinary and widely reported privacy breach; absent documentation or reliable sources the claim is unsubstantiated and implausible.

claim: Supported in-state tuition in Arkansas for illegal immigrants "if you'd sat in our schools from the time you're 5 or 6 years old and you had become an A-plus student," among other things.
rationale: I could not verify this specific quoted support or attribute it to any known Arkansas official or public record. Arkansas has had debates about in‑state tuition for undocumented students at various times, but the exact phrasing and claim as presented lack a reliable source and appear to be an unverified paraphrase. Without a named speaker, date, or sourcing, the statement cannot be confirmed as factual.

claim: Says George LeMieux was one of two Republicans who voted for President Barack Obama's jobs bill.
rationale: George LeMieux served in the U.S. Senate from January 2009 to January 2011 and therefore was not present for the high-profile 2011 vote on President Obama’s American Jobs Act when “two Republicans” is often referenced. There is no record of LeMieux being one of two GOP senators voting for that jobs package, and he left the Senate before that legislation was considered.

claim: On financial reform, there is "a million dollars being spent, per congressman, in lobbying expenses on this issue. (The) industry has four lobbyists per member of the House and Senate working on this."
rationale: The statement presents precise per-member figures without a clear timeframe or definition of “industry.” While financial firms did spend hundreds of millions on lobbying around major financial reform debates and employed thousands of lobbyists, available totals vary by year and by which firms/activities are counted; they do not reliably support the categorical claim of exactly $1,000,000 per congressman and exactly four lobbyists per member. Because the numbers are time- and definition-dependent, the blanket assertion as stated is not supported.

claim: Says "Monica Lewinsky Found Dead" in a burglary.
rationale: This claim is false. There have been no credible reports from major news organizations that Monica Lewinsky was found dead in a burglary, and she has been publicly active in recent years. Similar hoaxes about celebrity deaths have circulated online before and were debunked.

claim: Says Elizabeth Warren has a racist figurine in her kitchen.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Elizabeth Warren displayed a racist figurine in her kitchen; viral images and claims have been misattributed or taken out of context and have been debunked by fact-checkers. Independent reporting found no reliable documentation that she owned or promoted a racist 'mammy' or similar figurine in her home.

claim: Before 2005, "the percentage of" Texas high school "students meeting the college readiness standards of the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board stood at 28% in English and 42% in math. Those figures stood at 65% and 66% in 2013."
rationale: The specific percentages given do not match the published Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board and Texas Education Agency reports and widely cited summaries: THECB measures of college readiness and TEA accountability results show different baseline and 2013 values, and reported gains are not as large and are measured differently by subject and cohort. Additionally, the state changed assessments and readiness cutoffs over this period, so a simple before/after pair of percentages is misleading and likely incorrect.

claim: "Here are the facts: there is no massive wave of migrants pouring into California. Overall immigrant apprehensions on the border last year were as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years (and 85 percent of the apprehensions occurred outside of California)."
rationale: Contemporary U.S. Customs and Border Protection data show recent annual border encounters were much higher than multidecade lows—indeed recent years saw millions of encounters, not the lowest in nearly 50 years. While it is true that a large majority of encounters occur outside California (California accounts for a relatively small share), the claim that overall apprehensions were “as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years” is contradicted by federal data, so the combined statement is false.

claim: "In West Virginia alone, overdoses have increased by 50% during the #COVID-19 pandemic."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by available state and federal data: while West Virginia did experience an increase in drug overdoses during the COVID-19 pandemic, publicly reported year-to-year increases for the state were substantially less than a 50% jump in most official counts. Without a specified timeframe (e.g., particular months vs. full year) or whether the claim refers to fatal vs. nonfatal overdoses, the blanket statement that overdoses increased 50% in West Virginia is misleading.

claim: Says Barack Obama had "huge majorities" in Congress during his first two years in office and "did nothing with them to create jobs in America."
rationale: The claim is false. While Democrats held comfortable House and Senate majorities after the 2008 elections (a large House majority and a Senate majority that briefly reached 60 seats mid‑2009), Congress and the Obama administration passed major job‑focused legislation in 2009–2010, most notably the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (February 2009) and other measures to stabilize the auto sector and extend unemployment benefits. Saying they 'did nothing' ignores these enacted efforts intended to preserve and create jobs.

claim: "Kids are less likely to get it (COVID-19). You know, they’re less likely to spread. So I think there’s some pretty good data out there that will help alleviate some of the concerns."
rationale: The statement is an overly broad generalization. While early surveillance showed children, especially very young ones, had lower reported symptomatic case rates and some studies suggested lower susceptibility, substantial evidence from household and school studies shows children—particularly older children and adolescents—can and do get infected and transmit SARS-CoV-2. Transmission patterns also changed with newer variants and depend on age, mitigation, and vaccination, so the blanket claim that kids are less likely to get and spread COVID-19 is misleading.

claim: "We got a million jobs."
rationale: The claim as stated is ambiguous and cannot be verified because it fails to specify who "we" refers to or the timeframe for the million jobs. Verifiable claims about job creation require a defined geography, period, and metric (e.g., net payroll jobs per BLS), none of which are provided, so the statement as presented is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The State Department asked all secretaries of state to send their emails over." Hillary Clinton's "the only one who’s done it."
rationale: The State Department did ask living former secretaries to turn over work-related emails, and Hillary Clinton did hand over her work-related emails, but she was not the only former secretary to provide records. Other former secretaries either had archived records with the National Archives or cooperated with requests (for example, Colin Powell and others provided or had already preserved work-related materials). Therefore the claim that Clinton was "the only one who’s done it" is incorrect.

claim: Says his barehanded catch posted on YouTube is real.
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to accept the assertion that a claimed bare‑handed catch on YouTube is genuinely unassisted. Video content can be staged, edited, or misrepresented, and without original footage metadata, independent eyewitness accounts, or expert verification the claim remains unverified and therefore treated as false. Verification would require concrete provenance and corroboration.

claim: Says Tucker Carlson said, "What if these bodies of tortured, dead civilians were staged? What if they’re fake? What if the Ukrainian military killed them & then blamed Russia? I’m not saying any of this is true, I’m just asking the questions. Why can’t we ask these questions?"
rationale: In April 2022 Tucker Carlson aired segments in which he explicitly suggested as hypotheticals that the bodies shown after the Bucha killings could have been staged or fake and asked why such questions couldn’t be asked, framing the ideas as questions rather than assertions. Major news organizations and fact-checkers quoted and summarized his on-air language and noted he repeatedly prefaced such suggestions as hypothetical.

claim: Women are paid 77 cents for every $1 men get for the same work.
rationale: The oft‑cited "77 cents" figure refers to the raw median annual earnings of women versus men (commonly for U.S. full‑time workers) and does not control for job, hours, experience, education, or occupation. Studies that compare men and women in the same job with similar qualifications and hours find a much smaller pay gap, so saying women are paid 77¢ "for the same work" is a mischaracterization.

claim: "666,000 teachers have been laid off already since March."
rationale: There is no credible national data showing exactly 666,000 teachers laid off since March. BLS employment figures and contemporaneous fact-checks showed declines in education-sector jobs during the pandemic, but those losses were smaller, often included non-teaching staff, and were sometimes furloughs or temporary reductions rather than permanent teacher layoffs. The precise 666,000 figure appears to be a misleading or unsupported aggregation.

claim: Says opponents of proposed Austin school district bonds say the district’s "debt load doubles with these new bonds."
rationale: The statement that the district’s “debt load doubles with these new bonds” is unlikely to be accurate without showing that the proposed bond principal equals the district’s entire existing outstanding debt. Issuing bonds increases outstanding debt by the bond principal, but doubling would require the new bonds to match current debt levels; most school bond packages are far smaller than a district’s full debt stock and are phased over time. Without specific numbers from the district’s debt schedule and the bond proposal, the doubling claim is not supported.

claim: "The United States was energy independent in 2019 for the first time since 1957. In just 10 days we are sent back 50 years."
rationale: The claim's first part is correct: the U.S. was a net energy exporter in 2019 for the first time since 1957 (per EIA). The second part — that "in just 10 days we are sent back 50 years" — is vague and unsupported; there is no clear evidence that U.S. energy independence was reversed within a 10‑day period or that such a reversal literally sent the country back 50 years.

claim: "I’ve never supported legislation that invades people’s choices about contraception."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about a person's entire legislative record but no speaker or timeframe is provided, so it cannot be verified as true. Many public officials have supported legislation that affects contraception access or funding, and proving a universal "never" requires exhaustive review of the named person's voting history and public statements. Absent that specific evidence, the claim is not supported.

claim: Florida is "second in the nation in the uninsured."
rationale: The claim is presented without a year or whether it means uninsured rate (percentage) or raw number, and recent national data do not consistently place Florida second on either measure. Historically Texas has had the highest uninsured rate and Florida’s ranking has varied by year and by whether one counts percent uninsured or total uninsured people, so the blanket statement that Florida is "second in the nation in the uninsured" is unsupported. Without a specific timeframe or metric the claim is misleading.

claim: Says "I never billed a single hour of my time to the City of Portland in the last 10 years -- so, no revolving door."
rationale: This claim cannot be validated from the statement alone and therefore should be treated as false until corroborated. Determining whether someone billed the City of Portland in the past 10 years requires checking city payroll, vendor/contract invoices, and lobbying or ethics disclosures; without those records the assertion is unsubstantiated. Additionally, asserting “no revolving door” from a single claim about billing hours is logically weak because revolving-door concerns can arise from employment, consulting, or other compensated activity that isn’t captured solely by billed city hours.

claim: While the smoking rate nationally has fallen, more than 18 percent of Georgians still light up.
rationale: Recent nationally and at the state level, adult cigarette smoking prevalence has been declining. State surveillance data (BRFSS/NHIS) in the last several years have shown Georgia's adult smoking rate in the mid-teens rather than above 18 percent, so the claim that “more than 18 percent of Georgians still light up” is not supported by recent estimates.

claim: "Back in the Great Recession, when millions of  jobs across America hung in the balance, Donald Trump said rescuing the auto industry didn’t really matter very much. He said, and I quote again, ‘Let it go.’ "
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and Trump's own 2008 remarks show he opposed rescuing the automakers during the Great Recession, telling interviewers he would let Detroit/automakers go bankrupt rather than support a bailout. The paraphrase "let it go" captures the substance of those statements opposing an auto-industry rescue when jobs were at stake.

claim: "Actress Emma Stone: ‘For the first time in history we have a president that…"
rationale: The claim is an incomplete, unattributed partial quote and there are no reliable records or reputable news reports through mid-2024 showing Emma Stone made this statement. Because the fragment lacks context, a date, or a source, it cannot be verified and is likely misattributed or fabricated.

claim: "The Simpsons" predicted Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that The Simpsons explicitly predicted Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The show frequently satirizes political figures and events, and isolated images or clips have been retrofitted or taken out of context to suggest a “prediction,” but that is coincidence or misinterpretation rather than a true forecast. Without a specific, verifiable episode showing that invasion before it happened, the claim is false.

claim: George Allen voted for budgets that increased the national debt by $16,400 for every second he served in the U.S. Senate.
rationale: This claim is inaccurate and misleading. George Allen served in the Senate from Jan 2001–Jan 2007; depending on the debt series used, federal debt rose roughly $2.6–3.1 trillion over that period, which would equal about $13,000–$16,000 per second — the precise $16,400 figure depends on choice of start/end dates and whether gross debt or debt held by the public is used. Moreover, attributing the entire increase to “budgets he voted for” misstates causation because many votes, policies, and economic factors beyond a single senator’s votes determine the debt trajectory.

claim: Says North Carolina "hospital beds are typically 85% full across the state."
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or definition and does not match typical statewide occupancy data. Historically, average inpatient bed occupancy for states (and the U.S.) is generally lower—often in the ~60–75% range for staffed beds—and 85% represents a high level more typical of temporary surges rather than a normal, statewide level.

claim: "We [the city of Atlanta] are overbuilt on housing."
rationale: The blanket statement that Atlanta is "overbuilt on housing" is not supported by broad, recent indicators. Atlanta has seen population and job growth and sustained rental demand with historically low vacancy and rising rents in many years, so while some neighborhoods may have high new-construction concentrations, citywide evidence points more to continued demand than a clear, citywide oversupply.

claim: "We’ve still had more deaths to the flu this year than we've had COVID-19."
rationale: The statement is presented without a location or time frame and is misleading as a general claim. In most countries (and globally) since 2020 COVID-19 has produced substantially more reported deaths than a typical influenza season; for example, U.S. COVID-19 deaths have exceeded annual flu deaths by large margins in each pandemic year. Therefore the blanket claim that “we’ve still had more deaths to the flu this year than we've had COVID-19” is false in typical contexts.

claim: Says that Tim Pawlenty eliminated health insurance for 33,000 to 35,000 people when he was governor of Minnesota.
rationale: Multiple contemporary news reports and fact-checks record that during Tim Pawlenty’s governorship his administration cut the state program (commonly cited as General Assistance Medical Care/MinnesotaCare changes), resulting in roughly 33,000–35,000 people losing that state-subsidized coverage. The rounded 33,000–35,000 figure is the commonly reported estimate of those affected by the policy change.

claim: Says Republican gubernatorial candidate Adam Laxalt "tried to cut a deal with big pharma" in a lawsuit.
rationale: There is no clear, verified public record that Adam Laxalt ‘tried to cut a deal with big pharma’ as a general factual claim. Public reporting shows Laxalt, as Nevada Attorney General, participated in litigation against pharmaceutical companies (notoriously opioid suits) rather than being documented as negotiating a secret favorable deal; without a specific lawsuit or reliable sourcing the assertion is unsubstantiated. Because the claim is vague and lacks citation, it cannot be treated as established fact.

claim: The "top ten most unhealthy U.S. cities" are San Francisco; Seattle; Portland, Oregon; San Diego; Honolulu; Washington; Austin, Texas; Irving, Texas; Portland, Maine; and Denver.
rationale: The claim is incorrect: the named cities are commonly ranked among the healthiest U.S. cities in multiple public‑health and lifestyle surveys rather than the most unhealthy. There is no well‑known authoritative list that labels San Francisco, Seattle, Portland (OR and ME), San Diego, Honolulu, Washington (DC), Austin, Irving, and Denver as the top ten most unhealthy, and many of these places have low obesity rates and high access to health care and physical activity opportunities.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that U.S. military forces are at the White House arresting members of Congress. Such an action would be a major, widely reported constitutional crisis and would violate longstanding legal and constitutional norms, and no reputable sources have reported it. The claim appears to be false or a misinterpretation or rumor.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "took away $1.6 billion from schools and handed it off as over $2 billion in tax breaks to the rich."
rationale: The claim bundles and overstates disparate budget actions into a single direct transfer that independent analyses do not support. Walker’s budgets included reductions in state K–12 aid in some years and enacted tax cuts (including business and income tax changes), but the totals, timing, and beneficiaries are more complex than “took $1.6 billion from schools” and “handed over $2+ billion to the rich.” Nonpartisan budget summaries show cuts and tax changes spread over multiple years, with offsets from local levies and varied beneficiaries, so the precise one-to-one figures are misleading.

claim: Says "combined doses of vaccines" have never been tested.
rationale: This claim is false: vaccines are routinely evaluated in combination. There are licensed combination vaccines (e.g., MMR, DTaP‑IPV‑Hib, pentavalent vaccines) and numerous clinical studies and post‑licensure surveillance assess safety and immune responses when multiple vaccines are given together or concomitantly. While not every conceivable pairing may have been tested, the blanket statement that combined doses have “never” been tested is incorrect.

claim: "The conviction rate is almost exactly the same" for whites and blacks who commit murder.
"At least 450,000 ballots in the key states ... miraculously only have a mark for Joe Biden on them, and no other candidate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that at least 450,000 ballots in unspecified “key states” were exclusively marked for Joe Biden with no other choices; post‑election audits, recounts, and fact‑checks found these large figures to be erroneous or misinterpreted. Instances of ballots showing only a presidential selection are explainable by voter behavior (undervotes or skipping down‑ballot races), straight‑party voting, or reporting errors, not proof of mass fraud producing 450,000 Biden‑only ballots.

claim: "As soon as Chris Christie was governor, he gave tax cuts to millionaires."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Chris Christie took office in January 2010 and did not immediately sign a law specifically cutting taxes for millionaires; New Jersey tax changes affecting high earners occurred later and state budgets during his early years focused on spending cuts and shifting costs rather than an immediate targeted millionaire tax cut. Saying he 'as soon as ... gave tax cuts to millionaires' overstates the timing and specificity of any benefits to the wealthy under his administration.

claim: Fifty-three percent of graduates from liberal arts colleges these days can’t find jobs.
rationale: Broadly available labor statistics and graduate outcome surveys do not support a claim that 53% of liberal arts college graduates currently 'can't find jobs.' Typical employment rates for recent bachelor's degree recipients (including liberal-arts fields) usually show the majority employed or in further education within months of graduation, with unemployment for college graduates far below 53%. The 53% figure appears to conflate different measures (e.g., underemployment, jobs unrelated to major, or a specific small-sample finding) rather than representing a general unemployment rate.

claim: New food safety legislation will regulate backyard gardening.
rationale: The claim is too general and unsupported: unspecified "new food safety legislation" does not inherently mean backyard gardens will be regulated. In most jurisdictions food-safety laws target commercial food production, processing, and retail (restaurants, farms selling to the public), not private backyard gardening. While some local ordinances can restrict specific practices (e.g., keeping poultry or selling home-grown produce), blanket regulation of backyard gardens is uncommon and would require explicit statutory language or rules.

claim: "The biggest contribution" behind a decrease in U.S. unemployment "was 1.2 million people leaving the workforce"
rationale: The statement asserts a specific numeric cause without a time frame and is not generally true: changes in the unemployment rate can come from either job gains or people leaving the labor force, and most documented declines have been driven primarily by employment growth rather than a one-time 1.2 million exit. Verifying a claim like this requires referencing a particular month’s BLS household and payroll data; absent that context, the claim is unsupported and misleading.

claim: "Zach Nunn took money from Adventureland’s CEO, then sponsored legislation to loosen amusement park safety rules. A child died. Zach Nunn put his big donor first, ahead of the safety of Iowa families."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Zach Nunn sponsored legislation to loosen amusement-park safety rules or that he put an Adventureland CEO’s donation ahead of public safety leading to a child’s death. Nunn is a federal representative (and earlier a state legislator), and major news and legislative records do not document him authoring a bill to relax amusement-park safety standards tied to a donor-funded decision or a related fatality. The claim conflates donation, specific legislation, and a death without substantiation.

claim: Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 mail-in ballots
rationale: No credible state or county election reports show 372,000 mail‑in ballots rejected in Pennsylvania; official rejection counts in recent elections have been in the low tens of thousands, not hundreds of thousands. The claim omits a year or definition and appears to conflate different categories (requested, returned, undeliverable) with 'rejected.'

claim: "ABC News has confirmed that attendees to Trump WH Rally were paid. $150. ea and had to sign an NDA."
rationale: There is no credible record that ABC News “confirmed” attendees at a Trump White House rally were paid $150 each and required to sign NDAs. Major news organizations did not report such a confirmation, and the claim appears to stem from social-media rumor or conflation with unrelated instances of paid attendees at other events. Without an identified ABC News article or corroboration from other reputable outlets, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Rhode Island has the highest percentage of uninsured adults of any state in New England."
rationale: This is false. Since the Affordable Care Act and state Medicaid expansions, Rhode Island has generally had one of the lower uninsured-adult rates in New England; other states such as New Hampshire or Maine have typically reported higher uninsured adult percentages in recent years. Available state-level estimates do not show Rhode Island as the highest in the region.

claim: "In Oregon, students are skipping math class to learn about the Bible."
rationale: The claim is a broad, statewide statement without verifiable evidence; there are no credible reports that Oregon schools as a whole are permitting students to skip math class to receive Bible instruction. Public schools are barred from school‑led religious instruction, and while isolated 'released time' programs or off‑campus religious activities may occur with parental permission, those do not support a claim that students across Oregon are skipping math class to learn the Bible.

claim: Says Dr. Robert Gallo, the man who helped discover the HIV virus, confessed he was "forced" to "create the HIV virus as a secret weapon to wipe out the African race."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Dr. Robert Gallo ever confessed to creating HIV or being forced to do so as a racial weapon. Scientific consensus and historical research show HIV emerged from cross-species transmission of simian viruses, and Gallo’s documented role was in identifying and characterizing the human retrovirus and developing diagnostic tests—not creating it. Numerous reputable investigations and fact-checkers have debunked this claim as a baseless conspiracy theory.

claim: Says a photo shows Adam Schiff and Jeffrey Epstein.
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that a genuine photo exists showing Rep. Adam Schiff with Jeffrey Epstein; images circulated online were debunked as doctored or misidentified by fact-checkers and no reliable media or photographic record corroborates such a meeting. Given the lack of independent verification and the prevalence of manipulated images, the claim that a photo shows the two together is false.

claim: "Ten years ago, John McCain offered a bill that said he would ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. John McCain introduced a bill about ten years ago (circa 2015) that would categorically ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists. McCain was known for anti-lobbying and campaign-finance reforms (e.g., McCain-Feingold and other disclosure/gift limits), but I find no evidence of a 2015 bill that expressly prohibited candidates from paying registered lobbyists.

claim: "West Linn has one of the highest per capita rates of home-based businesses in the United States."
rationale: There is no widely cited national data or reputable ranking that identifies West Linn, Oregon, as being among the U.S. leaders in home‑based businesses per capita. The statement is a broad, strong claim that is unsubstantiated without a specific dataset, year, or definition of "home‑based business."

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "collaborated with Marxist regimes in the Soviet Union, Nicaragua and Cuba."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bernie Sanders engaged in formal or substantive collaboration with the governments of the Soviet Union, Nicaragua, or Cuba. While Sanders has participated in international delegations, met with activists or officials, and at times praised specific social programs (for example health care) in other countries, those activities do not constitute collaboration with those regimes. Sanders has also publicly criticized authoritarianism and human-rights abuses.

claim: The "3 red stripes" in Joe Biden’s campaign logo refer to a Chinese socialist slogan.
rationale: There is no evidence the Biden campaign intended the three red stripes to reference any Chinese socialist slogan. The stripes are a common graphic device (used to stylize the letter E and evoke the U.S. flag) and campaign materials and reporting do not tie them to Chinese political slogans. While China’s Mao-era “Three Red Banners” is a historical phrase, that is unrelated to the Biden logo’s documented design intent.

claim: "When I was speaker, we had four consecutive balanced budgets."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which “speaker” is referenced, which government level (federal, state, local), or how a “balanced budget” is being defined. Without that context the assertion cannot be confirmed; continuous four-year stretches of formally balanced budgets are uncommon at the federal level in recent decades. Because of the missing specifics I treat the claim as likely false in its presented, absolute form.

claim: Says North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis "called Obamacare ‘a great idea.’ "
rationale: There is no clear on-the-record instance where Thom Tillis flatly and unqualifiedly said “Obamacare is a great idea.” Public reporting and fact-checks show he praised certain goals or specific provisions of the Affordable Care Act (for example expanding coverage or protections) while opposing the law as enacted. Claims that he called the entire law “a great idea” conflate limited praise for aspects of reform with an endorsement of Obamacare as a whole.

claim: "Wisconsin Republicans have not passed a single bill in 6 months."
rationale: This claim is false. The Wisconsin Legislature, controlled by Republicans, regularly considers and passes bills and resolutions; legislative records show multiple bills advanced or enacted within any recent six‑month period. The statement appears to be political exaggeration or missing key context about what "passed" or which lawmakers and timeframe are meant.

claim: The health care law could cost up to $2 trillion, "double what we were promised."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Nonpartisan budget offices (CBO and Joint Committee on Taxation) produced decade-long estimates for the Affordable Care Act that were in the range of hundreds of billions and in some analyses reduced projected deficits, not a $2 trillion net federal cost. Saying it "could cost up to $2 trillion, double what we were promised" mixes different measures (gross vs. net, federal vs. state spending) and overstates mainstream official estimates.

claim: The Senate Republican education plan is an unfunded mandate for local school districts.
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify because it does not identify which specific Senate Republican education plan is meant. Whether a bill is an "unfunded mandate" depends on the particular provisions and whether the Senate/appropriations provided funding or preemption; different GOP education proposals have included varying funding levels and requirements. Without the specific bill text or year, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false as stated.

claim: Says David Dewhurst skipped nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate candidacy.
rationale: I cannot verify the precise claim that David Dewhurst skipped nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate candidacy. Contemporary news accounts from his Senate races reported that he skipped multiple events, but the reported number of forums missed varies by source and depends on how 'forum' is defined and the time window used. Because the exact figure 'nine' is not corroborated by a consistent, authoritative source, I judge the specific numeric claim as unverified and therefore likely false.

claim: "Oregon school districts are directing 24 percent of their food budgets to purchase local foods. That’s the highest percentage in the country."
rationale: I could not confirm a reliable, current national ranking showing Oregon school districts direct 24% of their food budgets to local foods and that this is the highest in the country. USDA Farm to School Census and state surveys collect related metrics, but results vary by year, definition of “local,” and sample; no authoritative source consistently lists Oregon at 24% and top among all states. Given the ambiguity in source, year, and measure, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Spending increases, not tax cuts, are the major cause of the federal budget deficit.
rationale: The claim is too categorical. Federal deficits have multiple causes: spending growth (especially Social Security, Medicare/Medicaid, and rising net interest) is a major long-term driver, but tax cuts have also materially reduced revenues and raised deficits in specific periods (e.g., early-2000s and after the 2017 tax law). Which factor is “major” depends on the time window and economic conditions, so it is incorrect to say tax cuts are not a major cause.

claim: A president must "obtain Congress' consent before formally accepting the Nobel Prize."
rationale: This is false. The Constitution's foreign emoluments clause bars acceptance of gifts or offices from foreign states without Congress' consent, but the Nobel Prize is awarded by private Nobel committees and the Nobel Foundation, not by a foreign state. U.S. presidents (e.g., Theodore Roosevelt, Barack Obama) have accepted Nobel Prizes while in office without seeking Congressional consent, and legal commentary generally treats Nobel awards as not triggering the consent requirement.

claim: Says Adam Putnam "was for amnesty."
rationale: Adam Putnam has publicly disavowed ‘amnesty’ and consistently emphasized enforcement-first immigration policies (such as E‑Verify and stronger border security) rather than blanket citizenship for undocumented immigrants. Although he has sometimes endorsed limited or 'earned' legal-status proposals, he has not embraced what opponents label as wholesale amnesty, so the broad claim that he 'was for amnesty' is inaccurate.

claim: "We only have 2 percent of the oil reserves in the world, and we consume 25 percent of the world's oil on a daily basis."
rationale: If “we” means the United States, the first part is approximately right (U.S. proven crude reserves are on the order of 2–3% of global proved reserves). However the second part is inaccurate: recent U.S. daily oil consumption has been about 18–22% of world oil use (roughly 20%), not 25%, so the overall claim is misleading. Variations by year and by how “reserves” or “oil” are defined can change exact percentages.

claim: "Dandelion root is able to kill 98% of cancer cells within 48 hours."
rationale: The claim overstates and generalizes limited laboratory findings. Small in vitro studies (cell cultures) have reported that certain dandelion root extracts killed high percentages of specific cancer cell lines under controlled conditions, but there is no robust clinical evidence that dandelion root “kills 98% of cancer cells within 48 hours” in humans or across cancers. In vitro results do not prove safety or effectiveness as a cancer treatment in patients.

claim: "An attack on a healthy 22-year-old homosexual man would be more protected under the law than an attack on an eight-year-old child."
rationale: This is false in general: most legal systems impose special protections and harsher penalties for crimes against minors (including child abuse and sexual offenses) and require mandatory reporting, so an assault on an eight‑year‑old is typically treated more severely than an assault on an adult. While hate‑crime laws can add penalties when an adult victim is targeted because of sexual orientation, those enhancements do not generally make an attack on a healthy 22‑year‑old "more protected" than an attack on a child.

claim: Says FEMA is giving essential workers $1,000.
rationale: This is false. FEMA has not announced or run a program that pays a universal $1,000 bonus to “essential workers.” FEMA’s mission and public programs center on disaster response and individual assistance tied to declared disasters, not blanket cash payments to entire worker categories, and similar claims have been debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: Says images show migrants on trains and buses heading toward the United States, not walking.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because no specific images, sources, timestamps, or geolocation are provided; without provenance, images claimed to show migrants on trains/buses heading to the U.S. may be miscaptioned or from other times/places. Past fact-checks have shown similar circulating photos often originate elsewhere or depict different contexts, so the blanket assertion is unreliable.

claim: Says the House Rules Committee is the only panel, other than the Intelligence and Ethics committees, not able to telecast proceedings in its main hearing room.
rationale: The claim asserts an exclusive restriction but is not accurate. Most House committees routinely have their main-room proceedings televised, and the House Rules Committee’s meetings are commonly carried by C-SPAN; Intelligence and Ethics are known to have special camera restrictions, but they are not the only committees that can face limited broadcast ability depending on room configuration or classified/closed sessions. Without a specific timeframe or definition of “able to telecast,” the exclusivity claim is unsupported.

claim: Iowa has "the highest high-school graduation rate in the country."
rationale: The claim is presented as a timeless fact but is not consistently true. State high-school graduation rankings (measured by the NCES Adjusted Cohort Graduation Rate) change year to year and in recent years several states (for example New Jersey, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Wisconsin) have equaled or exceeded Iowa’s rate; Iowa is often near the top but not universally the single highest state. Without a specific year or data source the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "When the union says I want to eliminate tenure, that’s not true."
rationale: The claim denies a specific assertion but provides no identifying context (who 'I' is or which union). Without a named speaker, union, or source, the statement is unverifiable; positions on eliminating tenure vary across individuals and organizations, so it cannot be confirmed as fact. Given the lack of evidence, the safe assessment is that the claim is not demonstrably true.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar vowed "to remove senior’s ‘entitlements,’ Social Security/Medicare."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Ilhan Omar vowed to eliminate Social Security or Medicare for seniors. Both have supported proposals like Medicare-for-All that would restructure how health coverage is provided, and they have publicly defended Social Security; viral claims that they vowed to ‘remove’ seniors’ entitlements misrepresent those positions.

claim: "The barber regulation here in Missouri is 10,000 words long….the book of Revelation is (also) 10,000 words long."
rationale: The statement presents two precise equal word counts but is misleading. The number of words in the Book of Revelation varies by Bible translation (typically roughly 9,000–12,000 words depending on the version), and there is no single Missouri “barber regulation” universally documented as exactly 10,000 words — licensing rules are spread across statutes and administrative code and their length depends on what is counted. Thus the paired claim as stated is not accurate.

claim: Says a "Canadian provincial prime minister came to Ohio for his medical treatment because of the delay in Canadian health care which would have endangered his life."
rationale: There is no verifiable, credible reporting of a Canadian provincial premier traveling to Ohio specifically because Canadian wait times would have endangered his life. High‑profile medical travel by a sitting premier would be widely reported and documented; the claim provides no name, date, or reliable source and conflicts with known transparency around premiers' health issues. Because the statement is vague and unsupported, it is best judged false until concrete evidence is provided.

claim: Since he and Scott Walker took office in 2011, "60,000 new jobs have been created in this state -- 40,000 of them were created in Madison and the Madison area."
rationale: Official employment series and state labor reports show Wisconsin added substantially more than 60,000 jobs after 2011, and it is implausible that roughly 40,000 of those occurred only in the Madison area. Madison is a growing metro but cannot plausibly account for about two-thirds of the state's job growth; statewide BLS nonfarm payroll increases and other metro gains (Milwaukee, Green Bay, etc.) contradict the claim.

claim: Says "Barcelona terrorist" is cousins with former President Barack Obama.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable reporting that any participant in the Barcelona attacks is a cousin of former President Barack Obama. Obama’s family genealogy is well-documented in public records and media investigations, and such a close familial tie would have been reported by major news organizations if substantiated. The claim appears to be a social-media rumor without supporting documentation.

claim: "The cost of living is going up, but paychecks aren't keeping up."
rationale: Broadly true: in many countries over recent years consumer prices (housing, food, energy) rose faster than median wage growth, causing real paychecks to decline for large segments of the population. While some wages increased nominally, inflation-adjusted pay often lagged, so purchasing power fell for many households.

claim: "Flip Flop! After opposing term limits for decades, Adam Putnam adopts Donald Trump and Ron DeSantis’ position."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes Putnam’s record. There is no clear evidence that Adam Putnam spent “decades” opposing term limits; his political career in Florida government is limited to the 2000s–2010s and he has not been a long-standing, well-documented opponent of term-limit proposals at the federal level. The statement also conflates actors and timelines (Trump/DeSantis positions) without specifying which term limits are meant, making the “flip flop after decades” framing inaccurate and misleading.

claim: Says "former Democrat Kelli Ward attacked President Trump's plans to crack down on illegal immigration, saying Trump was making a mistake."
rationale: This claim is false as stated. Kelli Ward is a Republican and known Trump ally who has generally supported strong immigration enforcement; there is no widely reported instance of her attacking President Trump’s plans to crack down on illegal immigration and saying he was making a mistake. The assertion appears to misattribute criticism to someone who has not publicly opposed that aspect of Trump’s agenda.

claim: With voting by mail, "you get thousands and thousands of people sitting in somebody's living room, signing ballots all over the place."
rationale: This statement is a broad and unsupported generalization. While isolated incidents of illegal ballot collection or assistance have occurred, there is no credible evidence that mail voting routinely produces "thousands and thousands" of people congregating in private homes to sign ballots. Mail voting systems generally rely on voters completing and signing their own ballots, with signature checks, witness or notarization rules in some states, and legal limits on third‑party collection that vary by jurisdiction.

claim: A Texas police department bought an ad telling drug dealers, "We can take your competition off the streets for FREE."
rationale: There is no verifiable reporting from reputable news sources confirming any Texas police department officially ran an ad with the exact wording “We can take your competition off the streets for FREE.” Images with that phrase have circulated on social media and appear to be doctored or misattributed. While police do run anti-drug/tip campaigns, this specific provocative line is not substantiated.

claim: Since the stimulus package was passed, "Ohio’s lost over 100,000 more jobs."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and cannot be verified as stated: it does not specify which "stimulus package" or the time period for counting jobs. Public BLS and state payroll data show employment changed substantially at different points (large losses in early 2020 followed by partial recovery), so a blanket statement that Ohio has "lost over 100,000 more jobs" since an unspecified stimulus package is not supported without a clear baseline and date range. Because the claim lacks necessary context and is not a verifiable factual statement as written, it is rated false.

claim: "We're experiencing a net outflow of illegal, undocumented workers from America back to Mexico."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization and not supported by recent migration data. While Mexican net migration to the U.S. declined and the Mexican-born unauthorized population fell compared with the 2000s, recent years have seen large numbers of arrivals and border encounters (including many non‑Mexicans), and overall unauthorized population dynamics do not show a clear, sustained net outflow “back to Mexico.” Thus it is misleading to claim we are experiencing a current net outflow of undocumented workers to Mexico.

claim: Says Virginia Del. Mark Cole "wants schools to check children’s genitals before using bathroom."
rationale: The claim is an exaggeration. While Mark Cole has backed policies enforcing bathroom use by biological sex and supported measures to verify sex, there is no credible evidence he proposed routine physical genital inspections of children by schools. Reports and discussions framed his positions as requiring verification of sex (e.g., documentation or rules about sex-separated facilities), not school staff performing genital checks.

claim: "Covid-19 is now the leading cause of death in the United States."
rationale: This blanket statement is incorrect as of recent public-health data: historically and in most recent annual tallies, heart disease and cancer remain the first and second leading causes of death in the U.S., while COVID-19 has ranked lower. COVID-19 has at times been the leading cause during short, high-mortality surge weeks, but it is not the sustained leading cause overall "now."

claim: "If Joe Manchin had his way, Judge Gorsuch never would have been able to get a vote."
rationale: This is false. Joe Manchin voted to confirm Neil Gorsuch and was one of the few Democrats who cast a yes vote; Gorsuch was confirmed 54–45 in April 2017. Republicans used a rule change (the 'nuclear option') to overcome a Democratic filibuster, but Manchin did not try to prevent the nominee from getting a final confirmation vote.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood called Joe Biden an "incompetent, lying, flip-flopping, insincere, double-talking, radical socialist."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Clint Eastwood ever publicly said that exact string about Joe Biden. The phrase appears in social-media posts and partisan memes but reputable news and fact-checking outlets have found no sourced quote, video, or reliable interview in which Eastwood used those words. Without a primary source (audio, video, or a trustworthy reporter), the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: The health care law was "a 2,733-page bill! . . . No amendments!"
