The claim appears to stem from misinterpretation or deliberate misinformation rather than documented fact.

claim: "President Trump has lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont, overseeing a 11,742 decline of Vermont residents on food stamps."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and phrased ambiguously: it attributes a specific decline of 11,742 Vermont residents on food stamps directly to President Trump without providing a timeframe or source. Public SNAP caseloads do change over time for many reasons (economic conditions, state and federal policy changes, administrative actions), and I cannot confirm the precise 11,742 figure or that Trump personally 'oversaw' or caused that decline.

claim: Says Scott Walker is proposing to add 485 employees "in the category of supervisor and management" to his Department of Administration.
rationale: The claim misstates the proposal. Available fact-checking and budget summaries indicate Walker’s plan did not add 485 new "supervisor and management" jobs specifically to the Department of Administration; the number and character of positions cited were either reclassifications, statewide adjustments, or distributed across agencies rather than 485 new managers in DOA.

claim: A photograph shows Joe Biden with a Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan.
rationale: There is no credible, authenticated photograph showing Joe Biden with a person identified as a Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan. Viral claims appear to conflate or mislabel images (for example, Biden photographed with the late Senator Robert Byrd, who had been a KKK member early in life but was not a Grand Wizard) or rely on doctored/misattributed photos; independent fact-checks have found no verified image meeting the claim.

claim: "Our income, our GDP per capita, is almost 50 percent higher than (it is for) the average European."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and generally misleading: GDP-per-capita gaps depend heavily on the measure and the comparator group. Using common datasets (IMF/World Bank) the US does have higher GDP per capita than many European averages, but the difference is not universally “almost 50%” — using PPP the gap is often smaller (roughly a few tens of percent), while nominal comparisons vary greatly by which European countries are averaged. Because the claim presents a single precise-sounding number without specifying year, metric, or which European average, it is not reliably true as stated.

claim: "The senior senator from Arizona (John McCain) said he couldn't support repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' because of the economy."
rationale: John McCain did express opposition to the timing of repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' and argued repeal was unwise while the country was at war and focused on military readiness. He did not publicly justify his opposition by saying it was because of the economy; contemporaneous statements and votes cited timing/war/readiness concerns, not economic reasons.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court decided in 1982 that non-citizen children must get free K-12 education.
rationale: In Plyler v. Doe (1982) the U.S. Supreme Court held that states may not deny public K–12 education to children based on their immigration status, finding such denial violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The ruling effectively requires that public elementary and secondary schooling be made available to children regardless of citizenship or undocumented status, though it does not address higher education or private schooling.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: This is false. Phil Scott is the Republican governor of Vermont and is not a member of the U.S. House, so he could not have cast a vote in a federal impeachment. He has publicly criticized Trump at times, but he did not 'vote to impeach' in any congressional proceeding.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: This claim is not supported by national health-insurance data. Survey-based sources (ACS and KFF state comparisons) show Missouri’s child uninsured rate has generally been near or only slightly above the national average rather than among the very highest states — the largest child-uninsurance rates are usually found in states such as Texas, Oklahoma, and Florida. Missouri’s Medicaid/CHIP coverage and recent Medicaid expansion also have pressured its uninsured rate downward.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: The claim is almost certainly false: congressional districts do not exclusively produce electricity from a single fuel. U.S. electricity generation is regionally integrated and typically includes a mix of coal, natural gas, nuclear, hydro and renewables, and no known 18th Congressional District produces 100% of its electricity solely from coal based on available plant-level and regional data. Even coal-dominated localities usually have some non-coal generation or import power from neighboring areas.

claim: "Biden invested the entire family fortune in Ukraine gas and oil. Then shuts down Keystone pipeline. Starting to get the picture."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden "invested the entire family fortune" in Ukrainian gas and oil. While Hunter Biden served on the board of Ukrainian energy firm Burisma, that is not equivalent to Joe Biden investing the family's wealth; additionally, President Biden revoked the permit for the Keystone XL pipeline (a planned new line) early in his term, but he did not 'investigate' or shut down existing U.S. oil infrastructure as part of a quid pro quo with Ukraine.

claim: "If they made no changes whatsoever, the [state employees pension] plan still had enough money to go forward for approximately the next 16 years."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it does not identify which state pension plan, valuation date, or the actuarial assumptions used to project solvency. Whether a plan could run for ~16 years with no changes depends critically on its funded ratio, assumed investment return, payroll growth, and scheduled benefits; different official valuations produce very different exhaustion timelines. Without those specifics, asserting a precise 16-year horizon is unsupported.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
rationale: Archival video from McCain’s earlier campaigns shows him endorsing privatizing aspects of Social Security through private/personal accounts, while during the 2008 campaign he publicly denied ever supporting privatization. Contemporary fact-checking and news reports documented the apparent contradiction between his denials and the earlier footage.

claim: "So Trump comes to Nashville to oversee damage from the tornado. He flies into the area in a helicopter to get there without further traffic problems in the city. He writes PERSONAL checks to those in need, with his personal accountant in tow."
rationale: The composite claim mixes plausible actions (a presidential visit and use of a helicopter) with an unsupported and unlikely allegation (handing out personal checks with his personal accountant present). Contemporary news accounts of Trump’s visits to tornado sites report official travel and federal relief coordination, but do not document him writing personal checks to victims or bringing a personal accountant to distribute funds. Because the central, unusual element (personal checks/accountant) lacks evidence, the overall claim is false.

claim: "Youth usage of marijuana has actually gone down in states that have fully legalized."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes: research is mixed rather than showing a uniform decline in youth marijuana use across all jurisdictions that legalize recreational use. National surveys (Monitoring the Future, NSDUH, YRBS) and state-level studies generally show stability or mixed outcomes—some states or age groups have seen declines, others show no change or inconsistent patterns. There is no clear, consistent across-the-board decrease in youth use tied to full legalization.

claim: "Thanks to President Trump and Republican leadership, the number of people collecting food stamps has declined by more than two million."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it omits timeframe and causal evidence. SNAP (food stamp) enrollment has fluctuated with the economy and the COVID-19 emergency; short-term declines or increases over specific periods can occur, but attributing a drop of “more than two million” directly to President Trump and Republican leadership is not supported without a defined period and ignores other factors (economic conditions, pandemic relief, administrative changes). Public USDA SNAP data and independent fact-checkers show variation by year and that causation is not solely political leadership.

claim: Under Republican-backed state budget, the state education agency estimates expansion of Wisconsin’s school voucher program "could cost nearly $2 billion annually"
rationale: Reporting and state analyses during consideration of the Republican-backed Wisconsin budget showed the state education agency (DPI) estimated a broad expansion of the voucher program would cost on the order of $1.8–$1.9 billion per year, commonly described as “nearly $2 billion.” The estimate was tied to the scope of eligibility expansions proposed by Republican lawmakers rather than a small incremental change.

claim: A proposed San Antonio ordinance will allow men into women’s restrooms in the city.
rationale: The claim is misleading: city nondiscrimination proposals in San Antonio have typically aimed to prohibit discrimination based on gender identity and to allow transgender people to use facilities consistent with their gender identity, not to broadly authorize cisgender men to enter women’s restrooms. Such ordinances address protections in public accommodations and employment and do not change criminal statutes or explicitly state that “men” may use women’s restrooms.

claim: Says his administration balanced "two budgets with over $13 billion in deficits without raising taxes."
rationale: The assertion is unverifiable as presented because it names no official, jurisdiction, or fiscal years and so cannot be checked against budget documents or audits. Claims of balancing two budgets that began with over $13 billion in deficits without raising taxes would require detailed evidence of specific spending cuts, reserve use, federal aid, or other accounting adjustments; without that documentation the claim is unsupported. Given the specificity of the numeric claim and absence of corroborating public records, it should be treated as false until substantiated.

claim: Kelly Ayotte "voted for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. Kelly Ayotte cast a vote specifically for a budget that contained $90 billion in Pell Grant cuts. The $90 billion figure has been associated with certain Republican budget proposals (notably versions of the Ryan budget) over a 10-year window, but the claim ties that specific dollar figure directly to an Ayotte vote without identifying the exact measure or showing she voted for that text. Without that linkage, the statement is misleading.

claim: "We are within the margin of error."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no data or context. Whether a result is "within the margin of error" depends on the specific measurement, the poll or study's stated margin of error, sample size, and confidence level; without those numbers the claim cannot be confirmed and thus should be treated as false.

claim: "The deficit was on track to top $1 trillion the year I took office."
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who “I” is or which year is meant; without that context it cannot be confirmed. Historical budget projections vary by presidency — baseline projections entering 2017 did not show a >$1 trillion deficit that year, while the COVID-era 2020–21 deficits did exceed $1 trillion — so the blanket statement is misleading as stated.

claim: Allen West called Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" and said "this country's got to get on sound footing by destroying it."
rationale: I found no reliable evidence that Allen West uttered that exact formulation. While West has criticized entitlement programs and called for reforms, the specific quote calling Social Security a “Ponzi scheme” and saying “this country's got to get on sound footing by destroying it” does not appear in reputable reporting and reads like a misquote or fabrication. Because the exact phrasing is not documented in credible sources, the claim is not supported.

claim: States with voter ID laws have seen "zero decrease" in participation. "Most have seen an increase."
rationale: The blanket claim is not supported by the evidence. Peer-reviewed research and multiple empirical analyses find mixed effects of voter ID laws: some studies show modest decreases in overall turnout—especially among Black, Hispanic, young, and low-income voters—while other studies find little or no effect; it is therefore incorrect to say there has been “zero decrease” everywhere or that “most” ID states saw increases without controlling for other factors. Aggregated results do not support the categorical, universal statement in the claim.

claim: Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted the continued taxation on residents’ properties over 70 percent of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific quantitative claim as stated. It asserts that Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted" continued taxation over 70% of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same, but no jurisdiction, time period, or primary vote records were provided; without official meeting minutes or roll-call data this percentage and the legal characterization cannot be confirmed. Additionally, seconding motions is often a procedural act and votes to maintain a millage rate do not by themselves establish criminal aiding/abetting.

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Frank Marshall Davis was Barack Obama’s biological father. Barack Obama’s father is documented as Barack Obama Sr. in contemporary records, family testimony, and Obama’s own memoir; claims tying Davis to paternity are conspiracy theories without genealogical or documentary support.

claim: "Richard Nixon was the last president to be impeached."
rationale: This is false. Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 before the full House of Representatives voted on articles of impeachment, so he was never formally impeached. Subsequent presidents, notably Bill Clinton (1998) and Donald Trump (2019 and 2021), were impeached by the House of Representatives.

claim: U.S. debt is "now equal to 100 percent of the GDP."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and therefore not correct as written. “U.S. debt” can mean different measures: gross federal debt (total publicly held debt plus intragovernmental) has been above 100% of GDP for several years, while the commonly cited “debt held by the public” has hovered around but not exactly equal to 100% of GDP and varies by reporting date. Without specifying which debt measure and which date, the flat claim that U.S. debt is "now equal to 100 percent of the GDP" is misleading.

claim: The New York Times published an old stock photo of a young girl and claimed Israeli forces killed her during its recent war with Hamas.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that The New York Times published an old stock photo of a young girl and explicitly claimed Israeli forces killed her during the recent Israel–Hamas war. Independent fact-checkers and published clarifications around disputed images from the conflict show that viral social posts misrepresented or recycled images, but the NYT's published photos were credited to news agencies/photographers and subjected to standard captioning and metadata checks.

claim: Says West Virginia is "down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working now because of addiction or conviction."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes the situation. West Virginia has a relatively low labor-force participation and employment-to-population ratio compared with other states, but recent data do not show only ~50% of adults working nationwide or in the state, and researchers attribute workforce shortfalls to multiple factors (aging population, disability, family care, economic opportunities) in addition to substance use and criminal records. The specific assertion that the workforce is “down to around 50 percent… because of addiction or conviction” is not supported by available labor-market statistics or causal analyses.

claim: Putin beheaded bioweapon engineers in Ukraine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Russian President Vladimir Putin personally beheaded anyone in Ukraine, nor verified reporting that Russian forces systematically beheaded alleged 'bioweapon engineers.' Major independent news organizations, international monitors, and credible investigators have not substantiated such claims. The allegation appears to stem from unverified or propagandistic sources and contradicts available reporting on the conflict.

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: The claim that “both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes” is incorrect. Public Senate roll-call records show that Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio participate in most votes; while they have missed some (for travel, campaigning, or scheduling), those absences are a small fraction of total votes rather than a majority. Saying they miss the “vast majority” greatly overstates their actual absence rates.

claim: "Calling for the assassination of the president is a federal crime."
rationale: Federal law makes threatening or soliciting the death of the President a federal offense (for example 18 U.S.C. § 871 criminalizes knowingly and willfully threatening to kill the President, and other statutes criminalize solicitation, conspiracy, and attempts). While not every hyperbolic statement will be prosecuted, calling for the President's assassination can fall squarely within these federal crimes when it amounts to a true threat, solicitation, or incitement to imminent lawless action.

claim: "South Korea sprays rioters with dye so they can be identified & arrested later."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading. While some police forces worldwide have used colored dye in water cannon to mark demonstrators in specific incidents, there is not widespread, well-documented evidence that South Korean authorities routinely spray rioters with dye to identify and arrest them later. Absent credible, repeated reporting of this being standard practice in South Korea, the general claim is false or at least an overgeneralization.

claim: AIDS was transmitted to humans because "one guy" had sex with "a monkey" and then started "having sex with men."
rationale: This claim is false. Scientific evidence shows HIV arose from simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) that crossed into humans (zoonotic spillovers) — most likely via exposure to infected blood during hunting/butchering of primates — and there were multiple independent transmissions in early 20th-century Central Africa, not a single person who had sex with a monkey. The idea that one individual (the so-called “patient zero”) introduced AIDS by bestiality has been debunked by phylogenetic and historical research; subsequent spread occurred through human-to-human sexual and blood-borne transmission.

claim: Says 2010 video clip showing coffins in a field proves "COVID was planned."
rationale: A 2010 video predates the emergence of SARS‑CoV‑2 by nearly a decade, so it cannot by itself demonstrate that COVID‑19 was planned. Footage of coffins in a field can represent many unrelated events (e.g., drills, cemetery prep, other disasters) and does not provide direct evidence linking organizers or intent to the later pandemic.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: The phrase "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit" is contradictory and implausible: governments procure certified PPE from specialized manufacturers, not luxury fashion houses like Saint Laurent. Hazmat suits carry specific certification labels and sourcing records, and there is no evidence that Saint Laurent produces government-issued certified hazardous-materials protective gear. Without provenance for the photo, the claim appears to conflate designer branding with official government equipment and is therefore very likely false.

claim: Undocumented immigrants "pay $12 billion a year into Social Security."
rationale: Multiple government and independent analyses estimate that unauthorized immigrants pay roughly $11–$13 billion a year in Social Security (FICA) payroll taxes; $12 billion is within that commonly cited range. The amount depends on the year and methodology, but the general claim that they pay about $12 billion annually is supported by Social Security and tax-revenue estimates.

claim: In Texas, "sexting is a felony sex offense for teenagers — that can mean up to 10 years in prison."
rationale: Under Texas law, creating, possessing, or distributing sexually explicit images of minors can be prosecuted under child sexual performance/child pornography statutes and may be charged as felonies. Certain promotion/possession offenses are third‑degree felonies carrying penalties in the 2–10 year range, and prosecutors have in practice charged teenagers for sexting under those statutes.

claim: The man in a mugshot is "responsible for lighting 32 of the wildfires" on the West Coast.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated: no credible, specific reporting supports that a single man shown in an unspecified mugshot was proven to have ignited 32 West Coast wildfires. Viral social media posts frequently misattribute mugshots to large-scale crimes, and law enforcement and major news outlets would document and detail an extraordinary arrest like a single person starting dozens of wildfires. Without a name, date, location, or authoritative source tying that exact mugshot to that specific crime, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: The statement asserts a categorical legal prohibition — that Attorney General guidelines prevent release of an internal affairs record. In reality AG guidance does not universally bar release; public-records and law-enforcement personnel-record rules vary by jurisdiction and many internal-affairs files are presumptively subject to disclosure except where specific statutes, court orders, or narrow exemptions (privacy, active investigations) apply. Without jurisdiction-specific law or an order, the blanket claim is misleading and therefore false.

claim: "Oregon, once again, remains among the top five hungriest states in the nation."
rationale: Based on national food-insecurity and food-insufficiency data from sources like USDA and Feeding America, Oregon does not consistently rank among the top five states with the highest hunger rates; the highest rates are typically in states such as Mississippi, Louisiana, New Mexico, Arkansas, and Alabama. Oregon's food-insecurity rate has historically been lower than those top-five states, so the claim that it 'remains among the top five hungriest' is not supported by typical annual rankings.

claim: U.S. military involvement in Libya "allowed thousands of surface-to-air missiles to fall into the hands of radical Islamists."
rationale: While large quantities of weapons were looted from Libyan stockpiles after the 2011 intervention, authoritative reporting and UN assessments do not support the claim that ‘thousands of surface-to-air missiles’ were handed to radical Islamists. Some man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) were unaccounted for and did leak into the region, but documented numbers are far lower and the claim overstates both the scale and direct causal responsibility of U.S. forces.

claim: "You couldn’t buy a cannon when, in fact, the Second Amendment passed."
rationale: The claim is false: at the time the Second Amendment was ratified (1791) cannons and other artillery were manufactured, sold, and in many cases privately owned by militias, merchants, privateers and landholders. While heavy artillery was expensive, difficult to transport, and sometimes subject to local regulation, it was not categorically unavailable or prohibited for private purchase.

claim: Says Google Earth blocked people from seeing the Suez Canal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Google Earth intentionally blocked viewing of the Suez Canal. During incidents like the Ever Given grounding, satellite imagery availability varied due to update timing and provider coverage, which some users misinterpreted as being 'blocked.' Google publishes imagery refresh schedules and only censors a few sensitive sites for legal/security reasons, and the Suez Canal is not among those routinely obscured.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: State personal income tax revenues in New York are highly concentrated downstate; New York City together with Westchester, Nassau and Suffolk have in recent years contributed roughly seven-in-ten of the state's PIT collections. The exact percentage fluctuates by tax year, but 70% is a commonly cited approximate share in official fiscal analyses.

claim: Photo shows "Myrtle Beach 30 minutes ago."
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify that a given photo actually depicts Myrtle Beach taken 30 minutes ago. Without the image, its metadata, source, or corroborating situational details (geolocation, timestamp, eyewitnesses), the claim cannot be substantiated and may be a miscaption. Therefore the claim is treated as false due to lack of verifiable evidence.

claim: "President Trump just saved Christmas for 13 million retirees."
rationale: The claim is vague and there is no evidence that a single unilateral action by President Trump "saved Christmas for 13 million retirees." Major benefits for retirees (like Social Security or stimulus payments) are set by law and/or administered by agencies and Congress, not by a sole presidential act that would uniquely affect exactly 13 million retirees. Reported counts of Social Security beneficiaries are far larger than 13 million, and no verifiable source ties a specific Trump action to "saving Christmas" for that precise group.

claim: "Trump wins the award Obama never could."
rationale: The claim names no specific award, so it is unprovable as stated and therefore unsupported. Moreover, public knowledge shows Barack Obama received awards (notably the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize) that Donald Trump did not, and Trump has received other honors Obama did, so a blanket assertion that “Trump wins the award Obama never could” is misleading without specifying which award.

claim: Says "99 percent of the time police officers aren't charged when they kill young people of color."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise 99% non‑charging rate for police who kill "young people of color," but there is no authoritative national statistic that supports that exact figure. Independent databases and investigative reporting show that criminal charges against officers in killings are relatively rare, especially for people of color, but estimates vary by dataset, year, definition, and age group and do not reliably establish a 99% non‑charging rate.

claim: "Most of Ted Cruz’s money comes from Washington, from outside the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and unsupported as stated. Campaign-finance records across Cruz’s election cycles show he raises significant funds from both in-state Texas donors and from across the country, but there is no clear evidence that a majority of his money specifically comes from “Washington” (likely Washington, D.C.) or that most of his receipts come from outside Texas in every cycle. Donor geography varies by year (e.g., presidential vs. Senate fundraising), so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "A golf course closes somewhere in America every 48 hours."
rationale: There is no sustained, verifiable statistic that a U.S. golf course permanently closes every 48 hours. While many courses have closed over past decades and some reports cite high rates in particular years or regions, closure rates fluctuate and recent data point to a few hundred closures per year—not a steady ~182 closures annually implied by "every 48 hours." The claim treats a variable, time‑dependent trend as a constant fact.

claim: Says "Biden wants a nationwide lockdown to combat a virus that has a 99%+ survival rate."
rationale: The claim mixes two misleading assertions. President Biden did call for a national COVID response and certain restrictions early in the pandemic, but he did not explicitly advocate for a blanket, indefinite nationwide lockdown as policy; his positions emphasized federal coordination, mask guidance, vaccinations and targeted measures. Also, stating the virus has a uniform "99%+ survival rate" is misleading: COVID-19 infection fatality and survival rates varied substantially by age, comorbidity, time period and variant and in many populations the IFR exceeded 1% for older or high-risk groups.

claim: North Carolina has "the strictest anti-gerrymandering standards in the entire country."
rationale: While North Carolina has state constitutional provisions limiting partisan districting (voter-approved standards requiring contiguity, compactness, and limits on favoring a party), calling them "the strictest in the entire country" is unsupported. Several other states have more robust or different anti-gerrymandering regimes (independent redistricting commissions, neutral algorithmic rules, or clearer bans on using political data) and enforcement varies, so NC cannot be conclusively ranked as the strictest. The claim is an absolute comparative assertion that is not backed by clear, objective evidence.

claim: "Greg Abbott said it would be a ‘waste’ to expand pre-k to all Texas children."
rationale: I found no verified instance of Gov. Greg Abbott using the exact phrase that expanding pre-K to all Texas children “would be a ‘waste’.” Abbott has publicly critiqued universal pre-K proposals and favored targeted early-childhood investments and fiscal restraint, but the precise quoted wording appears unsupported. The claim presents a direct quotation without an attributable source and likely misstates or paraphrases his position.

claim: "Due to ... tax cuts and lower (property) values, 2009 property taxes were almost $3 billion below 2007 property taxes."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable and likely false as presented because it gives no jurisdiction and no source for the figures. Property-tax collections differ by locality and year and depend on assessed values, tax rates, assessment timing, and accounting rules; without official levy/collection data for the named place in 2007 and 2009 the claim cannot be confirmed. To be true it would require corroboration from a specific local or state audit or budget report showing nearly $3 billion less in 2009 than 2007.

claim: "Jim Renacci cheated on his income taxes" and is a "deadbeat citizen."
rationale: There is no publicly documented evidence that Jim Renacci was convicted of income tax evasion or criminally charged for cheating on his personal income taxes. Calling him a "deadbeat citizen" is a subjective allegation about civic behavior and likewise lacks objective, verifiable support in the public record. Without specific, credible documentation of tax fraud or willful nonpayment, the claim is not supported.

claim: "McCain lobbied for (a) $10-million pork project honoring conservative justice."
rationale: There is no clear, documented instance that Sen. John McCain lobbied for a $10 million earmark to honor a conservative Supreme Court justice. The claim conflicts with McCain’s long public record as an opponent of “pork” and an advocate for earmark reform, and no specific project, justice, or credible source is identified to support the allegation.

claim: "The Lancet peer-reviewed study confirms vaccine efficacy, not as 95% stated by the vaccine companies, but as: AstraZeneca 1.3%; Moderna 1.2%; J&J 1.2%; Pfizer 0.84%."
rationale: The claim is incorrect — no Lancet peer‑reviewed paper confirmed vaccine efficacies as AstraZeneca 1.3%, Moderna 1.2%, J&J 1.2%, Pfizer 0.84%. The major randomized trial results reported in peer‑reviewed journals described efficacy as relative risk reductions (e.g., ~94–95% for Pfizer/Moderna, lower but substantially higher than 1% for AstraZeneca and J&J), and the ~1% numbers appear to be a misinterpretation or miscalculation (likely confusing absolute risk reduction with relative efficacy and depending on baseline incidence).

claim: The Wisconsin state Assembly chambers extend to the bathroom and the parlor, and rules allow members to vote for each other if the member is in the chambers.
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Wisconsin Assembly voting rules require members to be physically present in the legislative chamber or at their assigned voting station to cast a vote; there is no general rule that the chamber "extends" into private spaces like bathrooms or parlors, nor that members may routinely vote on behalf of absent colleagues. Past walkouts and quorum disputes in Wisconsin demonstrate that absence prevents participation, which would be unnecessary if the chamber legally included bathrooms or allowed proxy voting for absent members.

claim: A video clip from the Notre Dame cathedral fire shows a man walking alone in a tower of the church "dressed in Muslim garb."
rationale: This claim misidentifies a person seen in viral footage; reputable fact-checkers and news organizations found the clip was miscaptioned and there is no evidence the individual was a Muslim or that an Islamist was present in the tower during the Notre Dame fire. Official inquiries into the fire attributed it to accidental causes linked to restoration work and did not report any suspect matching that description. The viral claim therefore conflates or misrepresents the video content.

claim: "Breaking: Santa Fe killer expresses his love for Obama."
rationale: No credible news outlets or official reports from the widely covered Santa Fe school shooting mention the attacker publicly expressing 'love for Obama.' The claim appears to be an unverified social-media rumor or misattribution and is not supported by available factual reporting.

claim: "Iceland declares all religions are mental disorders."
rationale: There is no evidence that the Icelandic government or any Icelandic medical authority has officially declared all religions to be mental disorders. Iceland's constitution and laws protect freedom of religion, and major diagnostic authorities (e.g., WHO ICD) do not classify religions as mental illnesses. The claim appears to be a false or satirical assertion rather than a documented legal or medical determination.

claim: ICE está en Uvalde, Texas, "entonces los padres indocumentados tienen que temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos están vivos".
rationale: No hay evidencia creíble de que ICE estuviera llevando a cabo operativos de deportación en Uvalde que obligaran a padres indocumentados a temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos estaban vivos. Coberturas periodísticas y declaraciones oficiales tras el tiroteo en Uvalde indicaron que no se realizaron detenciones masivas en la escena y que las agencias no ejecutarían acciones de aplicación migratoria en sitios de tragedias. Que la presencia de agentes pueda generar miedo es plausible, pero la afirmación se presenta como un hecho comprobado cuando está exagerada o no documentada.

claim: "BREAKING: Pennsylvania initiated a FULL audit of the RIGGED ELECTION"
rationale: Pennsylvania did not initiate a statewide “full audit” that validated a ‘rigged’ election. After the 2020 election, officials and courts rejected widespread fraud claims; some counties conducted limited recounts or reviews, but there was no statewide forensic audit overturning results. The claim conflates local reviews with an official statewide audit and asserts fraud without evidence.

claim: Says "CNN host Fareed Zakaria calls for jihad rape of white women."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Fareed Zakaria, a mainstream CNN host and commentator, ever called for "jihad rape of white women." Such an extreme and criminal exhortation would have been widely documented and repudiated by major news organizations and by Zakaria himself, but no reliable sources corroborate this claim. The allegation appears to be a fabricated or malicious misattribution.

claim: Video shows Biden saying "salute the Marines" after hearing the words in an earpiece before his inauguration.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Biden heard and then repeated the phrase "salute the Marines" from an earpiece before his inauguration. Independent reviews of the footage and fact-check reporting found the viral clip to be misleading or edited; unedited video does not support the claim that he was parroting words fed to him through an earpiece.

claim: "What I have done -- and this is unprecedented ... is I've said to each agency ... 'look at regulations that are already on the books and if they don't make sense, let's get rid of them.'"
rationale: The speaker did direct agencies to review existing regulations, but claiming that this is 'unprecedented' is incorrect. Multiple prior administrations have issued formal orders and policies requiring retrospective review and removal of obsolete or burdensome rules (for example, Reagan's regulatory orders and later EOs such as Clinton's EO 12866 and Obama's EO 13563). Thus the novelty claim is false even if the action occurred.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: General, long-running public-opinion polling shows approval/trust in the U.S. Congress is typically at or near historic lows (often in the single digits or low teens), whereas approval/trust in the news media is usually higher (commonly in the 20s–40s depending on poll and year). Therefore the blanket claim that “the media has a lower approval rate than Congress” contradicts the usual pattern in major polls.

claim: "The number of SWAT raids have gone up by 1,400 percent since the 1980s."
rationale: The 1,400% figure is not supported by clear, reproducible national data on SWAT raids. That large percentage is often traced to advocacy reports or conflated metrics (e.g., counts of SWAT teams or deployments in select studies) rather than a consistent, nationwide count of raids since the 1980s. Independent researchers and official sources do show increases in militarized policing, but not a reliably measured 1,400% rise in SWAT raids across the country.

claim: Says Sen. Thad Cochran "voted to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on ... the Bridge to Nowhere in Alaska instead of shifting the money to repair a bridge damaged by Hurricane Katrina."
rationale: The claim implies a specific vote by Sen. Thad Cochran to divert hundreds of millions to Alaska’s 'Bridge to Nowhere' rather than to a Katrina-damaged bridge. Public records show the Gravina Island 'Bridge to Nowhere' was a controversial ~$200–$300M earmark, and there were later proposals to redirect those earmarked funds after Hurricane Katrina, but there is no clear contemporaneous record that Cochran cast a decisive vote to fund the Alaska project instead of shifting that specific money to Katrina repairs. Cochran generally supported Katrina relief measures, and the appropriations/earmark process and votes involved multiple bills and amendments, so the claim overstates and misattributes a single direct vote.

claim: "A gallon (of gasoline) delivered to the front lines for our troops in Afghanistan cost more than $400."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading. While some press reports and military estimates have cited extremely high per‑gallon “costs” (approaching or exceeding $400) for fuel delivered to a handful of very remote, heavily defended outposts when all logistics, convoy security and airlift costs were allocated per gallon, that was an exceptional, accounting‑style upper bound—not the normal price to deliver gasoline to frontline units. Most delivered fuel costs were far lower, and the $400 figure is often taken out of context or presented as a routine cost when it reflected specific extreme cases and accounting methods.

claim: "The U.S. has now spent more on reconstructing Afghanistan than was spent on the Marshall Plan and the reconstruction of Europe."
rationale: U.S. agencies tracking Afghanistan aid (SIGAR) report roughly $140–150 billion spent on reconstruction and assistance in Afghanistan, while the Marshall Plan totaled about $12.4 billion in 1948–52 (which converts to roughly $130–150 billion using common inflation adjustments). By common inflation-adjusted comparisons, U.S. reconstruction spending in Afghanistan is slightly higher than the Marshall Plan-era U.S. assistance for rebuilding Europe.

claim: Says the names of CNN anchors Chris Cuomo, Brian Stelter and Jake Tapper were on the flight logs of Jeffrey Epstein’s private plane.
rationale: Publicly released Epstein flight logs and multiple fact-checks do not show Chris Cuomo, Brian Stelter, or Jake Tapper as passengers; viral social-media claims were debunked as mistaken or unverified. Major news organizations and detailed passenger lists would have documented such high-profile names if they appeared, but there is no reliable evidence supporting the claim.

claim: Says he is the "ranking member" of the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it uses an unnamed pronoun (“he”) with no identification or date, so it cannot be verified as written. Additionally, the term “ranking member” is a formal title that is not universally used for select committees and the Jan. 6 select committee’s leadership roles were specifically designated (e.g., chair and vice chair), so a blanket statement that an unspecified male is the “ranking member” is not supportable. Without a named individual and timestamp the assertion fails verification.

claim: Says Mark Kelly wants to "defund the police."
rationale: This is false. Senator Mark Kelly has publicly said he does not support ‘defund the police’ and has positioned himself in favor of police reform and community investments rather than dismantling or defunding police departments. There is no credible evidence he has advocated abolishing or defunding police agencies.

claim: Under Gov. Scott Walker, "unemployment is increasing in Wisconsin at twice the rate it is nationally."
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely false because statewide and national unemployment generally fell during most of Scott Walker’s tenure rather than Wisconsin rising at twice the national rate. Without a precise time window or whether it means percentage points versus percent change, the statement cannot be supported; short-term month-to-month spikes could differ but do not establish the asserted sustained 2× increase. Overall labor‑market data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and Wisconsin state reports show no sustained period where Wisconsin’s unemployment rose at twice the national rate under Walker.

claim: "Any Floridian who has ever requested an absentee ballot henceforth gets one automatically."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. In Florida, voters do not automatically receive all future absentee (vote-by-mail) ballots simply because they once requested one; voters must request permanent vote-by-mail status or re-request absentee ballots for future elections, and election offices may remove voters from lists for inactivity or other reasons. Recent state laws have modified absentee processes but do not create a blanket automatic lifetime entitlement from a single past request.

claim: Video shows Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pouring shots for a group of people "days before testing positive" for COVID-19.
rationale: The claim implies the footage was taken just days before Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tested positive, but fact-checks established the video was misdated/miscontextualized and not demonstrably filmed immediately prior to her positive test. The timing presented in the viral posts is misleading and does not prove she was pouring shots to strangers in the days before infection.

claim: Says Ronald Reagan "was behind in the polls in 1980 going into the debate with Jimmy Carter and then turned around 10 days later and won 40 states."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on the outcome and oversimplifies the polling situation. Reagan did not win only 40 states — he carried 44 states in the 1980 election — and while polls were close in late October, nationwide polling was mixed rather than showing a clear Carter lead immediately before the debate; Reagan’s debate performance did help widen his lead.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: This phrasing is misleading. UN officials did warn (around 2017) that about 20 million people across four countries could be pushed to the brink of famine without urgent aid, but agencies clarified the number described people at extreme risk of famine or severe food insecurity and was contingent on funding — it did not mean more than 20 million would unavoidably die within six months.

claim: "Close to half of the folks in this country illegally entered legally (but) overstayed (their ) visas."
rationale: Multiple reputable analyses estimate that a substantial share—on the order of four in ten—of the unauthorized population entered legally and then overstayed visas, so describing that share as “close to half” is a reasonable characterization. Exact percentages vary by year and methodology, but most recent DHS, Pew, and Migration Policy Institute assessments place the overstayer share in the roughly 40–50% range.

claim: Says only seven percent of 2009’s stimulus bill went toward transportation projects, yet they created over one-third of the bill’s total jobs.
rationale: The statement is misleading. It is true that transportation-related spending in the 2009 ARRA represented roughly 6–7% of total outlays, but official OMB/CBO tracking and independent analyses do not support the claim that those projects produced over one-third of the bill's total jobs; transportation/infrastructure generated a significant but much smaller share of estimated job-years. The discrepancy likely comes from differing definitions of 'jobs' (peak jobs, job‑months, or job‑years) or selective use of short‑term estimates.

claim: "According to ATF data, 70 percent of firearms recovered and traced in drug cartel crimes in Mexico originated from the United States."
rationale: ATF trace records and multiple analyses have shown that a large majority of firearms recovered and traced in Mexico were originally sold in the United States, with figures around 70% cited for certain periods. However, ATF itself warns trace data are limited to guns submitted for tracing, vary by year, and do not represent all weapons used in Mexican crimes.

claim: Says after Hurricane Sandy, New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg "refused to allow the National Guard into the city to restore civil order because Guardsmen carry guns!"
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. After Hurricane Sandy in October 2012, the New York National Guard was activated and thousands of Guardsmen were deployed to the region to assist with security, logistics, and recovery; Mayor Bloomberg did not “refuse to allow” them into the city because they carried guns. Deployment decisions for the National Guard are made by the state governor (and can be federalized), not solely by a city mayor, and multiple reports from the time describe Guard assistance in New York City.

claim: Wisconsin ranks 48th out of all 50 states in venture capital investment.
rationale: The claim states an absolute current ranking without specifying year or metric; available state VC rankings fluctuate by year and source and Wisconsin is not consistently as low as 48th. In most recent national VC reports Wisconsin typically falls higher (better) than 48th—often in the mid-30s to low-40s in total dollars or deal counts—so the blanket statement is inaccurate. Without a specific year and measure the claim is misleading.

claim: The home-mortgage deduction is widely thought to be "a middle-class benefit. It's not -- 73 percent of it goes to people making a quarter-million dollars or more a year."
rationale: The mortgage interest deduction is indeed skewed toward higher-income households, but authoritative distributional analyses do not support the specific claim that 73% of the deduction goes to taxpayers earning $250,000 or more. Pre-2017 data typically show a large share of the benefit going to the top quintile, but the share accruing to filers above $250k is substantially lower (commonly in the ~30–40% range depending on year and methodology) and was altered further by the 2017 tax-law changes. Therefore the precise 73% figure is not supported by mainstream data.

claim: Alison Alter "has exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars to fund her campaign."
rationale: I am not aware of credible reporting or official records showing Alison Alter illegally 'exploited a campaign finance loophole' to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars. Public financing programs and campaign filings are typically documented and any abuse would likely have generated news coverage or enforcement actions; no such evidence is documented in mainstream sources up to my knowledge cutoff. The claim appears to conflate routine, legal public matching or voucher receipts with intentional exploitation without supporting facts.

claim: Says many public-employee unions falsely told their Wisconsin members his budget-repair bill sought 12 percent to 13 percent of their incomes for health insurance premiums.
rationale: Contemporaneous fact-checking and news coverage found that many public‑employee union mailings and statements presented a 12–13% figure as what workers would pay, and that characterization was misleading. The budget‑repair bill required employees to contribute toward health insurance premiums (a share of the premium), not 12–13% of their wages, so portraying the measure as taking 12–13% of income was false or deceptive.

claim: "If we pass immigration reform, it will make wages go up on average $250 for the average household."
rationale: The claim gives a precise dollar increase without specifying which immigration bill, timeframe (monthly/annual), or assumptions; scholarly and government analyses produce a range of outcomes that depend heavily on the policy details and modeling assumptions. While many economists find that legalization/immigration reform can raise aggregate GDP and produce small average wage gains for some groups, results are modest and distributional, and there is no robust, universally accepted estimate that passing "immigration reform" will raise wages by exactly $250 for the average household. Because of the vagueness and mixed evidence, the specific $250 claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The statement gives no specific dates and so cannot be verified as a current fact. Monthly private‑sector job counts come from the BLS and vary month to month; claiming “30 straight months” and exactly “4.6 million” requires a defined start/end period and citation. Without that context the claim is unverified and likely inaccurate as presented.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: Sanctioning a country's central bank can severely restrict its ability to transact internationally and greatly damage export revenues (especially oil), but it does not literally 'shut down' all domestic economic activity. Historical cases (e.g., sanctions on Iran's central bank in the 2010s and reimposed measures in 2018) caused deep contraction, currency collapse, and hardship yet economic activity, trade via workarounds, and domestic markets continued. Thus the claim is an overstatement of the direct causal effect.

claim: "Ohio has lost more population than every other state in the country except for two."
rationale: The statement is too broad and inaccurate as written. For commonly used reference periods (for example the 2010–2020 census decade), Ohio actually gained population; in more recent annual estimates Ohio has lost residents but several other states (e.g., New York, California, Illinois) have experienced equal or larger absolute losses, so Ohio is not unambiguously second-worst across standard measures.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton and Tim Kaine "want to shut down shale, and shut down natural gas."
rationale: This is an exaggeration. During the 2016 campaign Hillary Clinton repeatedly said she would not support a blanket federal ban on fracking and instead promoted stronger regulation, methane limits, and a transition to cleaner energy; Tim Kaine has supported natural gas development and did not call for shutting down shale gas. Neither politician advocated an explicit policy to 'shut down' shale or natural gas production.

claim: Says Fox News gave Republican senators twice the air time as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State.
rationale: There is no well-documented, credible analysis showing Fox News specifically gave Republican senators exactly twice the airtime as Democrats during “a hearing about the Islamic State.” Media airtime claims require a named hearing, a defined time window, and a transparent measurement methodology; without a cited study or transcript analysis this asserted 2:1 ratio is unsupported. Broad media-monitoring studies of partisan guest balance show mixed results and do not verify this precise claim.

claim: Says Kanye West got 40,000 votes in the presidential election in Kentucky.
rationale: The claim is incorrect: in the 2020 U.S. presidential election Kanye West received roughly 60,000 votes nationwide, not 40,000 in Kentucky alone. Kentucky’s official 2020 results show third‑party/independent totals far below 40,000 in the state, making a 40,000 vote total for Kanye in Kentucky implausible.

claim: "Corporate income has increased as a share of" gross domestic product.
rationale: The claim is stated as a general, timeless fact but is ambiguous and not uniformly true. Corporate income (corporate profits) as a share of GDP is cyclical and varies by country, time period, and accounting definition, and there is no consistent, universal upward trend across all periods and jurisdictions. Therefore the blanket assertion that corporate income "has increased as a share of GDP" is misleading without further specification.

claim: "Car thefts (are) increasing in 8 of the 10 most populous (Wisconsin) counties."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim as stated. Public reporting and crime data show vehicle-theft increases in some large Wisconsin counties (for example Milwaukee and a few others) but trends vary by county and year; the claim that 8 of the 10 most populous counties saw increases is unsourced and not verifiable without a defined timeframe and official county-by-county statistics, so I judge it false given the uncertainty.

claim: Obama served on a board with former Weather Underground member William Ayers and "that relationship with Mr. Ayers on this board continued after 9/11."
rationale: Obama and William Ayers did serve together on the Chicago Annenberg Challenge board in the mid-to-late 1990s, but Ayers’ board service ended in 2001 while Obama remained on the board into 2002. Contemporary fact-checking and board records do not support the claim that their board relationship continued beyond Sept. 11, 2001, so the statement is misleading.

claim: Congressman Jeff Denham "has agreed all illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Jeff Denham explicitly endorsed a blanket policy that every undocumented immigrant be detained, arrested and deported. His public record emphasizes stronger border enforcement and removal of criminal aliens, but he has not been documented calling for universal detention/arrest/deportation of all undocumented people. The claim overstates and universalizes his position beyond available statements and votes.

claim: "We could cut unemployment in half simply by reclaiming the jobs taken by illegal workers."
rationale: This claim is false because undocumented/illegal workers make up only a minority of the labor force in most countries, so reclaiming their jobs could not by itself eliminate or halve overall unemployment. Labor-market research shows hiring is not a simple one-to-one transfer — many jobs held by undocumented workers are in specific locations, industries, or low-wage niches that unemployed workers may not be qualified for or willing to take, and removing undocumented workers would also change labor demand and prices. Empirical studies generally find immigration has small effects on native unemployment, not dramatic reductions when undocumented workers are removed.

claim: "There have been more than 300 mass shootings in the United States this year – more than any other country in the world."
rationale: The claim is imprecise — it omits the specific year and does not define "mass shooting." Counts vary widely by definition; U.S. trackers that use a 4+ shot threshold (e.g., Gun Violence Archive) have recorded several hundred such incidents in recent years, often exceeding 300, and the U.S. does generally report far more mass shootings than other countries. Because the statement lacks a date and a definition, it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: "Speaker Gingrich for 20 years supported a federal individual mandate" for health insurance.
rationale: Gingrich did endorse the idea of an individual mandate at various points in the 1990s and discussed mandatory coverage as a conservative alternative, but he did not continuously endorse a federal individual mandate for a straight 20-year period. In later years (notably around the ACA debate) he publicly opposed the federal mandate and emphasized alternative/state-based or market approaches, so the claim of uninterrupted 20-year federal support is inaccurate.

claim: Says Bill White is refusing to debate.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous (no date, forum, or which Bill White) and there is no corroborated reporting that a Bill White publicly refused to debate. Historically, Bill White (former Houston mayor and 2010 Texas gubernatorial candidate) did participate in debates, so absent a specific, sourced incident the blanket claim is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: "The United States was paying for anywhere from 70 to 90 percent of (NATO), depending on the way you calculate."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The United States does not pay 70–90% of NATO overall: it historically contributes about 20–25% of NATO’s relatively small common-funded budgets, while its share of total NATO members’ combined defense spending is large (often roughly 60–75% in recent years) but well below 90%. The statement conflates different metrics and overstates the upper bound.

claim: President Obama was "raised Muslim."
rationale: This is false. Barack Obama was born in Hawaii and was raised primarily by his mother and maternal grandparents; although his father was Muslim and Obama spent a few childhood years in Indonesia with exposure to Islam, he has said he was not raised in the Muslim faith and later became a Christian. Public biographical records and Obama's own accounts contradict the claim he was "raised Muslim."

claim: "24 of every 100 kids in school today speak Spanish."
rationale: The claim gives a precise 24% figure without specifying jurisdiction or how “speak Spanish” is defined (home language, proficiency, or enrollment in Spanish class). U.S. data show Hispanic students are roughly mid-to-high 20% of public-school enrollment but the share of children who speak Spanish at home or are Spanish speakers is typically lower and varies by year and state, so the blanket 24 of 100 statement is unsupported. Because of the missing context and differing measures, the claim cannot be verified as stated.
